Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets up nice and cozy, and let me tell you about two best friends, a very silly mix-up, and the longest, most adventurous train journey you can possibly imagine. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in the big, bustling, absolutely wonderful city of London, there lived a boy named Raj. Now Raj was... how do I put this nicely... a little bit of a goofball. A loveable goofball, but still a goofball. He was always late, always laughing, always getting into some sort of silly situation. His dad, a big warm teddy bear of a man, would shake his head and chuckle at him every single day. Raj had grown up in London, but his dad always told him stories about their home country of India, about the golden fields of Punjab, about the music and the colours and the festivals. And even though Raj had never been there, those stories made his heart feel all warm and glowy inside.

Now across the city, in another cozy little house, lived a girl named Simran. Simran was wonderful. She was brave and smart and had the most sparkly imagination you have ever seen. She would daydream about adventures, about wide open spaces, about seeing the whole wide world. Her dad, whose name was Bauji, loved her very very much, but he was also, and I say this kindly, a little bit stubborn. Like a very loveable, very confused goat who had made up his mind about something and simply would not budge. Can you imagine? He had already decided that when Simran grew up, she would go to India and marry a boy from their village back home, a boy she had never even met. Poor Simran.

But before any of that happened, something exciting was on the horizon. A trip! A grand, glorious, Europe trip with a whole group of friends for a whole month. Trains and mountains and castles and beautiful countryside, oh my!

And guess what happened? Raj was going on the VERY SAME TRIP. What are the chances!

Now the trip started off a little rocky, mostly because Raj, being Raj, was late to the train station. He came running and puffing and sliding across the platform with his enormous backpack wobbling all over the place, and he just barely leaped onto the train as it was pulling away. Simran, who was already sitting very properly in her seat, watched this whole performance and thought, this boy is an absolute disaster. And honestly? She was not entirely wrong.

But here is the thing about trips, my sleepy little ones. When you spend a whole month travelling with someone, seeing beautiful snowy mountains and cobblestone streets and twinkling little towns, sometimes the person you thought was an absolute disaster turns out to be your very best friend. Raj made Simran laugh until her tummy hurt. He knew all the funniest games, all the best songs, and he always somehow found the best food in every single city they visited. Simran showed Raj how to actually look at things, to really see them, to notice the beautiful little details he was always too busy goofing around to see. They were, in a word, the most perfect pair of best friends the world had ever produced.

They explored and adventured and had the most magical time. They got lost in the Swiss mountains once, which sounds scary but was actually hilarious because Raj's GPS was completely upside down the whole time and they still somehow ended up at the most beautiful lake you have ever seen in your life. They danced in the rain in Paris. They watched the stars from a tiny little village in Austria and talked about all their biggest dreams.

And then, as all wonderful things do, the trip ended.

And that is when the real adventure began.

Because Simran went home and her dad announced it was time to pack up everything, leave London, and move to India so she could meet the boy from the village she was supposed to be friends with forever. His name was Kuljeet. Now Kuljeet was not mean, exactly. He was just... let me think of the right word... magnificently clueless. He strutted around like a rooster who thought he was the most important rooster in the entire barnyard. He had big hair and a very loud laugh and was absolutely convinced that everyone in the world found him as wonderful as he found himself. Can you imagine? Hilarious.

Simran was very sad. She did not want to leave. She did not want to be best friends with a strutting rooster boy she had never met. She wanted to go on more adventures. She wrote in her diary and looked out the window and missed her fun, goofy, wonderful friend Raj terribly.

But then! THEN! Guess what happened!

Raj showed up.

Because THAT is what best friends do.

Raj had been thinking about everything, about their adventures and their conversations and how Simran was the most genuinely wonderful person he had ever known, and he thought, I am not going to just let my best friend disappear to another country forever. No no no. So he packed his bag, told his dad the whole story, and his dad, the big warm teddy bear, grabbed his OWN bag and said, I am coming too, obviously.

So off they went to Punjab, India. The golden fields! The colours! The music! Everything his dad had always told him about, right there in front of his eyes. It was even more beautiful than the stories.

Now the tricky part was that Simran's dad, Bauji, did not know Raj. And Bauji had, as we mentioned, made up his mind about things in a very goat-like way. So Raj could not simply walk up and say, hello sir, I am Simran's best friend, please reconsider your plans. That would not work at all.

So instead, Raj did something clever. He decided to become part of the village, to help out, to show everyone what kind of person he really was. He helped with the farm work. He fixed things that were broken. He joined in the celebrations with so much joy and enthusiasm that everyone in the whole village absolutely adored him. Even Bauji secretly thought this boy had a very good heart, although he was not quite ready to admit that yet because, well, goat.

Kuljeet, meanwhile, was busy being magnificently useless. He kept trying to show off and things kept going hilariously wrong. He tried to lift a very heavy bag to impress everyone and dropped it directly on his own foot. He tried to ride a horse and the horse looked at him, decided absolutely not, and walked away. He was not bad. He was just wonderfully, completely, perfectly silly.

Now Simran's mum, she was smart. Mums always are, right? She could see exactly what was happening. She saw how happy Simran was whenever Raj was around, how her eyes sparkled and she actually laughed again for the first time in weeks. And she thought, hmm, I think I need to have a quiet word with Bauji.

And the word she had was this. She said, do you remember why you left India all those years ago? You wanted a better life. You wanted Simran to be happy. And happiness, my dear stubborn wonderful husband, is standing right there in that field helping old Mr. Singh fix his fence.

Bauji went very quiet.

He stood at the window and he watched Raj in the field, working hard, laughing with the neighbours, being so completely and genuinely himself. And something in that stubborn goat heart of his went soft. Just a little. Like a biscuit that has been sitting near a warm cup of tea.

And then came the most important moment of the whole story.

Simran came to say goodbye to Raj, because she thought it was over, she thought he would have to go home. But Raj said no. He said he was going to do this properly. He walked right up to Bauji, looked him in the eye, and said, I am not going anywhere without your blessing. Because your daughter is my very best friend in the whole world and I will wait right here for as long as it takes for you to see that.

There was a very long pause.

And then Bauji, that wonderfully stubborn man, looked at his daughter's face, bright and hopeful and so full of life, and he looked at this silly brave boy who had crossed the world for her, and something finally clicked loose inside him.

He nodded. And he said, ja, Simran. Go.

And Simran ran.

She ran to catch the train that was just beginning to pull away, and Raj reached out his hand, and she grabbed it, and off they went into the most wonderful future you can possibly imagine. Best friends. Adventure partners. Two people who had found in each other something that made the whole world feel bigger and warmer and full of possibilities.

And back in the village, Bauji smiled a very small, very quiet smile. And Kuljeet tripped over absolutely nothing and fell into a hay bale. And everyone had a lovely cup of chai.

Now then, my little ones. The fields of Punjab are very quiet tonight. The train is rocking gently on the tracks. Raj and Simran are watching the stars go by through the window, just like they did in Austria, and everything is perfectly, wonderfully fine.

You close your eyes now. Think of all the adventures waiting for you. Think of the friends who will make you laugh until your tummy hurts. Think of the big beautiful world out there, full of golden fields and snowy mountains and trains going clickety clack into the dark.

Sleep tight. I love you to the moon and all the way back. Goodnight.

Okay little one, snuggle up tight. Pull that blanket all the way to your chin. Yes, just like that. Are you cozy? Good. Because tonight I have a really really wonderful story for you. It's about a boy named Raj, a girl named Simran, and the most exciting adventure across two whole countries. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in the big beautiful city of London, there lived a girl named Simran. She had the longest, floatiest hair you ever saw, and she loved to twirl in fields of bright yellow flowers. Yellow! Like sunshine. Like butter. Like the very best kind of happy.

Simran lived with her papa, her mama, and her little sisters. Her papa was a funny, round, very serious man named Baldev. He always wore the same mustache. A big, bushy, wiggly mustache. And he always talked in a very loud, very important voice. LIKE THIS. Even when he didn't need to. Even at breakfast. Even about toast.

Now Papa loved Simran very very much. But he was also a little bit silly, the way grown-ups sometimes are. He had decided, long long ago, that Simran would one day go to India to marry a boy she had never ever met. His name was Kuljeet. And Kuljeet, well, we'll get to Kuljeet later.

But first. There was Raj.

Raj lived in London too. He was funny and loud and bouncy, like a puppy who just woke up from a nap. He had the biggest smile you can imagine. Just enormous. Like if you stretched a smile all the way from one ear to the other and then a little bit more. That was Raj's smile.

Raj's papa was also very funny. He was always saying dreamy, floaty things about love and life and trains. He loved trains very much. Trains and feelings. That was Raj's papa.

Now one day, Simran and Raj and a whole big group of friends went on a trip across Europe. Europe! So many countries! So many trains! So many sandwiches!

And on this trip, Raj and Simran became the very very best of friends. The kind of friends who make each other laugh so hard their tummies hurt. The kind of friends who share their snacks and their secrets. They ran through Swiss mountains together. They chased each other through markets in France. Raj was always doing something silly, and Simran was always shaking her head but also giggling. Always giggling.

But then the trip ended. And Simran had to go to India. Because Papa had decided. And Papa's mustache had decided too.

Simran felt very sad on the airplane. She pressed her nose against the little oval window and watched London get smaller and smaller and smaller until it was gone.

Raj felt sad too. He stood on a train platform in a big coat and watched the train pull away. And he thought and he thought and he thought.

And then he had an idea.

The biggest, bounciest, most wonderful idea.

He would go to India too! He would find Simran! He would show her papa, the very serious mustache man, that he was a good and kind and trustworthy friend. And maybe, just maybe, Papa would say yes. Yes, Simran can choose her own path. Yes, Raj is good. Yes, everything will be okay.

So off Raj went to India. To a tiny little village with golden fields and busy kitchens and the smell of warm spices floating through the air like a hug.

Now when Raj got there, he met the family. And oh, he was SO charming. He helped in the kitchen. He carried heavy bags. He made everyone laugh. Even the grumpy uncle who never laughed. Even the dog.

But then there was Kuljeet. Remember Kuljeet? Oh, Kuljeet was something else entirely. He was very very proud of his own hair. He spent a lot of time looking at himself. A LOT of time. He was loud and boastful and he walked around like he was the most important person in every single room, even rooms he had just walked into, even rooms that were empty before he arrived.

Kuljeet had big friends who were also very silly. They bumbled around and tripped over things and argued about nothing. They were not scary even a little bit. They were more like a bunch of confused chickens than anything else.

But Raj was clever. And kind. And patient. He didn't do anything loud or showy. He just kept being good. Day after day after day.

And slowly, slowly, slowly, like the sun coming up in the morning, Simran's mama saw it. She saw how happy Simran was. She saw how good Raj was. And she went to Papa.

She sat beside the big mustache man. And she spoke very gently. She said, our daughter has a good heart. Trust her heart. Let her choose.

And Papa sat very quietly for a long time.

His mustache twitched.

And then, at a train station, on a golden afternoon, Papa looked at Simran and said go. Go, my child. Go and be happy.

And Simran ran. She ran and ran down the platform, her floaty hair flying behind her, and Raj was there, on the train, with that enormous smile, and he held out his hand, and she took it, and off they went together. Best friends. On the greatest adventure. Into the most beautiful tomorrow.

And everyone in that little village had a big feast. With dancing and music and so much food that even the dog was happy.

Now close your eyes, little one.

Can you picture those yellow flowers? Those golden fields?

That's where you're going tonight, in your dreams.

Soft and warm and safe.

Just like Simran. Just like Raj.

Just like you.

Goodnight, my love. Sleep tight.

Alright, alright, scootch over and make some room, pull that blanket up nice and snug, and let me tell you about one of the greatest adventures ever to happen to two best friends who found each other in the most unexpected way. This is the story of Raj and Simran, and trust me, by the end of it, you're going to believe that some friendships are just written in the stars.

Once upon a time, in the big, beautiful, buzzing city of London, there lived a girl named Simran. Now Simran wasn't just any ordinary girl. She was the kind of person who could find magic in absolutely everything. She'd press flowers between the pages of her diary, she'd close her eyes on the Tube and imagine she was somewhere completely different, and she had this wonderful habit of twirling around in open fields whenever she got the chance. Her bedroom walls were covered in pictures of mountains and meadows and places she dreamed of going. She was a dreamer, our Simran, through and through.

Her Papa, Baldev Singh, was a big, round, wonderfully dramatic man who ran a little Indian grocery shop on a London street. He was the kind of dad who cried at literally everything. A beautiful sunset? Tears. A particularly good samosa? More tears. The thought of his daughter growing up? Absolute Niagara Falls. He loved Simran more than anything in the whole world, but he also had this funny little habit of being just a tiny bit, how do we say it, overprotective. Okay, very overprotective. He still checked if she'd packed her umbrella. She was seventeen.

Now, Papa Baldev had a dream of his own. He wanted Simran to marry the son of his oldest, dearest friend back in India, a boy named Kuljeet. He'd never really met Kuljeet properly, but in his head, Kuljeet was absolutely perfect, practically a prince, probably had lovely hair, definitely very responsible. Simran wasn't so sure about all this, but she loved her Papa too much to argue. Not yet, anyway.

Then one day, Simran's best friend Sheena came bounding over with the most exciting news. A group of friends was going on a big Interrail trip across Europe. A whole month of trains and cities and castles and absolutely incredible food. Simran's eyes went wide as dinner plates. This was exactly the kind of adventure her diary had been waiting for.

She asked Papa. Papa said no. She asked again with slightly bigger eyes. Papa wavered. Mama stepped in, because Mama always stepped in at exactly the right moment, and Mama pointed out that their little girl was growing up and needed to see the world before the world passed her by. Papa looked at Mama, then at Simran, then at the ceiling, then he cried a little bit, and then he said yes.

Simran nearly knocked him over with her hug.

So off she went, backpack stuffed to bursting, heart full of excitement, and a little notebook to write every single thing down in.

Now, on the very same morning, at a very different house across the city, a boy named Raj was also getting ready for a trip. Raj was the kind of person who made every room slightly louder and significantly more fun the moment he walked into it. He had the most contagious laugh you've ever heard, the sort that made strangers on the street smile without knowing why. He was clever and quick and just a little bit cheeky, and he'd grown up in London with his Papa, who was his absolute best friend in the whole world.

Raj's Papa was a jolly, big-hearted man who told even bigger stories and laughed at every single one of them himself. He told Raj every single day to go out and grab life with both hands, to be kind, to be brave, to be someone worth knowing. Raj had listened very, very carefully to all of this advice, and it showed.

Raj and his friends were also taking the exact same Interrail trip across Europe, because that, my sleepy little friends, is exactly how stories work.

The two groups of friends ended up on the same train, and through one of those wonderfully chaotic series of events involving a spilled bag of crisps, a very confused conductor, and an argument about whether Switzerland or Austria had better chocolate, Raj and Simran ended up sitting across from each other.

Now, I won't tell you it was instant friendship. In fact, Simran thought Raj was the most annoying person she had ever encountered in her entire seventeen years of life. He was too loud, too confident, told too many jokes, and he kept stealing the window seat. Raj, on the other hand, thought Simran was brilliant but also possibly the most serious person on the planet and he made it his personal mission to make her laugh at least once before they reached the next station.

He succeeded, for the record, somewhere just outside Brussels, and it was a very good laugh indeed.

And so it began. Days and days of adventures across Europe. They visited castles that looked like they'd been drawn by a child who'd had too much imagination and not enough sleep. They got spectacularly lost in a little Swiss town and ended up having the best hot chocolate of their lives in a bakery run by a tiny elderly woman named Helga who spoke no English but communicated entirely through enthusiastic gestures and extra pastries. They ran for trains they definitely should have caught earlier, they argued about maps, they shared snacks, they stayed up talking while the train moved through the dark countryside and the stars appeared one by one outside the window.

Raj told Simran about his Papa and how much he admired him. Simran told Raj about her dreams, the real ones, the ones in her diary. Raj told her they were brilliant dreams. He said them back to her like they were facts, not wishes, and something about that made Simran feel like maybe they could be.

By the time the trip was over and the train pulled back into London, these two were absolutely, completely, one hundred percent best friends. The kind of best friends where you don't really have to explain yourself because the other person already sort of knows. The kind that feel like you've known each other for years even when it's only been weeks.

But then came the part that made Simran's heart sink all the way down to her shoes.

When she got home, Papa was waiting with very exciting news in his opinion. They were moving back to India. Not in a few months. Soon. And the wedding with Kuljeet was being arranged. Simran stood in the kitchen and felt the whole adventure drain right out of her. She'd only just found this brilliant friendship and now she was being packed into suitcases and shipped across the world.

She told Raj. Raj stood very still for a moment, which was unusual for Raj who almost never stood still. And then he said something that Simran thought was either very brave or completely bananas or possibly both.

He said he was coming too.

Not because he had to. Not because anyone asked him to. But because real friends don't just wave goodbye at train stations. Real friends show up.

So Raj went to India.

Now, Simran's family in the Punjab lived in a farmhouse so pretty it looked like it had been painted by someone who really loved golden light and fields of mustard flowers. There were chickens wandering about, and a dog named Tuffy who was deeply suspicious of everyone, and relatives absolutely everywhere, and the air smelled like fresh bread and marigolds and just the faintest hint of someone's grandmother's very strong perfume.

And right next door was Kuljeet's family.

Oh, Kuljeet. Where to begin with Kuljeet. He was tall and he knew it, and he walked around like he expected everyone to applaud when he entered a room. He was the kind of person who flexed his muscles when he thought no one was looking and then looked around to check if anyone had noticed. His best friends were two boys named Sukhwinder and Pappu who functioned mainly as a personal cheering squad and weren't very good at thinking for themselves. Kuljeet liked to make speeches about how wonderful Kuljeet was. He was not, in anyone's objective opinion, wonderful. He was just very loud about it.

Raj, being Raj, somehow managed to charm absolutely everybody at the farmhouse within about forty-five minutes of arriving. He helped carry things, he made people laugh, he learned three Punjabi phrases and used them at completely wrong moments which was somehow even more endearing, and Tuffy the suspicious dog was sitting in his lap by sunset, which everyone agreed was basically a miracle.

Simran's family adored him. Her little sister followed him everywhere like a duckling. Her aunties kept feeding him second helpings of everything. Even Grandma, who didn't approve of most things, nodded at him once, which was apparently the highest honour available.

The only ones who were not charmed were Kuljeet and his crew, who had figured out that this cheerful boy from London was Simran's very good friend and they did not like that one bit.

Kuljeet tried all sorts of silly tactics to make Raj look bad. He challenged Raj to an eating contest at a family dinner, convinced this was his moment to shine. Raj ate so enthusiastically and with such obvious joy that everyone applauded him and Kuljeet ended up with hiccups for the rest of the evening. Sukhwinder and Pappu tried to sneak into Raj's room and rearrange his belongings to confuse him, but they got so confused themselves that they ended up locked in a cupboard and had to be rescued by Grandma, who was not impressed.

Then Kuljeet decided he would tell Simran's Papa that Raj was up to no good. He marched over with his chest puffed up and his speech all prepared and dramatically announced that this London boy could not be trusted.

Papa Baldev looked at Kuljeet. Then he looked at Raj, who at that exact moment was helping Simran's Mama carry a very heavy pot of dal and making her laugh while doing it. Papa Baldev was many things, but he wasn't completely unobservant.

He didn't say anything just yet. But he was thinking. Papa Baldev, underneath all the drama and the crying and the overprotectiveness, was actually a very good man with a very good heart. He just needed to figure some things out.

Meanwhile, Raj and Simran had one of those very important conversations that best friends sometimes have to have. They sat outside under an absolutely ridiculous number of stars, and Simran told Raj that she was scared. Scared of saying no to Papa. Scared of disappointing everyone. Scared that wanting her own path made her a bad daughter.

Raj was quiet for a moment. Then he said that the bravest thing in the world wasn't climbing a mountain or fighting a dragon. The bravest thing was being honest about what you truly wanted, especially when it was hard. He said that a good parent, a truly good parent, didn't want their child to be happy in spite of them. They wanted to be part of what made their child happy.

Simran thought about this for a very long time.

And then she did the bravest thing she'd ever done. She went to Papa Baldev and she sat down across from him and she told him the truth. All of it. About the trip, and the friendship with Raj, and the dreams in her diary, and how she wanted to choose her own path. She didn't yell. She didn't argue. She just told him, honestly and lovingly, exactly who she was and what she hoped for.

Papa Baldev listened. And as he listened, something on his face shifted, slowly, like clouds moving away from the sun. Because he heard in his daughter's voice the exact same longing that had lived in his own heart when he was young, before he'd buried it under worry and tradition and the fear of things going wrong.

He sat there for a very long time. And then his eyes went a bit watery, which was not unusual. But this time they went watery in a different kind of way.

He looked at Simran, this brilliant, dreaming, twirling, diary-keeping girl who somehow had the whole world inside her. And he thought about what kind of father he wanted to be. Not the kind who held on so tight that the thing you loved most couldn't breathe. The kind who loved bravely enough to let go.

He called Raj over. Raj came, looking a bit uncertain, which was possibly the first time he'd looked uncertain about anything.

Papa Baldev looked at him for a long, long moment. Then he said, gruffly but warmly, that anyone who made his daughter laugh like that, who showed up for her the way Raj had, who ate dal with that much enthusiasm, was clearly someone worth knowing.

And Kuljeet, to absolutely nobody's devastation, was very politely told that the wedding was off. He took it with considerable drama and some very theatrical sighing, and then Sukhwinder and Pappu suggested they go find some snacks and everyone agreed that was the best idea anyone had had all week.

The farmhouse that evening was full of lights and music and the smell of Mama's cooking and Tuffy running around causing chaos and Simran's little sister dancing in the courtyard. And in the middle of it all was Raj, laughing his big contagious laugh, and Simran, actually twirling, just like she always did when she felt like everything was exactly right.

And it was. It really, really was.

So here is what that story teaches us, my sleepy ones. It teaches us that real friendship is one of the most powerful forces in the whole universe. It teaches us that bravery isn't about being loud or bold or never being scared. Sometimes bravery is just being honest, just saying the true thing even when your voice shakes. And it teaches us that the people who love us most, the really good ones, they don't want us to be smaller than we are. They want to cheer for the fullest, most wonderful version of us.

And now the stars are out, just like they were over that farmhouse, and the night is warm and soft, and somewhere out there someone is having a great adventure of their own, maybe on a train across beautiful countryside, maybe in a bakery with too many pastries, maybe just sitting with a very good friend under a very large sky.

But right now, the most important thing is you, all tucked in, warm and safe and loved. And that, my darling sleepy ones, is the very best place in the world to be.

Close your eyes now. Dream something wonderful.

Goodnight.

Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets up nice and tight, and let me tell you one of my absolute favourite stories. It's about friendship, and bravery, and a very, very silly bad guy who could never quite get things right. Are you ready? Good. Close your eyes if you want, but keep your ears wide open.

Once upon a time, in a little village called Ramgarh, tucked between big golden hills and dusty winding roads, there lived a kind and wise old man named Thakur. Now Thakur had a magnificent white moustache — the kind that wiggled when he talked — and he loved his village more than anything in the whole wide world. He was like the grandfather everyone wished they had. The kind who always had a sweet in his pocket and a story on his lips.

But Ramgarh had a problem. A big, silly, ridiculous problem. And that problem had a name. His name was Gabbar.

Now listen, Gabbar thought he was very, very scary. He wore dusty old clothes and had a big loud laugh that went "Ha ha ha HA!" and he stomped around the hills with his gang of bumbling, clumsy followers. Can you imagine? His gang was always tripping over their own feet, dropping things, and arguing about whose turn it was to make the tea. They were, honestly, more like a group of confused pigeons than actual bad guys. But they made a lot of noise, and they kept bothering the people of Ramgarh, stealing their vegetables and scaring their goats, and that was not very nice at all.

So Thakur came up with a brilliant plan. He was going to find two of the cleverest, funniest, most adventurous friends in the whole country and ask them to come to Ramgarh and sort Gabbar out once and for all. And he knew just who to call.

Their names were Jai and Veeru.

Oh, these two. Where do I even begin? Jai and Veeru were best friends — the absolute best kind of best friends. The kind who finished each other's sentences and made each other laugh until their tummies hurt. Jai was quiet and clever, always thinking, with a little harmonica that he played the most beautiful tunes on. And Veeru was loud and bouncy and enthusiastic, the kind of boy who would jump into a pile of leaves just because it was there. Together, they were completely unstoppable.

Thakur went and found them and said, "Boys, I need your help. My village needs clever people, not just strong people. Will you come?" And Jai and Veeru looked at each other, grinned those big matching grins, and said, "We're in!"

So off they went, rattling along on a train toward Ramgarh, already joking and laughing and probably eating too many snacks. When they arrived at the village, everyone peeked out from behind their doors. The village had been so quiet and nervous for so long that they'd almost forgotten what laughter sounded like.

But Jai and Veeru brought the laughter back.

Veeru, bless him, immediately became best friends with absolutely everyone. He befriended the horses, he made friends with the children who followed him around like little ducklings, and he struck up the most wonderful, giggly friendship with a cheerful young woman named Basanti who drove a horse cart and talked — oh my goodness — she talked more than anyone you have ever met in your life. She could talk about anything! The weather, the horse, the road, a leaf she saw, a cloud that looked like a fish. Veeru thought she was absolutely wonderful, and they became the silliest, funniest pair of friends, always chattering away together.

And Jai, quiet lovely Jai, he found a friend too. Her name was Radha, and she was gentle and soft-spoken and kind. She didn't say much, but when she did, every word mattered. Jai would sit on the steps in the evenings and play his harmonica, and Radha would sit nearby, and they didn't even need to talk. That's the best kind of friendship, isn't it? When you can just sit quietly with someone and feel completely happy.

Now, meanwhile, Gabbar had heard that two clever strangers had come to Ramgarh. And did this worry him? Well, it should have. But instead, Gabbar puffed out his chest and said, "HA! Two strangers? I am GABBAR! Nobody can outsmart ME!" And his gang all nodded and clapped, even though two of them bumped heads doing it.

One time, Gabbar's gang came stomping into the village, trying to look menacing, and Veeru had sneakily tied all their bootlaces together. Can you imagine? They got about three steps before they all went tumbling into a big heap like a pile of socks falling out of a drawer. The whole village giggled from behind their windows.

Another time, Jai played such a spooky, mysterious tune on his harmonica in the dark that Gabbar's gang became completely convinced the hills were haunted. They ran all the way back to their hideout, tripping over rocks, with their hats flying off their heads. Gabbar was furious, but what could he do? His gang was hiding under their blankets.

Slowly, slowly, something magical started happening in Ramgarh. The people began to come out of their houses. They started talking to each other again. They began to smile. Children played in the streets. The old women brought out their best recipes. There was music and colour and the smell of good food drifting through the village in the evenings. Jai and Veeru hadn't just come to deal with a silly bad guy — they had brought an entire village back to life.

Thakur watched all of this with his magnificent wiggling moustache and felt very proud indeed.

But Gabbar was getting more and more frustrated. His plans kept failing. His gang kept coming back with ripped trousers and dented hats and silly stories about harmonicas and haunted hills. Finally, he stomped his feet and said, "ENOUGH! I will come up with the most brilliant plan anyone has ever seen!" His gang all looked at each other nervously because Gabbar's brilliant plans had a funny way of going very, very wrong.

And this one was no different.

Gabbar's grand plan involved sneaking into the village during the big harvest festival when everyone was celebrating. But Jai and Veeru had known something was coming. They were clever like that. So they prepared the whole village. Everyone had a job. The children were in charge of making noise with pots and pans. The old women were in charge of the water buckets. Basanti, wonderfully unstoppable Basanti, was in charge of creating a distraction — and if you've ever met someone like Basanti, you'll know that a distraction is absolutely her speciality.

When Gabbar and his bumbling gang crept into the village, they walked straight into the most magnificent, chaotic, wonderful confusion they had ever seen. Pots were banging, water was splashing everywhere, Basanti was talking at approximately a million words per minute, and Jai and Veeru appeared from two different directions at exactly the same moment, which completely baffled everyone because how did they always know?

It was a magnificent muddle. Gabbar's gang slipped, stumbled, got splashed, got completely confused, and ended up sitting in a big bewildered bunch in the middle of the village square, looking very sorry for themselves. Gabbar himself had somehow ended up with a bucket stuck on his foot.

The whole village came out and looked at him. And then someone started laughing. And then someone else. And soon everyone was laughing, because honestly, a villain with a bucket on his foot is very hard to take seriously.

Gabbar looked around at all the laughing faces, and at his hopeless gang, and at Jai and Veeru grinning at him, and something in him sort of... deflated. Like a balloon that had been puffed up too big. He was taken away to be looked after by people who could help him learn to be better, and the hills around Ramgarh became peaceful again.

That night, the whole village celebrated. There were lights strung everywhere, and wonderful food, and music, and Veeru danced so enthusiastically that he knocked over a table, which was very on-brand for Veeru. Jai played his harmonica, and it was the most beautiful sound floating up into the night sky, like a little piece of happiness sent up to the stars.

Thakur stood in the middle of it all, his moustache wiggling with joy, watching his village alive and bright and full of laughter. He looked at Jai and Veeru and felt something so warm in his heart that he could barely find the words. He didn't need many. He just said, "Thank you, boys." And that was enough.

Jai and Veeru looked at each other, and then at Ramgarh, all lit up and glowing in the night, full of the people they'd come to love. And they knew that this little dusty village between the golden hills had become something very precious to them. A home away from home.

And somewhere out in those quiet peaceful hills, a little harmonica tune drifted on the warm breeze.

Now then, my darling ones, the village of Ramgarh went to sleep that night feeling safe and happy and loved. The stars were out, very bright, watching over everyone. The horses were resting. The children were tucked in, just like you are now.

Your eyes are getting heavy, aren't they? I can see that. That's good. That's just right.

Remember, the bravest thing you can do is be kind. And the cleverest thing you can do is make people laugh. And the very best thing in the whole wide world is to have a really, truly wonderful friend.

Sleep now, little ones. The stars are watching. Goodnight.

Okay little one, snuggle up tight. Pull that blanket all the way up. Are you cozy? Good. Because I have a really, really good story for you tonight. It's about two best friends, a kind old man, and the silliest bad guy you ever heard of. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in a little village called Rampur, there lived a very kind old man named Thakur. Thakur had the biggest, warmest heart in the whole village. He loved his family. He loved his neighbors. And he had the most magnificent white mustache you have ever seen in your life. It was very, very impressive.

Now Thakur had a little problem. There was a silly, silly man causing trouble near his village. This man's name was Gabbar. Oh, Gabbar thought he was very scary. He wore a big hat. He made very loud noises. He stomped around going HA HA HA. But honestly? He was not scary at all. He was just very, very silly. His boots were too big and he kept tripping over them. His hat fell over his eyes all the time. His helpers were even sillier than he was. They bumped into each other. They dropped things. One of them was always hiccuping at the wrong moment. They were basically a bunch of silly geese in boots.

But still, Gabbar and his silly gang were bothering the village. They were sneaking in and taking all the laddoos from the sweet shop. Every single laddoo. Can you imagine? That is simply not okay.

So Thakur said, I need some help. I need two very clever, very brave friends to come and save my village.

And that is where our two heroes come in. Their names were Jai and Veeru. And oh, these two were the best friends in the whole wide world. They did everything together. Everything. They laughed together. They ate together. They got into little bits of mischief together. Jai was quiet and clever and always thinking. Veeru was loud and funny and always talking. He never ever stopped talking. Even in his sleep he was probably talking.

Jai would say something very wise with just four words. And Veeru would say the same thing but with four hundred words and three jokes and a little song. They were perfect together. Like roti and butter. Like chai and a rainy day. That is how good friends they were.

Thakur sent them a letter that said, please come and help us. And Jai and Veeru said, of course we will help. Friends help friends. And so off they went to Rampur.

When they arrived, the whole village was so happy to see them. There was a funny man named Soorma Bhopali who wore a very large coat and told very big stories about himself that were probably not true. There was a cheerful young woman named Basanti who drove a horse cart and talked even more than Veeru did, which was honestly quite an achievement. She and Veeru became the very best of friends immediately because they both loved talking more than anything in the world. They could talk and talk and talk and the horse, whose name was Dhanno, would just sigh very patiently.

Jai became good friends with Radha, who was gentle and kind and very wise. She did not say much but when she did say something it really meant a lot. Jai liked that. Quiet people understand each other, you know.

Now Jai and Veeru had a plan to deal with Gabbar and his silly gang. They were not going to do anything scary. They were going to be clever. Very, very clever.

First they hid all the laddoos in a secret place so Gabbar could not find them. Gabbar and his gang searched and searched and found nothing. They looked very confused. They bumped into each other some more.

Then Jai played a little trick using some rope and some tin cans and a very startled goat. I will not explain all the details but I will tell you that Gabbar's gang got completely tangled up like a ball of yarn and fell into a big pile. They were all fine. Just very confused and a little dizzy.

Then Veeru climbed up the water tower and made a very long and very dramatic speech. It was so long that Gabbar's gang all sat down and actually fell asleep listening to it. That gave everyone time to call the proper authorities to come and take Gabbar away.

And do you know what happened to Gabbar in the end? He had to come to the village every single day and help fix things he had bothered. He swept the roads. He carried heavy bags for the old grandmothers. He learned to bake and he actually turned out to make quite good laddoos, which was a nice surprise for everyone. His boots still did not fit properly but he got used to it.

The village had the biggest celebration. There was music and dancing and so many sweets. Basanti talked for approximately six hours straight. Veeru listened happily because he loved her very much as his best friend. Thakur laughed so hard his magnificent mustache actually wobbled. Jai sat quietly and smiled that little smile of his.

And all was well in Rampur. All was very very well.

Now little one, can you feel how cozy and safe everything is right now? The village is all tucked in for the night. Jai and Veeru are resting under a big starry sky, side by side like always. The horses are sleeping. The flowers are sleeping. Even Gabbar is sleeping, probably dreaming about laddoos.

And you, my little one, you are safe and warm and so very loved. Close those beautiful eyes now. Let the story settle around you like a soft blanket. Tomorrow there will be more adventures. But right now, it is time to sleep.

Goodnight sweetheart. Sweet sweet dreams.

Alright, snuggle up tight, pull that blanket all the way up to your chin, and get comfy, because tonight I have a really, really good one for you. This is the story of two best friends, a grumpy old man with a heart of gold, and the silliest, most ridiculous villain you have ever heard of in your entire life. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in a little village called Ramgarh, tucked between rolling golden hills and dusty red roads, there lived a retired police officer named Thakur Baldev Singh. Now, Thakur was the kind of man who had a moustache so impressive that birds considered building nests in it. He walked with his chest puffed out like a proud rooster, and everyone in the village respected him enormously. He had a big beautiful haveli, which is a grand old house, with a courtyard where marigolds bloomed and his grandchildren ran around making a glorious amount of noise.

But something was troubling Thakur's village, and had been for quite some time. You see, there was a fellow named Gabbar Singh who lived up in the rocky hills outside the village, and Gabbar was, well, how do I put this kindly... he was an absolute buffoon. A complete nincompoop. The most dramatically ridiculous man in the entire history of dramatic ridiculous men.

Gabbar had a gang of followers who weren't particularly bright either. They wore mismatched clothes, they could never agree on anything, and their horses were constantly wandering off in the wrong direction. Gabbar himself had a big bushy beard that he was enormously proud of, and he had this habit of laughing very loudly at his own jokes, even when nobody else found them funny at all. Which was basically always.

What Gabbar loved most in the world was swooping down into Ramgarh and demanding that the villagers hand over grain and sweets and generally causing everyone a big, annoying headache. He wasn't dangerous, exactly, he was more like that one relative who shows up uninvited, eats all the good snacks, and refuses to leave. Deeply, profoundly irritating.

The villagers were completely fed up. They had tried everything. They had tried reasoning with Gabbar. They had tried ignoring Gabbar. Old Rameshwar the farmer had once tried bribing Gabbar with an extra large bag of peanuts, and Gabbar had taken the peanuts AND still caused trouble. Something had to be done.

So Thakur put on his best kurta, polished his walking stick until it gleamed, and set off on a mission. He was going to find help. Specifically, he was going to find two young men he had once crossed paths with, two absolute scoundrels with hearts surprisingly full of goodness, named Jai and Veeru.

Now, Jai and Veeru. Oh, where do I even begin with these two.

Jai was the quiet one. Tall, lean, with eyes that were always watching everything thoughtfully, like he was solving a puzzle that nobody else could see. He didn't talk much, but when he did, it was usually something clever or something funny, delivered so casually that it took you a moment to realize how brilliant it was. He always had a coin that he liked to flip in his fingers, and he had this habit of flipping it whenever he had to make a decision. Heads or tails. That was Jai's philosophy of life.

Veeru was... the opposite. Veeru was loud, cheerful, enthusiastic about absolutely everything, and talked approximately four hundred words per minute. He had a smile so wide and bright that people standing near him occasionally had to shield their eyes. He was the kind of person who made friends with everyone he met within thirty seconds, including the horse they were riding, which he had also named and given a full personality to. Veeru loved life the way a puppy loves a tennis ball. Completely and without any reservations whatsoever.

These two had been best friends for so long that they had developed their own secret language of looks and signals. A raised eyebrow from Jai meant one thing. A slight nod from Veeru meant another. They could have entire conversations without saying a single word, which drove everyone around them absolutely mad in the most entertaining way possible.

Thakur found them, explained the situation with great seriousness and dignity, and offered them a job. Help us deal with Gabbar, he said, and we will make it worth your while.

Jai flipped his coin. Veeru grinned his enormous grin.

They said yes.

And so, with their little bundle of belongings each, Jai and Veeru arrived in Ramgarh, and I promise you, the village was never, ever the same again.

From the very first morning, Veeru had made twelve new best friends, learned everyone's names, their children's names, their goats' names, and had somehow gotten himself invited to three different houses for dinner simultaneously. He bounced through the village like a cheerful little comet, spreading laughter and chaos in absolutely equal measure.

Jai, meanwhile, wandered quietly and observed. He walked through the dusty lanes, watched how the village worked, noted where Gabbar's lookouts were posted in the hills, and filed everything away in that calm, thoughtful mind of his. Jai's brain was like a very organized library. Everything had its place. Everything would be useful eventually.

They stayed with Thakur in his big haveli, and this is where things got wonderfully, beautifully complicated, in the best possible way.

Thakur's granddaughter Raji was basically the unofficial mayor of the haveli as far as the children were concerned, incredibly sharp, bossy in that warm and loving way that only the most caring people can be bossy, and she saw through Veeru's cheerful nonsense immediately. She was not impressed by his big smile or his constant jokes. She told him so, directly, on their very first meeting.

Veeru was delighted. He found this extremely funny. He decided immediately that they were going to be great friends, whether she agreed or not.

And then there was Radha.

Radha was Thakur's daughter-in-law, a gentle, quiet young woman who helped run the household. She had a sadness about her that sat softly around her shoulders like a shawl. She moved through the haveli like moonlight, calm and a little distant. Jai noticed her the way he noticed everything, thoughtfully, without intruding. And slowly, gradually, over chai shared in the courtyard and quiet conversations in the evenings, a gentle friendship bloomed between them. Not loud, not dramatic, just warm and steady and real, like a lamp glowing in a window on a cold night. They would sit and talk about small things, about the stars, about the village, about what makes a place feel like home, and it was the kind of friendship that makes you feel understood in the deepest and most important way.

But let us talk about the main event. The business with Gabbar.

Gabbar, up in his rocky hideout, had heard about Jai and Veeru arriving in Ramgarh, and he was not pleased. He paced around dramatically, his boots going CLONK CLONK CLONK on the rocks, his beard bristling with annoyance.

He sent his best men down to Ramgarh to deal with these newcomers. His best men were named Sambha and Kaalia, and I say best men only because they were the most organized among a very, very disorganized lot, which is a bit like being the tallest person in a room full of very short people. It is technically an achievement, but let us not get carried away.

Sambha's entire personality was saying "yes, boss" to everything Gabbar said, even when it made no sense. Kaalia was convinced he was much more intimidating than he actually was, which is a very specific kind of silliness that you might recognize from certain people in your own life.

Jai and Veeru saw them coming from half a mile away. They had a whispered conversation that lasted approximately four seconds. Jai raised an eyebrow. Veeru nodded. Plan made.

What followed was one of the most glorious bits of clever mischief you can imagine. Jai and Veeru had spent the past week quietly, patiently, sneakily setting up the most elaborate series of tricks and traps around the village. Not harmful traps. Funny traps. Traps designed specifically to make everyone involved look extremely foolish in a perfectly harmless way.

Gabbar's men came charging into the village looking intimidating, and immediately Sambha ran straight into a fence that had mysteriously appeared where he was absolutely certain a fence had not been before. Kaalia tried to look menacing from atop his horse, and his horse sat down. Just simply declined to participate further and sat directly down on the ground. Kaalia sat there on a sitting horse looking deeply confused, which is a very hard expression to look fierce through.

The whole thing collapsed into wonderful, absolute chaos, and Gabbar's men eventually retreated back to the hills with considerably less dignity than they had arrived with.

Gabbar, watching from a distance through his little telescope, ground his teeth together. Fine. He would come himself.

In the meantime, life in Ramgarh was genuinely lovely in that way that only temporary things can be, where everyone knows something special is happening and tries to enjoy every single bit of it. There were evenings around fires with Thakur telling stories, the children of the village performing plays, Veeru being loudly and enthusiastically terrible at cooking while absolutely convinced he was brilliant at it.

Veeru and Raji's friendship had, through the magnificent force of Veeru's cheerfulness and Raji's gradually lowering defences, become one of those great friendships where two people argue constantly and enjoy every second of it. He called her his best critic. She called him impossible. Both of them grinned when they said it.

There was one night, a quiet, beautiful night, when Veeru climbed up onto the water tower in the middle of the village for reasons that are difficult to fully explain except that they made complete sense to Veeru, and announced his feelings about friendship and this village and these people so loudly and dramatically that every single person in Ramgarh woke up and leaned out their windows to listen. Even the grumpiest old man on the street was smiling by the end of it, even though he would absolutely deny it.

Jai watched from below, arms crossed, coin spinning between his fingers, shaking his head slowly, smiling in that quiet way he had that meant he was absolutely, completely delighted.

And then came the day Gabbar himself decided enough was enough.

He came with all his men, absolutely sure that this time he would simply walk into Ramgarh and that would be that. He had given himself a very motivating speech about it in the mirror that morning. He felt very prepared.

He was not prepared.

Because what Gabbar did not know, and what Jai had been quietly organizing for weeks, was that the entire village was ready. Every person in Ramgarh, even old Rameshwar with his peanuts, even the children, even the woman who sold flowers by the temple and who everyone had assumed wasn't paying attention, which was a mistake because she was extremely paying attention. Everyone had a part to play.

The plan involved misdirection, cleverness, the strategic deployment of Veeru being extremely loud in one place while important things happened very quietly somewhere else, and the most spectacular series of mix-ups and confusions that Gabbar and his gang had ever encountered.

Gabbar kept thinking he had cornered Jai, and then it was Veeru. He kept thinking he had found Veeru, and then it was a decoy. He went left and everyone went right. He went right and the entire village had somehow rearranged itself. His men kept bumping into each other, arguing about which direction they were supposed to go, and at one memorable point, Sambha and Kaalia spent a full fifteen minutes accidentally chasing each other around a well thinking the other one was Veeru.

In the end, Gabbar was outwitted so thoroughly, so completely, so gently and firmly and kindly that he didn't quite know what had happened until it was already over. He found himself sitting in the middle of the village square, his plans in ruins, his men scattered and confused, looking up at Thakur, who was standing there with his magnificent moustache and his polished walking stick, looking tremendously dignified and not even slightly out of breath.

It was Jai's coin flip that had determined the final piece of the plan. Heads or tails. The right choice at the right moment.

And Gabbar, deflated like a balloon that has met an unkind pin, finally accepted that perhaps a career change was in order. Perhaps something that didn't involve bothering people who were just trying to live their lives peacefully. Perhaps something quieter. He shuffled away with what remained of his dignity, which was admittedly not very much, followed by Sambha saying "yes boss" about the whole situation even though there was nothing left to say yes to.

Ramgarh was free.

There were celebrations, of course. Enormous ones. With food and music and dancing that lasted until very, very late. Thakur sat in the middle of it all with moisture in his eyes that he absolutely insisted was dust. The children ran in circles until they collapsed happily in heaps. Even the horses seemed pleased.

Jai and Veeru stood at the edge of the courtyard looking out at it all, the lights and the laughter and the warm golden glow of a village that felt safe again.

"We did alright," said Veeru.

Jai flipped his coin, caught it, didn't even look at it.

"Yeah," he said. "We did."

And somewhere out there under that same huge, generous sky, all the stars were out, every single one, like they had dressed up specially for the occasion.

The hills were quiet. The marigolds in the courtyard were golden and sweet-smelling. The village of Ramgarh breathed in and breathed out slowly, like a person who has finally set down something heavy and is enjoying the wonderful feeling of their own two hands being empty and free.

And that, my darlings, is where we leave them. Jai and Veeru, friends for always, Thakur proud and peaceful, Raji and Radha and all the people of Ramgarh safe under their blankets just like you.

Close your eyes now. Feel how heavy and warm and comfortable your blanket is. Feel how soft your pillow is against your cheek.

The stars are out tonight, every single one of them.

And somewhere in those golden hills, there is a village all lit up and happy, and everything is perfectly, beautifully, wonderfully alright.

Goodnight, my loves. Sleep tight.

Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull that blanket up nice and cozy, and let me tell you about three of the best friends the world has ever seen. Are you ready? Good. Close your eyes and imagine a big, grand school — the kind with tall buildings and long corridors and very, very serious professors who think laughing is basically against the rules.

This school was called ICE, the Imperial College of Engineering, and it was full of the smartest kids in all of India. Everyone there was trying to be the best, studying all night long, memorizing enormous books thick as your pillow. But among all those serious students, there were three friends who were about to turn the whole place upside down — in the most wonderful way.

Their names were Rancho, Farhan, and Raju.

Now Rancho — oh, you would have LOVED Rancho. He had this big bright smile and a brain that worked like a magic machine. But the thing about Rancho was that he didn't just memorize things. He actually understood them. He asked questions like "But WHY does it work that way?" instead of just writing things down without thinking. Can you imagine? In a school full of people copying from books, here was this one boy who wanted to actually figure things out for himself.

Farhan was Rancho's best friend and roommate. He had a secret — a beautiful, wonderful secret he hadn't told anyone. Farhan didn't actually want to be an engineer at all. What he really, truly loved with his whole heart was taking pictures of animals. Wildlife photography! He had a big dream of travelling through jungles and forests and photographing tigers and elephants and colorful birds. But his papa wanted him to be an engineer, so here he was, sitting in lectures about machines and circuits with a slightly sad look on his face.

And then there was Raju. Oh, sweet Raju. He worried about EVERYTHING. He wore little rings on his fingers for good luck and prayed every single morning because he was so scared of failing. His family back home needed him to do well, and that thought sat on his shoulders like a heavy, heavy backpack that he carried everywhere.

These three boys shared a little room together and became the best of friends. They laughed together, they ate together, they stayed up late talking about their dreams. Rancho always told his friends — "All is well! All is well!" Whenever things felt scary or hard, he'd say it, and somehow, it actually helped. It was like a little magic spell.

Now. The head of the school — the director, whose name was Viru Sahastrabuddhe, but everyone secretly called him Virus — was the silliest, most bumbling, most pompous man you have ever seen in your life. He walked around with his chest puffed up like a pigeon and he had this enormous mustache that wiggled when he was cross, which was basically always. He wore the same stiff, starched clothes every day and he had a very loud, very squeaky voice that he used mostly for telling students they were doing everything wrong.

Virus believed that life was a race. First place was everything! Second place was nothing! He'd hold up two flowers — one that survived and one that got eaten by a bug — and say the bug was the world and you had to be the strong flower. The bug is coming! Study harder! The bug is the world! Rancho once pointed out that actually, both flowers are important to nature, and Virus turned absolutely purple with outrage. His mustache wiggled SO hard. It was quite something to see.

Virus had a star student named Chatur — oh, Chatur was a piece of work. He had memorized practically every textbook ever written but he didn't understand a single thing in any of them. He called himself the Silencer and walked around with a very smug look on his face, convinced he was going to be the most successful person who ever lived. He and Rancho had a friendly little rivalry, which mostly involved Chatur announcing how great he was and Rancho nodding politely while trying not to giggle.

One time, there was a big speech competition, and Chatur practiced his speech over and over and over. But Rancho — being the clever, mischievous fellow he was — sneakily swapped some of the words in Chatur's speech with silly, ridiculous words. So there stood Chatur in front of the entire school, all proud and puffed up, and he gave this speech full of completely nonsense words without even realizing it. The whole hall burst out laughing. Even some of the professors had to hide their smiles. Chatur finished his speech with a big proud bow, completely confused about why everyone was in stitches. Rancho and Farhan and Raju were in the very back row, crying happy tears.

But here's where the story gets really important, little ones. Because underneath all the fun and the laughter, Rancho was always trying to tell his friends something. He'd say — don't chase success. Chase your passion. Do what you love with your whole heart, and success will come running after you. It was such a simple idea, but it was the most important idea in the whole world.

Farhan finally, finally found the courage to tell his papa the truth. He sat him down and he said — Papa, I love you and I know you worked so hard for me, but I don't want to be an engineer. I want to photograph animals. I want to go into the jungle with a camera and capture the most beautiful pictures the world has ever seen. And do you know what? His papa looked at him for a long, long moment. And then — because fathers love their children even when it's hard — he said yes. He said yes, my son, follow your dream. And Farhan cried happy tears and Rancho and Raju jumped around the room like absolute silly beans, celebrating.

Raju's story was harder, because Raju was so scared. He was so scared of failing that he couldn't do anything right. He'd sit in exams with his hands shaking. He'd worry so much at night that he couldn't sleep. And one day, things got so hard that it felt like the end of the world for Raju.

But then something extraordinary happened. Raju woke up, and his two best friends were right there beside him. They hadn't left. They were sitting there, holding his hand, making him laugh, telling him stories, reminding him that he mattered — not because of his grades, but because he was RAJU, their wonderful, kind, funny, worrying friend. And slowly, slowly, Raju started to believe it. He stopped being so scared. He walked into his next big test and instead of trembling, he was calm. He answered every question with a clear head and a peaceful heart. And guess what? He did wonderfully. Because when you stop being afraid, you can finally show the world what you've got.

Now, there came a very dramatic night — oh, you would not believe this part — when there was the most enormous thunderstorm, and Virus's daughter needed help, and there wasn't a proper doctor around, and who saved the day using actual engineering and science and cleverness? Rancho. He used the things he'd actually learned and understood to help, right there in the middle of all that chaos. Virus stood there afterward with his mustache completely still for once, looking at this young man who'd done something real and important with his knowledge, and for the very first time, something softened in that stiff old director.

And then Rancho disappeared.

Just like that, after they all graduated, Rancho was gone. Farhan and Raju looked everywhere but couldn't find him. Years passed. Farhan became a famous wildlife photographer — his pictures were in magazines all around the world. Raju became a confident, happy engineer who smiled easily and didn't shake anymore. But they missed their friend. They missed him every single day.

And then — THEN — Chatur came back, all grown up and still as smug as ever, saying he'd found Rancho and they should all go see him. He was convinced Rancho had failed in life. He drove them all the way to a tiny school in the most beautiful, faraway village you can imagine — green hills and blue sky and children running everywhere.

And there was Rancho. Except — surprise of all surprises — that wasn't even his real name! His real name was a long, complicated, wonderful name, but everyone who loved him just called him Rancho. And here he was, running a little school for village children, inventing things, teaching kids to think and question and wonder, just like he always had. All around him, children were laughing and learning and building things. He was doing exactly what he loved, and he was the happiest person in the whole wide world.

Farhan and Raju ran to him. They hugged for so long. There were tears and laughter all mixed up together, the way the best reunions always are. And Chatur stood there with his mouth hanging open, because this man he thought had failed had actually created something more beautiful than any fancy job or big salary could ever be.

And the lesson, my darlings, the lesson that Rancho had been teaching his friends all along, finally made complete, perfect, wonderful sense. Don't run the race everyone else is running. Find the thing that makes your heart sing. Be curious. Be kind. Be brave enough to be yourself.

All is well.

All is well.

Now you close those eyes, my little ones. Think about the things that make YOU happy — the things you love, the questions you want to ask, the dreams tucked up inside you like little seeds waiting to grow.

The stars are out. The whole world is quiet. Rancho and Farhan and Raju are somewhere out there, happy and together.

And you, my darling, are safe and loved and wonderful.

Sweet dreams. All is well. All is very, very well.

Once upon a time, there was a very big school called Imperial College of Engineering. It had tall towers and long hallways and oh so many rules. The teachers there were very serious. They wore very serious faces. They never ever smiled. Not even a little bit.

Rancho had the biggest, brightest smile you've ever seen. And he asked questions. So many questions! While all the other students tried to memorize big boring words from big boring books, Rancho wanted to know WHY things worked. He wanted to understand. He wanted to learn for real.

And that made the head teacher, Director Viru, very very grumpy.

Oh, Director Viru. He had a big round belly and tiny little glasses that sat on the very tip of his nose. He walked around going HMPH and HARUMPH all day long. He thought school was only about winning. About being number one. About getting the highest marks and the fanciest job. He had a big chart on his wall with everyone's names on it. He checked it every single morning and every single night.

But Rancho didn't care about the chart. Not one bit.

Now Rancho had two best friends in the whole world. Their names were Farhan and Raju.

Farhan was tall and funny and he secretly loved taking pictures of animals and birds. Not engineering at all! But his papa wanted him to be an engineer, so there he was at the big serious school, feeling all muddled up inside.

Raju was sweet and gentle and he worried about everything. He worried so much that he had pictures of all his gods on his desk, just to feel safe.

These three friends did everything together. They ate together. They studied together. They laughed together. Late at night, when the whole school was asleep and everything was quiet, they would talk and dream about who they really wanted to be.

And Rancho would always say the same thing. He said it like a little song. He said, "Follow what you love, my friend. Follow what you love, and everything will be okay." He said it so many times that Farhan and Raju started to believe it too.

Now Director Viru had a helper named Chatur. Oh, Chatur. Chatur was very very proud of himself. He slicked his hair down flat every morning. He practiced his serious face in the mirror. He memorized every single word in every single book. He wanted to be number one more than anything in the whole world.

Chatur did not like Rancho one bit. He thought Rancho was too silly. Too happy. Too different. So Chatur was always trying to catch Rancho doing something wrong. He would peek around corners. He would tiptoe down hallways. But every time Chatur tried to make trouble, something funny happened instead. A bucket would tip over. His papers would fly everywhere. He would slip on a wet floor and go whooooop right into a pile of cushions.

Rancho never even had to try. It just happened that way.

As the years went by, something started to change. Farhan found a little bit of courage inside himself. He wrote a letter to a famous animal photographer and said, I love what you do. I want to learn from you. And you know what? The photographer wrote back! Farhan couldn't believe it. He laughed and cried at the same time. And Rancho hugged him tight and said, see? Follow what you love, my friend.

And Raju, sweet worrying Raju, he learned something too. He learned that worrying so much was making him miss all the beautiful things happening right in front of him. He took a big deep breath. He stopped looking at his feet. He looked up instead. And the world looked so much nicer from up there.

Then one night, something very exciting happened. A baby was about to be born, right there at the school, in the middle of a big rainstorm. The lights had gone out. Everything was dark and wet and scary. But Rancho stayed very calm. He remembered everything he had ever learned, not from memorizing, but from really truly understanding. He got his friends together. He found a way. And that tiny baby came into the world safe and warm and perfect.

Even Director Viru, grumpy old Director Viru with his tiny glasses and his big belly and his HMPH and his HARUMPH, even HE had to admit that Rancho was something special.

And years later, when Chatur came back bragging about how successful he was, he found out something wonderful. Rancho, their happy curious Rancho who just wanted to understand things and learn things and love things, had become one of the most brilliant inventors in the whole world. He lived somewhere beautiful and peaceful and he was still smiling that same big bright smile.

And Farhan was taking the most gorgeous photographs of birds you ever saw.

And Raju was just fine. Really truly fine.

The three friends found each other again and they hugged and laughed until their tummies hurt.

And the lesson, sweet one, the lesson that Rancho always knew, was this. Follow what you love. Really love. Not what makes other people clap. Not what looks good on a chart. What makes your heart feel warm and full and light.

Now close your eyes, little one.

You are safe and warm and loved.

And somewhere out there, those three friends are probably still laughing under the stars.

Just like you'll be dreaming very very soon.

Goodnight, sweetheart. Goodnight.

Spoiler — it wasn't. But oh, he thought it was.

His favourite student was a slick, grinning boy named Chatur, who everybody called Silencer — and if you knew how much Chatur talked and bragged and recited facts without ever actually understanding a single one of them, you'd understand exactly why that nickname was funny in the most backwards way possible.

He was the kind of kid who would look at a broken fan and immediately want to take it apart just to understand how it spun. He wanted to trek through jungles with a big camera and take pictures of snow leopards and rare birds and beetles that nobody had ever seen before. But his father had dreamed of having an engineer for a son since before Farhan was even born, so here Farhan was, dragging his feet through physics equations when his heart was somewhere in the wilderness, trying to photograph a very confused-looking rhino.

Raju was the opposite kind of worried. He was so terrified of failing that he could barely breathe. His family was very poor, and the weight of their hopes sat on his shoulders like a very large, very heavy elephant — a kind elephant, mind you, one that loved him dearly, but enormous nonetheless. Raju wore a big cluster of rings on his fingers, one for each god he was praying to, just to cover all his bases. He prayed before exams, during exams, and probably a little bit after exams just to be safe.

So there they were. Rancho, who loved learning. Farhan, who loved everything except what he was studying. And Raju, who was so scared of everything that he'd forgotten how to love much of anything at all. Together, they became the three idiots — which, by the way, was a name people used to tease them, but which they wore like a badge of absolute honour.

Now, the trouble began almost immediately, because Rancho simply could not stop being Rancho.

On the very first day of class, when their professor was droning on about the definition of a machine and expecting everyone to write down exactly what the textbook said, Rancho raised his hand. Chatur's greatest moment, he believed, would come at the college's big annual speech night. He had been chosen to deliver a speech in Hindi — a language Chatur was not entirely fluent in — and he spent weeks memorizing every single word.
