What followed was the most accidentally ridiculous speech in the history of the college, full of words that Chatur proudly mispronounced, words that meant something completely different from what he thought, and lines that had the entire audience trying desperately to keep straight faces while their shoulders shook with suppressed laughter. Virus's mustache twitched so fast it was practically a hummingbird. Chatur finished, bowed deeply, looked up expecting applause, and was greeted by an auditorium full of people who were very, very pink in the face from the effort of not completely losing it.

Rancho, Farhan, and Raju walked back to their room that night laughing so hard they had to hold each other up. It was one of those laughs that starts in your belly and travels all the way up through your chest and out into the night sky and maybe even reaches the stars.

But here's the thing about those three friends — their story wasn't just about jokes and mischief. It was about something much more important than that.

Farhan, you see, was getting closer and closer to the moment when his father would expect him to graduate and become an engineer. And one night, sitting on the roof of their hostel under a big spilled-out sky full of stars, Rancho looked at Farhan and said something very simple. He said, "Have you ever actually told your father what you want?"

Farhan had not. Because he was afraid. Because he thought his dream was too small, too silly, not serious enough for the big sacrifices his parents had made. But Rancho shook his head slowly and said, "Farhan. Your pictures of animals aren't silly. They're incredible. And the world needs people who are incredible at things they actually love."

It took a long time. It took a lot of nervousness and a few deep breaths and one very important, very shaky conversation between a son and his father. But Farhan finally told his dad the truth. And his father — who, underneath all his stern hoping, simply loved his son — finally listened. Really listened. It was like watching someone take off a backpack they'd been carrying for years and realize how much lighter they could stand.

And then there was Raju.

There came a moment when Raju's fear got so big that it swallowed him up completely. He was so terrified of disappointing his family, so certain he was about to fail, that he just froze — like a computer that has too many windows open and simply stops working. And in that frozen, frightened moment, he did something rash.

But Rancho and Farhan were there. They stayed up all night. They talked to him and sat with him and refused to leave. And slowly, like the sun coming up over the edge of the world, Raju began to thaw. He began to realize something enormous and simple at the same time — that the people who loved him didn't love him because of his grades or his degree. They loved him because he was Raju. Nervous, ring-wearing, prayer-muttering, kind-hearted Raju. And that was more than enough.

When Raju finally went to his next interview — shaking like a leaf in a ceiling fan breeze — he walked in without pretending. He didn't say what he thought they wanted to hear. He said true things. Honest things. Things like, "I've been scared my whole life, and I'm working on it." And somehow, impossibly, wonderfully, that honesty was exactly what people wanted. Because it's rare. And it's beautiful.

Now, all of this time, Virus kept trying to squash their spirit the way you might try to squash a rather bouncy rubber ball — enthusiastically, repeatedly, and without success.

His greatest weapon was pressure. Exams. Rankings. Rules. A system where only the student at the very top was considered truly worthwhile. But Rancho kept quietly proving that a mind set free to wonder and invent could do things that a mind just trying to top a rankings chart never could.

And the proof came in the most dramatic, most absurd, most wonderful way possible.

It was a stormy night — the kind where the rain hammers on the windows and the thunder rolls around the sky like a very grumpy uncle who's lost his glasses. And in the middle of that storm, someone needed help urgently, and there was no way to get proper help in time. So Rancho did what Rancho always did — he looked at the problem, he thought about what he knew, about how things actually worked, and he built something. Right there. Out of parts and wires and sheer determined cleverness. And it worked. Of course it worked. Because it was built with understanding, not memorization.

Even Virus had to stand there in the rain, his mustache drooping, and admit — quietly, privately, in the tiny space of his heart where honesty lived — that this boy was something else.

Time passed, the way it does in all the best stories, and the three friends graduated. But then Rancho disappeared. Just like that — poof, gone, like a soap bubble. Farhan and Raju searched for him, asked about him, missed him every single day. But Rancho had simply gone off to live his life exactly as he wanted to — learning, building, wondering, inventing.

Years later, Farhan and Raju went looking for him. And this is where the story becomes a proper adventure, because Chatur — who had spent all those years getting rich and important and never quite getting over being outwitted by Rancho — declared, in his most puffed-up Chatur voice, that he had won their old competition. That he was richer and more successful and more impressive, and that Rancho was probably nowhere and nothing.

Oh, Chatur. Sweet, ridiculous Chatur.

Farhan and Raju followed the clues — through cities and dusty roads and finally to the most beautiful, tucked-away little school, hidden in the mountains, where children sat and learned not because they were afraid but because they were curious. And there, in the middle of it all, was Rancho. Older, just as bright-eyed, doing exactly what he'd always been meant to do — teaching kids the way he'd always wished someone had taught him. Helping small minds fall completely in love with how the world works.

And then Chatur arrived, ready to deliver his grand victory speech. He had prepared it. He had rehearsed it. He had probably memorized it.

But when he finally understood — really understood — who Rancho actually was, what Rancho had actually built, the patents he'd filed, the innovations he'd created, the lives he'd changed, Chatur's mouth opened and closed like a very confused goldfish experiencing something it hadn't been trained to swim through.

He had not won. He had been Chatur the whole time and had never once noticed.

Rancho just smiled. Because he hadn't been competing. He'd never been competing. He'd just been doing what he loved. And somehow, magically, inexplicably, that had been enough. More than enough.

Farhan became a wildlife photographer. A really, really good one. He once spent three weeks in a jungle waiting for a single bird to land in exactly the right light, and it was the happiest three weeks of his life.

Raju became an engineer — a good one, because he'd finally stopped being so scared that he could actually think. He got a job where his boss valued honesty and courage, which, it turns out, are rarer and more useful than any textbook fact.

And Rancho kept teaching, kept building, kept asking why and how and what if, up there in the mountains where the air was clean and the children laughed and every single day felt like a discovery.

The lesson, the real one underneath all the silly speeches and the rainy nights and the mischief and the tears and the laughter, is simply this — follow what makes your mind light up. Not out of fear. Not to impress anyone. Not to win a competition. But because when you do the thing you genuinely love, you become the very best version of yourself. And the very best version of yourself is worth more than any trophy, any rank, any tiny pen pointed in your direction by a puffed-up director.

Now. Your eyes are getting heavy. I can see them. You've been on quite an adventure tonight. You've been to a beautiful mountain school and sat under a star-filled roof and laughed at Chatur's speech and found Rancho in his perfect place.

Let all of that settle into you like a warm cup of something sweet. Think about the thing that makes your mind light up. Hold onto it gently.

The rain is soft on the window. Everything is quiet. Everyone found where they belonged.

And so can you.

Sleep tight.

And she whispered goodnight to her mama, somewhere up there among them, and she said thank you. And somewhere, floating gently through the night sky, Aman's balloons were still drifting along having a perfectly lovely time.

Now then, little ones. Your eyes are getting heavy, aren't they? That's alright. Let your eyelids flutter closed. Think about the people you love most, the friends who make you laugh, the family who holds you close. That love is always there, even when it's quiet, even when people are far away. Just like the stars.

Alright, snuggle up tight, pull that blanket all the way up, and get cozy, because tonight I have an absolutely wonderful story for you. It's got best friends, a little bit of silliness, a whole lot of heart, and one very special letter. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in a big, beautiful college called St. Xavier's, there were three best friends. Their names were Rahul, Anjali, and Tina. Now, St. Xavier's was the kind of college that looked like it had been painted by someone who really, really loved the color orange and the smell of fresh marigolds. It had wide green fields where students played basketball, cozy little corners where people read books, and a canteen that made the most magnificent samosas you have ever smelled in your entire life.

Rahul was the kind of boy who walked into a room and somehow made everyone smile without even trying. He had floppy hair that never quite sat where it was supposed to, a laugh that was louder than it needed to be, and the magical ability to make friends with absolutely anyone — whether it was the canteen uncle, the grumpy groundskeeper, or even the pigeons that sat on the college roof. He was charming, he was funny, and he was, without question, the most popular boy in all of St. Xavier's.

Now, Anjali was Rahul's absolute best friend in the whole world. She was loud, she was brilliant, she was sporty, and she wore her hair in two long braids that swung behind her like little pendulums whenever she ran, which was often, because Anjali was always running somewhere. She wore caps and jerseys and never once worried about what anyone thought of her, which made her, honestly, the coolest person on campus. She and Rahul had been best friends since their very first day of college, and they were the kind of friends who finished each other's sentences and knew exactly what the other one was thinking just by looking at their eyebrows.

They did everything together. They played basketball together and Anjali was, between you and me, quite a bit better than Rahul, though Rahul would never in a million years admit that. They sat together in lectures pretending to take notes while actually drawing funny cartoons of their professors. They had a secret handshake that took forty-five seconds to complete and involved three spins, a wiggle, and something that looked vaguely like a chicken flapping its wings.

Life at St. Xavier's was absolutely perfect.

And then, one fine sunny morning, Tina arrived.

Now, Tina was wonderful. She was kind and warm and had a smile that could light up an entire football stadium. She was elegant in the way that made people forget what they were saying mid-sentence, and she had a way of making everyone around her feel like the most important person in the room. She was genuinely, authentically lovely.

And Rahul, well. Rahul took one look at Tina and forgot his own name for about four and a half seconds.

Anjali noticed this immediately, because Anjali noticed everything. She saw the way Rahul's floppy hair seemed to stand up a little straighter around Tina. She saw the way he laughed a little too loudly at things that weren't particularly funny. She saw all of it, and she filed it away quietly in her heart like a little folded note.

You see, here's the thing. Anjali had realized something that she hadn't quite realized before. She realized that Rahul wasn't just her best friend. He was her favourite person. And favourite people are a very special category. They're the ones whose happiness matters to you more than almost anything, even when that happiness has nothing to do with you.

So Anjali did what only the very bravest and most generous people do. She swallowed her feelings like a rather large and uncomfortable piece of dry toast, put on her biggest smile, and decided that if Rahul was happy, then she would be happy too.

Meanwhile, there was also someone else in this story. A boy named Aman. Now, Aman was cheerful and sweet and had the kind of energy that made you feel like you'd just had three glasses of mango juice. He was perfectly nice. He was friendly to everyone. He once helped the canteen uncle reorganize the entire spice shelf just because he had twenty minutes free. Lovely boy, truly.

But he had a rival, or at least he thought he did. A boy named Rifat — and oh, you are going to love Rifat, because Rifat was completely, magnificently, extraordinarily useless when it came to trying to be cool. He wore sunglasses indoors. He practiced his hair flip in reflective windows. He once tried to slide dramatically into a chair during a debate competition and missed the chair entirely and landed on the floor with a sound like a bag of potatoes falling off a shelf. The entire room went silent. Then everyone laughed for about three minutes. Rifat straightened his sunglasses, stood up, and said, "I meant to do that," which made everyone laugh for another three minutes.

Rifat was not a bad person. He was just magnificently, spectacularly bad at being impressive.

Anyway, as the months went on, Rahul and Tina became very close friends, and eventually, the very best kind of friends — the kind who want to be together always. And Anjali, being Anjali, cheered for them with her whole heart, even though a small and quiet part of her felt a little bit like a balloon that had slowly let out all its air.

College ended the way all good things do — too quickly and with a lot of feelings.

And then life moved on, as life has a habit of doing.

Rahul and Tina got married and had the most beautiful little girl in the entire universe. They named her Anjali. Because some names are so full of warmth that you just have to pass them on.

But then, something sad happened, and I want you to know that even in the saddest parts of stories, there is always love holding everything together. Tina became very ill, and though the doctors did everything they could, she knew that she wouldn't be around for very long. And so, before little Anjali was even old enough to say more than a handful of words, Tina sat down and did the most extraordinary thing a person can do. She wrote her daughter letters. Eight of them. One for each birthday, so that even when Tina was no longer there, a little piece of her would still be present, still speaking, still loving her little girl through words on paper.

And then Tina was gone, leaving behind a heartbroken Rahul, a tiny Anjali who didn't quite understand yet, and eight sealed envelopes sitting in a little box, waiting to be opened one by one.

Now. Fast forward eight years.

Little Anjali has grown into a curious, bright, wonderful eight-year-old who lives with her father Rahul and her grandmother, who everyone calls Nani, and who is one of those grandmothers who has an opinion about absolutely everything and isn't even slightly shy about sharing it. Nani had opinions about the weather, about the neighbors, about the way Rahul parted his hair, about the temperature of tea, and especially about the fact that Rahul had spent eight years being sad and needed, in Nani's expert opinion, to cheer up immediately.

On little Anjali's eighth birthday, she opens the eighth and final letter from her mother. And in that letter, Tina says the most important thing. She says that she wants Rahul to be happy. She says that there is someone out there who loved him in a way that was quiet and steady and true. She says her name.

Anjali.

The big Anjali. The one with the braids and the basketball and the chicken-flap handshake.

And so little Anjali, being eight years old and therefore completely confident that she can fix absolutely anything, decides that she is going to find this person and bring her father's smile back. Not the polite smile he used at dinner or the tired smile he used when Nani lectured him about vegetables. The real one. The loud, floppy-hair, samosa-at-the-canteen smile.

What follows is one of the greatest friendship missions ever undertaken by a determined eight-year-old.

Little Anjali does some detective work, which mostly involves asking a lot of questions, making several very serious lists in a notebook with a duck on the cover, and recruiting her grandmother who is THRILLED to be involved and immediately starts referring to the whole thing as Operation Bring Papa Joy, which little Anjali thinks is a bit dramatic but also kind of perfect.

They discover that big Anjali — our Anjali, cap-wearing, braid-swinging Anjali — is now a sports teacher at a summer camp. A summer camp that, by extraordinary coincidence, little Anjali could attend.

Pack the bags, says little Anjali.
Finally, says Nani.
What is happening, says Rahul, who has somehow agreed to all of this without fully understanding any of it.

At camp, little Anjali spots big Anjali immediately. And she feels it right away — that particular warmth you feel around people who are genuinely good. Big Anjali is wonderful with the children. She's funny and patient and still wears a cap and her braids are still magnificent and she still has that laugh that fills up a whole room.

They become friends almost instantly, the little one and the big one. And little Anjali thinks, oh yes. This is right. This is exactly right.

But there is a complication. Of course there is. What is a good story without a complication?

The complication's name is Aman. Aman, you remember — the cheerful, sweet, mango-juice-energy boy from college? Well, Aman had never quite forgotten big Anjali. He had admired her from a distance at college, never quite brave enough to say anything because she and Rahul had been so thoroughly, completely best friends that it felt like trying to walk between two magnets. But time had passed and things had changed and now Aman was here at this camp and he was grown-up and kind and he was absolutely certain that big Anjali was the most wonderful person he had ever met.

He started leaving little notes for her. He learned that she liked a very specific kind of chai — extra ginger, no sugar — and started making sure there was always a cup ready for her. He was genuinely, sweetly devoted to making her smile.

And big Anjali? She thought Aman was lovely. Truly lovely. He made her feel seen and cared for in a way that she hadn't let herself feel in a long time.

And then Rahul arrived to drop little Anjali off properly at camp.

And time did that thing it sometimes does where it seems to pause for a moment and hold its breath.

Rahul saw Anjali.

Anjali saw Rahul.

And something that had been very quietly tucked away in both of their hearts for eight long years sort of rustled its wings, like a bird that had been sleeping and suddenly remembered it knew how to fly.

But of course, Rahul being Rahul, he didn't say any of this. He said something completely normal like, "Oh! Hi! You're here!" which is not exactly the stuff of great literature, but it was honest.

And Anjali said, "Hi," and smiled, and immediately went to fetch some extra ginger chai for approximately no reason whatsoever.

The days at camp were full of laughter and old memories and the kind of easy, comfortable conversation that you can only have with someone who already knows you — not the shiny polished version of you, but the real one, the one with the embarrassing habits and the too-loud laugh and the ability to eat four samosas in under three minutes.

Little Anjali watched all of this with the intense focus of someone who has a very important mission. She also watched Aman, who was watching Anjali and Rahul with an expression that slowly changed from cheerful to thoughtful to something a little bit like someone who has just realized the puzzle has more pieces than they expected.

Here is what I love most about Aman. When he understood, really understood, what was happening — when he saw the way Rahul looked at Anjali and the way Anjali's braids swung a little lighter when Rahul made her laugh — he didn't stomp his foot. He didn't plot anything ridiculous. He didn't put on sunglasses and sulk dramatically like a certain other person we know. He sat very quietly for a while and felt his feelings properly, which is a very grown-up and respectable thing to do, and then he got up and he smiled, because he was a genuinely good person, and good people want the people they care about to be happy even when it's hard.

And so one evening, as the sun dipped low and turned the whole camp the color of a perfectly ripe mango, Rahul said the things he should have said a very long time ago. He said that she was his favorite person. He said that he'd been walking through the last eight years carrying something he couldn't name and he thought perhaps it was the missing shape of her laugh in his days. He wasn't particularly smooth about it. He fumbled over his words a bit and went slightly red in the face and at one point said "what I mean is, um" three times in a row.

But Anjali didn't need smooth. Anjali had always known him exactly as he was.

And she smiled the smile that she had kept tucked away for a very long time, and said yes.

Little Anjali, watching from behind a conveniently placed bush with Nani — who had somehow appeared at camp at exactly this moment because Nani has a sixth sense for important events and also had taken a very fast train — pumped her fist so hard she nearly fell into the bush entirely.

"Operation Bring Papa Joy," whispered Nani triumphantly.

"Nani," whispered little Anjali, "you can not keep calling it that."

"I absolutely can," said Nani.

And so, my love, that is the story of how a best friendship — the truest, most patient, most generous kind — found its way back to itself. It's a story about how love isn't always loud. Sometimes it's quiet and steady and it waits, and it roots for you even when it hurts, because that's what real love does.

And somewhere, in a little letter in a little box, a mother smiled.

Now close your eyes. Let the story settle around you like a warm blanket. Think about your favourite person — the one whose laugh makes everything feel better. Hold that thought close.

Everything good is worth waiting for.

Goodnight, my darling. Sleep tight.

Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets up nice and cozy, and let me tell you a wonderful story about a little village, a very silly man, and the most exciting cricket match that ever, ever happened in the whole wide world. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in a beautiful village called Champaner, tucked away in the sunny hills of India, there lived a cheerful young man named Bhuvan. Bhuvan had the biggest smile you ever saw, hair that was always a little messy, and a heart so full of courage it could barely fit in his chest. He loved his village more than anything. He loved the people, the little houses, the dusty fields, and even the stubborn old ox who refused to walk in a straight line.

Now, the village of Champaner had a little problem. Well, actually a rather big problem. There was a man called Captain Russell who lived in a fancy fort nearby and thought he was terribly, terribly important. Captain Russell wore a stiff uniform, had a moustache that curled up at the ends like two little snails, and he walked around with his nose so high in the air that he probably couldn't even see his own boots. Can you believe that?

Captain Russell had decided that the villagers had to pay something called lagaan. Lagaan was like a big pile of grain that the villagers had to hand over every single year. And that year, because the rains hadn't come and the crops were sad and droopy, the villagers were having an enormously hard time. Bhuvan went to the Captain and very politely said, please sir, could we perhaps not pay the lagaan this year? Our tummies are rather empty already.

And do you know what Captain Russell did? He twirled his silly moustache, puffed up his chest like a big pompous pigeon, and said no. Not only no, but he said the villagers would have to pay DOUBLE the lagaan. Double! Oh, he was so very pleased with himself about that. He even did a little self-satisfied chuckle. He was not a very nice man, but he was also not a very smart one, which is important to remember.

But then, oh but then, Captain Russell had another idea. He pointed out to the cricket field behind his fort and he said, I'll tell you what. My soldiers and I will play a cricket match against your little village. If you win, nobody in the whole region pays any lagaan for three whole years. Three whole years! But if you lose, you pay three times the lagaan. Three times!

The whole village gasped. The old men shook their heads. The aunties looked worried. Nobody in Champaner had ever even played cricket before. They didn't even know what cricket was! It was a game the British soldiers played with a bat and a ball, and it looked very confusing and very difficult.

Everyone told Bhuvan, no no no, don't agree to this, it's a terrible idea. But Bhuvan looked at his village, looked at his friends, looked at the sad hungry faces around him, and he thought, we can do this. We just have to learn. And so, with the biggest grin on his face, he shook Captain Russell's hand and said yes.

Guess what happened next! Captain Russell went back to his fort laughing and laughing, because he thought it was the funniest thing in the world that a bunch of farmers wanted to play cricket against his trained soldiers. His assistant kept nervously adjusting his hat. His soldiers slapped each other on the back. Oh, they thought they had already won.

But Bhuvan got to work straight away.

First he needed a team. Now gathering a team was not the easiest thing, because the people of Champaner were all quite different. There was Deva, who was tall and strong and could throw anything very very far. There was Guran, who was a little clumsy but absolutely full of enthusiasm, and every time he tried to catch the ball he would spin around twice and fall over, but he kept getting right back up with a big laugh. There was a man called Bagha who never said much but had the most extraordinary aim you have ever seen. There was Lakha, who was a bit of a grumbler and whose eyebrows always seemed to be in a bad mood, but he could run quite fast when he wanted to.

And then, in a lovely twist, there was a girl called Gauri, Bhuvan's best friend from childhood, who was absolutely the most enthusiastic supporter the team had ever had. She cheered so loudly at every single practice that the birds flew off the trees in surprise. She brought everyone water and snacks and made sure nobody gave up when things got hard. She was the heart of the whole team, really.

And here is something rather wonderful. Captain Russell had a sister called Elizabeth, who had come to visit. Now Elizabeth was nothing like her brother. She was kind and gentle and she thought her brother's moustache was honestly a bit ridiculous too. When she saw how hard the villagers were working and how much they cared about their home, she wanted to help. She became a great friend to Bhuvan and the team, and she taught them the rules of cricket, drawing little diagrams in the dirt and explaining things very patiently while Guran kept asking the same question over and over again and she answered it every single time with a smile.

So the team practiced and practiced and practiced. They practiced in the morning when the sun was just waking up. They practiced in the evening when the fireflies came out. There were days when the ball went completely the wrong way and bonked someone on the head and everyone would dissolve into giggles. There were days when they felt tired and wondered if it was all too hard. But then Bhuvan would do that big bright smile of his and say, come on, one more time, and they would all pick themselves up and try again.

Captain Russell, meanwhile, was absolutely not worried. He was too busy admiring himself in the mirror and telling his soldiers how brilliant they were. His soldiers were actually quite good at cricket, which made things tricky. But you know what? The villagers had something the soldiers didn't have. They were playing for their home. They were playing for their families. They were playing for every hungry tummy and every tired face in Champaner, and that made them brave in a way that's very hard to practice.

Finally, the great big day arrived. Oh, the match was three whole days long! All the villagers came and sat in the sunshine. Some brought little flags. Some brought snacks. The aunties had made enormous amounts of food. There was cheering and gasping and holding of breath.

The soldiers batted first and they were very good indeed, and for a while it looked quite scary, except nobody was actually scared because Guran kept doing his funny little stumble every time he got excited and it was very hard to feel scared when Guran was around.

Then it was Champaner's turn. And oh, there were some brilliant moments and some heart-in-your-mouth moments. At one point Bhuvan hit the ball so hard it went sailing through the air like a little comet and everyone screamed with joy. At another point the whole team huddled together and Bhuvan said, we've got this, and you could feel the love they all had for each other just shimmering in the air.

Captain Russell kept making faces from the sidelines. His moustache twitched with irritation. He tried all his cleverest tricks. His best bowler bowled the trickiest balls. But the villagers had practiced so very hard and they knew each other so well and they trusted each other completely.

And then, on the very last ball of the very last day, with the whole crowd holding their breath so tightly that not a single person was breathing, Bhuvan stood there with his bat, and he looked at the ball coming toward him, and he swung with everything he had, and CRACK, off it went, soaring up into the blue sky, and it landed way, way out beyond the field, and everyone erupted. Jumping, hugging, crying, laughing, spinning around in circles. Even the grumpy-eyebrowed Lakha had tears running down his face. Guran fell over twice from sheer happiness.

Champaner had won.

Captain Russell stood there with his mouth hanging open like a fish, and his moustache drooped, and his assistant had to remind him to close his mouth. Then Captain Russell had to do the most difficult thing he had ever done in his very pompous life. He had to admit that the village had won, fair and square. He looked as though he had swallowed something sour. Then he turned around and marched back to his fort, and his snail-curl moustache never looked quite so confident again.

And for three whole years, not a single person in the whole region had to pay any lagaan. The rains came back, the crops grew tall and golden, and the village of Champaner was happy and full and grateful. They told the story of that cricket match to their children, and their children told it to their children, and it became the most wonderful legend of the most wonderful village that ever there was.

So you see, little ones, it doesn't matter if something seems impossible or too hard or too big. If you have good friends beside you, and you're brave enough to try, and you get back up every single time you fall down, just like Guran always did, then anything, anything at all, can happen.

Now close your eyes, my darlings. Let the warm feeling of that big cheering crowd carry you off to sleep. Dream of sunny fields and good friends and the sound of a cricket bat going crack against a ball and sailing up, up, up into the big beautiful sky.

Goodnight, little ones. Goodnight.

Once upon a time, in a tiny little village in India, there lived a boy named Bhuvan. Bhuvan had the biggest smile you ever saw, and he loved two things more than anything in the whole world. He loved his village, and he loved playing cricket with his friends.

Now the village was a happy place, full of laughing people and little mud houses and mango trees and fluffy little goats going baaaa in the morning. But there was a big problem. A very, very big problem.

The problem had a silly moustache.

His name was Captain Russell. He was the boss of the big fort on the hill, and oh my goodness, he was SO full of himself. He walked around with his chest puffed out like a pigeon who thought he was a peacock. His hat was too big. His voice was too loud. And he had a moustache that curled up at the ends like two little sleeping caterpillars on his face.

Now Captain Russell had decided that the villagers had to pay something called lagaan. That means tax, little one. It means giving away some of your food and grain to someone else. And the harvest had been very bad that year because the rain hadn't come. So the poor villagers had nothing extra to give.

Bhuvan went up to Captain Russell one day, very bravely, and said, please sir, we have no food to spare. Can you please not make us pay?

And do you know what Captain Russell did? He twirled his silly caterpillar moustache and he said, I'll make you a deal. If your little village team can beat my team at cricket, you won't have to pay lagaan for three whole years!

Now here was the funny thing. Bhuvan had never actually played a proper cricket match before. None of his friends had! But Bhuvan was brave and bold and he said YES! We will play!

All the villagers went a little wobbly at the knees when they heard that.

But Bhuvan just smiled his big smile and said, don't worry friends. We are going to learn. We are going to practise. And we are going to win.

Now Captain Russell had a sister named Elizabeth, and she was nothing like her grumpy brother at all. She had a kind heart and she thought her brother was being very unfair. So she decided to do something wonderful. She went to the village and she became friends with everyone there, and she helped teach them cricket! She showed them how to hold the bat, how to bowl the ball, how to catch and run and duck and cheer. She was a truly good friend, and the whole village loved her for it.

So every single day, Bhuvan and his friends practised and practised. There was big strong Deva who could bowl the ball so fast it made a whooshing sound. There was tiny little Tipu who was SO quick running between the wickets. There was Kachra, who had a wobbly arm, and everyone thought he couldn't play, but Bhuvan said oh yes he can, and guess what, that wobbly arm made the ball spin in the most surprising ways. Nobody could figure out where it was going! Not even Kachra himself sometimes.

They practised in the sunshine. They practised in the dust. They fell down and they got back up. They laughed and they tried again and again and again.

And then the big day came.

Oh little one, you should have seen it. The whole village came to watch. People came from all the other villages too. Everyone sat together and the sky was big and blue and beautiful.

Captain Russell's team looked very impressive in their crispy white uniforms. Captain Russell himself stood there twirling his moustache, looking terribly pleased with himself.

Bhuvan just looked at his friends, and his friends looked at Bhuvan, and they all smiled. They were ready.

The match went on for three whole days. Three whole days! Up and down, back and forth, sometimes Bhuvan's team was doing wonderfully and everyone cheered, and sometimes Captain Russell's team was winning and everyone held their breath. But Bhuvan never stopped believing. Not for one single second.

And then, at the very very end, with everyone holding their breath and squeezing each other's hands, Bhuvan hit the ball. He hit it so hard and so high that it sailed up up up into the big blue sky like a little bird flying away. And it landed so far away that they won the runs they needed.

They won! They actually won!

The whole crowd burst into the most wonderful cheering you ever heard in your life. People were jumping and dancing and hugging each other and laughing and crying happy tears all at the same time.

And then, something magical happened. The clouds which had been very shy for a very long time, suddenly decided to come out. And it began to rain. Cool, soft, beautiful rain. Right there on the cricket field. Everyone lifted their faces up to the sky and laughed and danced in the rain together.

Captain Russell went home very grumpy indeed, his caterpillar moustache all droopy and wet. But nobody was thinking about him anymore.

Bhuvan and his friends and his village had done it together. They had been brave together. They had tried together. And they had won together.

Because that's what happens little one, when you believe in your friends and you never ever give up.

Now close your eyes, my darling. The rain is falling softly outside. The village is safe and warm and full of happy people. And you, my sweet one, are right here, cozy and loved and safe.

Goodnight now. Sleep tight. I love you so much.
