Alright, snuggle up tight and get those pillows just right, because tonight I have a truly spectacular story for you. This one has brave villagers, a cricket match that changes everything, a bumbling British officer who can't stop twirling his mustache, and one boy who believed in something so hard that the whole world had to listen. Ready? Good. Here we go.

Once upon a time, in the heart of India, nestled between golden fields and a sky so blue it looked painted by hand, there was a little village called Champaner. Now Champaner wasn't famous for anything particularly grand. It didn't have a palace or a marketplace or a fancy fountain. What it had was good, honest people, and fields of crops that they loved and tended to like their own children. And the thing about those fields was that they needed rain. Good, proper, soaking rain that would make the seeds dance underground and push up into tall, swaying stalks of grain.

But this particular year, the rain was being very stubborn. It puffed up its clouds and said, "Not today, thank you," and then floated off somewhere else entirely. The fields were dry. The earth was cracked and thirsty. And the people of Champaner were worried.

Now, here's the part that made everything even trickier. The village of Champaner, like many villages in India at that time, was under the rule of the British Empire. And the British officer in charge of their region was a man named Captain Andrew Russell. Captain Russell was the kind of person who wore his uniform so stiffly that you half expected him to creak when he walked, which he basically did. He had a magnificent mustache that he was extremely, unreasonably proud of, and he spent a great deal of time looking at his own reflection in anything shiny, including his horse's saddle, which tells you quite a lot about him.

Captain Russell had decided, in his infinite and somewhat wobbly wisdom, that the villagers of Champaner needed to pay double taxes this year. Double! As in, twice as much grain as before, even though the rain hadn't come and the harvest was thin as a whisper. The villagers couldn't believe it. How could they pay double when they barely had enough to eat themselves?

Now, in this village lived a young man named Bhuvan. Bhuvan was not a king or a warrior or anyone particularly important, at least not yet. He was just a farmer's son with a wide smile, a stubborn chin, and the kind of energy that made everyone around him either inspired or exhausted, sometimes both at the same time. Bhuvan loved his village and his mother and he also, secretly, loved playing cricket. Just knocking a ball around with a stick, mind you, but he had a gift for it that nobody had quite noticed yet.

One day, Bhuvan went to the British cantonment, which was a grand and slightly ridiculous compound where the British officers lived with their flags and their fancy furniture that looked very out of place in the middle of dusty India. He went to speak up for his village, to ask Captain Russell to please, please cancel the taxes or at least reduce them, since the harvest had been so poor.

Captain Russell came out of his office, mustache bristling, eyes narrowed, and looked at Bhuvan the way a cat looks at a particularly annoying fly. He said absolutely not, he would not cancel the taxes, and furthermore, the villagers were lazy and needed to be taught a lesson.

Bhuvan, to his credit, did not say anything rude. But his eyes flashed, and something lit up inside him like a lamp being turned on, and that was the moment everything changed.

Because just then, through a strange twist of the afternoon, Bhuvan ended up watching the British soldiers playing cricket on their manicured little pitch. And Captain Russell, who fancied himself quite the cricket genius, sneered at Bhuvan and said something along the lines of, you Indians couldn't possibly understand a sport this sophisticated, and quite frankly your people are too simple to ever play it properly.

Now, that was a very silly thing to say.

Bhuvan watched the game with bright, clever eyes, and something clicked in his brain the way a key clicks in a lock. He turned to Captain Russell and made a proposal. He said, why don't we have a match? The village of Champaner against your British team. If we win, you cancel our taxes not just for this year, but for three whole years. And if you win, we'll pay triple.

Triple.

The whole cantonment went quiet. Captain Russell's mustache quivered. His junior officers looked at each other with big round eyes. And then Russell laughed, a big booming laugh that bounced off the walls, because he thought this was the funniest, most ridiculous thing he had ever heard.

He said yes.

And that, my dear sleepy ones, is when the real adventure began.

Bhuvan walked back to Champaner feeling about ten feet tall and also slightly terrified, because of course he had just agreed to something completely enormous on behalf of everyone without actually asking anyone first. When he told the villagers what he had done, the reaction was, let's say, mixed. Some people were furious. Some people were panicking. Old Uncle Bhura, who was grumpy about everything on a good day, looked like he might actually float away on a cloud of outrage.

But Bhuvan stood in the middle of the village square and talked to them all. He said, look, we're already struggling. We've already got nothing to lose but a little pride and some sweat. But what if we win? What if we actually do this? What if we show them that we are not small, that we are not nothing, that this village of ours is worth fighting for?

And slowly, one by one, like flowers turning toward the sun, the villagers began to nod.

But here was the delicious problem. None of them actually knew how to play cricket.

Not properly. Not the real rules. Not the bowling and the batting and the fielding and the wickets and all the complicated bits in between. They were farmers and weavers and potters, not sportsmen. They had their hands and their hearts and their willingness to try, and right now, that was going to have to be enough.

Help, however, came from a surprising direction.

Captain Russell had a younger sister named Elizabeth, who was visiting the cantonment. Now Elizabeth was nothing at all like her brother. Where he was pompous, she was kind. Where he was loud, she was thoughtful. And she thought what her brother was doing to these villagers was deeply, thoroughly unfair. So she made a decision. She decided to help.

Elizabeth found her way to Champaner and introduced herself, and what followed was one of the loveliest friendships you could imagine. She couldn't speak much Hindi, and the villagers couldn't speak much English, but she knew cricket better than almost anyone because she'd grown up watching the soldiers practice, and she taught them everything. Through gestures and demonstrations and a great deal of enthusiastic arm-waving and laughter, she taught them how to hold a bat, how to bowl, how to field, how to run between the wickets without bumping into each other, which took quite a lot of practice.

The children of the village adored her. They called her Lizzie and brought her flowers and she helped everyone remember which direction was which, because in the beginning, some people were running toward entirely the wrong end of the pitch and nobody could figure out why.

Now, Bhuvan was building his team, and this is my favorite part of the story because look at who ended up on it. There was Guran, who had only one arm but could field like a lightning bolt. There was Deva, a big quiet man who turned out to have a bowling arm like a catapult. There was Kachra, a young man with a differently shaped hand that everyone had rather unkindly ignored, but whose spinning ball turned out to be completely unplayable, twisting through the air in ways that made batsmen look utterly confused and slightly offended.

And there was Lakha. Now, Lakha is complicated, because at first, he said no to the team. He stomped around saying it was impossible and foolish. But the truth was, Lakha had made a secret, shameful deal with Captain Russell, who had promised him some grain and a bit of extra comfort if Lakha would spy on the team and make things go wrong. Captain Russell thought this was very clever. It was not, in fact, very clever. It was the sort of plan that only looks clever if you have never met the kind of people who live in small villages and love each other fiercely.

Because eventually, standing there at practice, watching his neighbors throw themselves onto the ground to stop a ball, watching Bhuvan encourage everyone with that enormous smile, watching children cheer and old men laugh and Elizabeth teach and Kachra bowl people out with his magic spinning deliveries, Lakha felt something shift inside his chest. Something warm and a little bit ashamed.

He came to Bhuvan quietly one evening and he confessed everything. He told him what he'd done, what he'd promised. And he waited, probably terrified, for Bhuvan to be furious.

Bhuvan was quiet for a long moment.

And then he said, join the team properly. No more secrets. Just play with us.

And Lakha's eyes filled up with relief the way a cup fills with water, and he joined the team, and he played with everything he had.

Meanwhile, Captain Russell was busy being magnificently overconfident. He polished his cricket whites. He practiced his victory speech. He told everyone at the cantonment that this match was basically already won and could someone please prepare a rather nice dinner for afterward because he intended to celebrate. His officers nodded and smiled and quietly thought their captain was perhaps getting ahead of himself.

The day of the match arrived.

Oh, I wish you could have seen Champaner that morning. Every single person in the village was up before the sun, dressed in their finest clothes, faces bright with nerves and excitement and pride. The match was to be played over three days, which in cricket is actually quite normal, because cricket is a sport that understands that good things take time.

Now, the British team was genuinely very good. They had trained soldiers, men who had played all their lives, a bowler so fast his ball was practically invisible. The first day did not go brilliantly for Champaner. Balls zoomed past bats. Wickets tumbled. Captain Russell strutted around like a particularly pleased peacock. His mustache was basically vibrating with smugness.

But Bhuvan held the team together. During the breaks, he sat with each person and talked to them, quietly and warmly. He reminded Guran of his incredible throwing arm. He reminded Kachra that his spin bowling was magic. He made each person feel like they were exactly the right person in exactly the right place, which is one of the most powerful things any leader can do.

And on the second day, Champaner began to find their rhythm.

It happened slowly, like music finding its tune. Bhuvan batted beautifully, reading the bowlers with those sharp eyes of his, sending the ball to all corners of the ground. The crowd of villagers watching erupted every time he hit, leaping to their feet and hollering with joy. Elizabeth cheered too, sitting among them, entirely on their side, which made her brother so grumpy that his mustache drooped to one side, which was quite something to see.

Kachra came in to bowl and Captain Russell's team simply could not figure him out. The ball would leave his hand and then do something strange and unexpected and bamboozling in the air, and the batsmen would swing hopefully and miss completely, looking very confused and a little embarrassed. One by one, wickets fell. The crowd went absolutely wild.

Russell kept fiddling with his lineup. He kept changing tactics. He kept having long, flustered conversations with his officers. But nothing seemed to work, and he was getting redder and more flustered by the hour, which some of the village children found very funny indeed.

On the third and final day, everything came down to the last few balls. Champaner needed just a handful of runs. The British team needed just one more wicket. The whole crowd was so quiet you could hear the wind moving through the dry grass.

Bhuvan stood at the crease. He took a deep breath.

He looked at his team behind him. He looked at his village watching, every face he had known all his life. He looked at the dry, parched fields in the distance that needed rain and needed time and needed this moment to be a beginning.

He faced the ball.

And he hit it. He hit it so cleanly, so perfectly, that it sailed over the boundary with the most satisfying sound in the world, and the crowd exploded. Not just polite applause. Absolute, joyful, hat-throwing, jumping-up-and-down, laughing-and-crying explosion of happiness. Elizabeth jumped up too and cheered louder than anyone.

Champaner had won.

Captain Russell stood in the middle of the pitch, mouth slightly open, mustache completely flat, looking like a man who cannot find his umbrella and it is raining. He had to cancel the taxes. Three whole years. He tried to maintain his dignity as he signed the papers, but his pen kept slipping and his hand was quite shaky, and he kept glaring at his mustache in the reflection of his pocket watch as if somehow it was to blame.

And then, as if the sky itself had been waiting for exactly this moment, the clouds rolled in.

Big, beautiful, heavy, wonderful clouds, dark and full and generous. And the rain came down on Champaner like a gift, like an answer, like the world saying, yes, you did it, here you go, here is everything you needed.

The villagers ran out into the rain and turned their faces up and laughed. The children spun in circles. Old Uncle Bhura, who complained about everything, actually smiled, which was possibly the most shocking thing that happened all day. Bhuvan stood in the rain and felt it soak into his hair and run down his face and he thought about his village and his neighbors and this ridiculous, impossible, wonderful thing they had all done together.

And that, my darlings, is where we leave them.

Happy and soaked to the bone and free.

The fields of Champaner would grow green again. The harvest would come back. The people would have three good years to breathe and rest and save and sing. And whenever any of them felt small or hopeless or like their voice didn't matter, they would remember the day they picked up cricket bats they barely knew how to hold, and they played, and they won, because they believed in each other.

Now, the stars outside are getting all soft and sleepy. The crickets are singing their own little night songs. And you, my brave and lovely ones, have a whole day of adventures waiting for you tomorrow, which means you absolutely need to rest.

Close your eyes. Let the story settle around you like a warm blanket. Dream of green fields and red cricket balls and rain falling on grateful earth.

Goodnight.

tzp.6-8:
Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets up nice and cozy, and let me tell you a really really special story tonight. This one is about a little boy who saw the whole world differently from everyone else, and how he found someone who finally understood him. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, in a busy, bustling city in India, there lived a boy named Ishaan. Now Ishaan was eight years old, just about your age actually, and he was absolutely, completely, one hundred percent magnificent. He had the most wonderful imagination you could ever dream of. When he walked to school in the morning, he didn't just see a puddle on the road. Oh no no no. He saw a shimmering ocean full of tiny fish and golden bubbles. When he looked up at the sky, he didn't just see clouds. He saw elephants and dragons and castles made of fluff. Can you believe that? What a brain this kid had!

But here's the thing. School was really really hard for Ishaan. Not because he wasn't smart, oh he was SO smart, but because the letters and numbers on the page did the most peculiar thing. They jumped around! They flipped and swirled and danced like they were having a little party right there on the paper, and by the time they stopped dancing, Ishaan had no idea what they said anymore. So when his teacher asked him to read aloud, the words came out all mixed up and muddled, and the other kids would giggle, and Ishaan would feel his tummy go all tight and his face go all hot.

His teachers at school were, well, let's just say they were not exactly the most understanding bunch. There was one teacher in particular, Mr. Grumbleface, and that wasn't actually his name but it should have been, because he always looked like he'd just bitten into a very sour lemon. He would tap his stick on the desk and boom in his big boomy voice, "Ishaan! Pay attention! Stop dreaming! Read the board!" And poor Ishaan would stare at the board and the letters would just wiggle and wink at him like naughty little gremlins. It wasn't funny for Ishaan, even though those letters were being quite ridiculous.

At home, Ishaan's older brother Yohaan was brilliant at everything. Top marks, trophies on the shelf, the whole lot. And Ishaan loved his brother, he really did, but sometimes it felt like everyone kept pointing at Yohaan's trophies and then looking at Ishaan's crumpled, scribble-covered homework and sighing the biggest, longest sighs you ever heard.

Ishaan's papa was a very hardworking man who really truly loved his sons, but he got so worried about Ishaan's school marks that he made a very hard decision. He decided to send Ishaan to a boarding school, far away from home. A place where Ishaan would have to stay and sleep and eat, away from his mama's warm hugs and his dog and his paints and everything he loved. Oh, little ones, I know, I know. It makes your heart squeeze a little bit doesn't it?

So Ishaan went to this new school, and at first it was SO hard. The teachers there were even more serious, walking around with their chests all puffed up like little pigeons who thought they were very important eagles. The classrooms were strict and silent and everything felt grey and cold. Ishaan stopped painting. He stopped imagining fish in puddles. He just sort of... went quiet inside.

But THEN. Oh, but then! Guess what happened next!

A new art teacher arrived at the school, and this teacher was like no one Ishaan had ever met before. His name was Ram Shankar Nikumbh, but everyone called him Nikumbh Sir, and honestly he deserved about ten thousand gold stars just for walking into that building. He came in on his very first day, not with a grumpy face or a stick to tap on desks, but with colours and music and a big bright smile that made the whole classroom feel warmer somehow.

Nikumbh Sir taught art like it was the most joyful, wonderful, spectacular thing in the whole universe. He let children splatter paint. He let them draw funny wonky faces. He told them that mistakes were just happy accidents in disguise. The other children absolutely loved him immediately.

But Nikumbh Sir noticed something. He noticed that one little boy in the corner wasn't smiling. One little boy was sitting very still and very sad, like a lamp that had forgotten it could glow. And that boy was Ishaan.

Now Nikumbh Sir was very clever and very kind, and he didn't make a big fuss or draw attention to Ishaan in front of everyone. Instead he quietly, gently started paying attention. He looked at Ishaan's old notebooks, the ones all covered in doodles and drawings, the most incredible drawings, dragons and fish and whole entire worlds drawn in the margins. He looked at how Ishaan read. He watched how the letters confused him. And slowly, slowly, a thought began to bloom in Nikumbh Sir's heart like a little flower opening up.

He understood. He actually truly understood what was happening with Ishaan.

You see, Ishaan had something called dyslexia. Now that's a big word for bedtime, I know, but it just means that Ishaan's brilliant brain was wired in a special, different way. The part that dealt with letters and reading worked differently, which made reading really hard. But the part that dealt with creativity and art and seeing the beauty in the world? Oh that part worked in the most extraordinarily spectacular fashion you can possibly imagine.

Nikumbh Sir knew all about this because when he was a little boy, the very same thing had happened to him! He too had seen letters dance and wiggle. He too had felt confused and silly in class when he was anything but silly. So he knew, he just KNEW, that Ishaan was not careless or lazy or naughty. Ishaan was magnificent. Ishaan just needed someone to help him learn in a different way.

So Nikumbh Sir became Ishaan's very special friend and helper. Every day he would sit with Ishaan and they would practice letters together, but in the most fun ways you can imagine. They made letters out of clay! Squishy, squashy, colourful clay letters that Ishaan could feel with his fingers. They traced letters in sand, all swooshy and smooth. They played games with sounds and rhymes. And slowly, oh so slowly, like watching a little seedling push up through the soil, things started to make sense for Ishaan. The letters stopped doing their naughty little dances quite so much.

And Ishaan started to glow again.

He started painting again, and oh my goodness, the paintings that came out of that boy were like sunrise and thunderstorm and rainbow all mixed together into something breathtaking. Nikumbh Sir showed everyone. He put Ishaan's work on the walls. He told anyone who would listen that this child had a gift that was rare and precious and should be celebrated.

Now Nikumbh Sir had a marvellous idea. He organised a big art competition at the school, where all the children AND all the teachers would compete to paint their very best picture. The puffed-up pigeon teachers thought this was absolutely absurd, they huffed and they puffed and one of them knocked over an entire bucket of yellow paint trying to prove he was a serious artist, which was quite funny actually. But they all joined in because Nikumbh Sir was very enthusiastic and also because yellow paint was now everywhere and things had sort of already started.

And when all the paintings were hung up and everyone walked around looking at them, there was one painting that made everyone stop. Made everyone go completely quiet. It was warm and swirling and full of life and wonder. It was painted by Ishaan Awasthi, age eight.

He won. Of course he did.

And when Ishaan's parents came to see the painting, when his papa looked at what his son had created, something shifted in his chest. He finally saw. He saw his wonderful, brilliant, different, glorious little boy. And Ishaan ran to his parents and they hugged him so tight, the kind of hug that fills you up all the way to the very top.

Ishaan still had to work hard at reading and writing. That didn't just disappear overnight like magic, because real life doesn't always work like a magic trick. But now he had help, and he had someone who believed in him, and most importantly he knew something true and important about himself. That being different wasn't something broken that needed fixing. It was something special that needed understanding.

And Nikumbh Sir and Ishaan stayed the very best of friends for a long long time, painting the world in colours that nobody else could quite see.

So you see, little ones, everyone's brain is its own special kind of wonderful. Some brains love numbers, some brains love music, some brains love words, and some brains love to look at a puddle and see an entire ocean. And every single one of those brains deserves a Nikumbh Sir, someone who looks at them and says, I see you, I understand you, and you are extraordinary.

Now your eyes are getting heavy, aren't they. I can see that. Those little eyelids are fluttering just like butterfly wings getting ready to rest. Let your arms go soft, and your toes go warm under that blanket, and as you drift off to sleep tonight, maybe you'll dream in the most beautiful swirling colours. Maybe you'll dream of fish in puddles and dragons in clouds and a little boy who learned that his light was always there, just waiting for someone kind enough to help it shine.

Goodnight, my darlings. Sleep tight. You are, every single one of you, magnificent.
tzp.3-5:
Okay little one, snuggle up tight. Pull that blanket all the way up to your chin. That's it. Are you cozy? Good. Because I have a very, very special story for you tonight. It's about a little boy named Ishaan.

Ishaan was eight years old. And Ishaan saw the world in the most magical way.

When other kids looked at a puddle, they just saw water. But Ishaan? He saw a whole universe of colors dancing around. Blues and greens and golds all swirling together like a painting come to life. When he walked to school, he stopped to watch a little duck waddling down the street. He stopped to look at a butterfly sitting on a red flower. He stopped to look at everything, because everything was so beautiful and interesting to him.

Ishaan loved to paint. He loved colors. He loved fish and dogs and mud and the sky. He loved so many things.

But school was very, very hard for Ishaan.

The letters on the page did something funny. They wiggled. They jumped around. They flipped upside down. When Ishaan tried to read the word "cat," the letters would do a little dance and end up looking like "tac" or "act" or something else entirely. It wasn't Ishaan being silly. His brain just worked in a very special, different way.

His teacher at school was called Mr. Grumps. Well, that wasn't really his name. But he was very grumpy! He had a big bushy mustache that wiggled when he talked. And he would say, in his big grumpy voice, "Ishaan! Pay attention! Ishaan! Why can't you read this simple word?" And his mustache would wiggle left and right and Ishaan would just stare at it because honestly, it was very funny looking.

But even though the mustache was funny, Ishaan started to feel sad. He started to feel like maybe he wasn't smart. Like maybe something was wrong with him. And that made his heart feel heavy, like a little stone sitting in his chest.

His parents were worried too. They didn't know how to help. So they decided to send Ishaan to a boarding school. A school where he would stay and sleep and eat, away from home.

And oh, little one, that first night away from home, Ishaan cried. He missed his mama. He missed his papa. He missed his big brother. He missed his dog. He missed his own pillow. Everything felt big and scary and strange.

The new school had new grumpy teachers too. They also said "Pay attention, Ishaan!" Their mustaches wiggled just like Mr. Grumps. Some of them didn't have mustaches, but they still made very grumpy faces. And poor Ishaan, he stopped painting. He stopped looking at puddles. That little light inside him went very quiet.

But then.

Oh, but THEN.

A new teacher arrived. His name was Ram Shankar Nikumbh. But everyone called him Nikumbh Sir. And Nikumbh Sir was absolutely, completely, wonderfully different from every other teacher Ishaan had ever seen.

He came bouncing into class one day with a big smile and bright eyes. He didn't carry a big heavy stick like the grumpy teachers. He carried art supplies! And he said, "Hello everyone! Today, we are going to have FUN!"

And all the children looked at each other like, fun? At school? Is that allowed?

Nikumbh Sir noticed right away that Ishaan was sitting very still and very quiet in the corner. That Ishaan wasn't smiling. He could see that something special was hiding inside this little boy. Something that just needed someone to see it.

So Nikumbh Sir started looking at Ishaan's old paintings and drawings. And his eyes went wide. Because they were beautiful. Really truly beautiful. Full of color and life and magic.

And then Nikumbh Sir discovered something important. He realized that Ishaan's brain worked differently. The letters danced for Ishaan. Lots of very brilliant, amazing, wonderful people had the same thing. It had a name. It was called dyslexia. And it didn't mean Ishaan wasn't smart. It meant Ishaan's brain was wired in a magnificent, special, creative way.

Nikumbh Sir sat with Ishaan. Very gently. Very patiently. He taught him little tricks to help the letters stay still. He practiced with him every single day. And slowly, slowly, like the sun coming up in the morning, Ishaan started to understand. The letters stopped dancing quite so much.

And most importantly, Nikumbh Sir told Ishaan, "You are not broken. You are brilliant. Don't you ever forget that."

And that little stone in Ishaan's heart? It melted away.

Ishaan started painting again. Oh, the paintings he made! Everyone stopped and stared because they were so, so lovely. The whole school put up an art show, and Ishaan's paintings made everyone go quiet in the best way. The way you go quiet when something is so beautiful it fills your whole chest up.

And his mama and papa came. And when they saw what their little boy had made, their eyes went all shiny with happy tears. They hugged Ishaan so tight. They understood now. They understood that their boy just needed someone to see him. Really see him.

And Ishaan smiled the biggest smile. That warm, sunshine smile that had been hiding for so long.

Because someone believed in him. And when someone believes in you, little one, you can do anything. Anything at all.

Now. Close your eyes.

You are so very loved. Just exactly as you are. Your brain is wonderful. Your heart is wonderful. YOU are wonderful.

The stars are out now, keeping watch over you.

Drift off to sleep, my darling.

Goodnight.
tzp.9-12:
Alright, snuggle up tight, pull that blanket all the way up, and get those pillows just right, because tonight I'm going to tell you about a boy named Ishaan Awasthi, and I promise you, by the end of this story, you're going to see the whole world just a little bit differently. Ready? Good. Here we go.

Ishaan Awasthi was eight years old, and his head was the most magical place you could ever hope to visit. Seriously, if you could shrink yourself down and take a little tour inside Ishaan's mind, you'd find entire galaxies spinning around up there. You'd find fish that glowed like lanterns, dogs that could talk in three languages, puddles that were secretly doorways to other dimensions, and clouds shaped like every wonderful thing you could possibly imagine. His imagination was so big, so bright, so absolutely bursting at the seams, that it was honestly a wonder his head didn't just float right off his shoulders and drift up into the sky like a balloon.

The only problem was, the world outside Ishaan's head was a very different story.

School, for Ishaan, was like trying to dance in shoes two sizes too small. The letters on the page — oh, those sneaky, slippery letters — they simply refused to stay still. The letter b would wink at him and do a little spin and suddenly become a d. The number 9 would flip itself upside down and giggle as it became a 6. Words would scramble themselves up like they were playing a game, rearranging their letters just to confuse him. While his classmates would look at the word "was" and read "was," Ishaan would look at it and see "saw," and no matter how hard he squeezed his eyes and tried, he just could not make those letters behave themselves.

His teachers, bless their hearts, were not exactly what you'd call patient or understanding. His main teacher, Mr. Patel, was a round little man who wore the same brown jacket every single day and whose mustache twitched like a caterpillar doing yoga every time he was annoyed, which, around Ishaan, was approximately all the time. Mr. Patel had one solution for every problem in the universe, and that solution was: try harder. Bad marks? Try harder. Can't read properly? Try harder. Still can't read? Well, have you considered... trying harder?

Ishaan's other teachers were similarly unhelpful. There was Ms. Shroff, who spoke so fast that her words sounded like a train that had lost its brakes, and Mr. Dubey, who had a habit of sneaking up behind students and clapping loudly right next to their ears, which startled absolutely everyone but seemed to delight him enormously. These teachers looked at Ishaan and saw a lazy, daydreaming, careless boy. They saw someone who wasn't paying attention, who didn't care, who simply wouldn't try.

But that wasn't Ishaan at all. Not even a little bit.

Ishaan cared so much it sometimes made his chest hurt. He tried so hard that by the end of every school day, he felt completely wrung out, like a cloth that had been twisted and squeezed until there was nothing left in it. He just couldn't seem to make the words and numbers do what everyone else could make them do, and nobody could figure out why, and nobody thought to ask, and that made him feel very, very alone.

At home, things weren't much easier. His father, Mr. Awasthi, was a serious, important, briefcase-carrying kind of man who believed very firmly that life was about results. He'd rattle off phrases like "competition" and "future" and "discipline" the way some people rattle off song lyrics. His older brother Yohaan was excellent at everything — sports, studies, making adults smile and nod approvingly — and Ishaan loved his brother very much but also sometimes wished, just a tiny bit, that Yohaan could be bad at something. Just once. Just so Ishaan wouldn't feel so completely on the wrong side of everything.

His mother was the warm, soft center of the family, the one who made everything feel slightly more bearable, the one whose hugs felt like the word "home." She knew something was wrong, she could feel it in her bones, but she didn't know what it was or how to fix it, and that helplessness made her heart ache in a way she couldn't quite put into words.

After Ishaan failed his exams for the third time and got into a particularly spectacular bit of mischief involving a neighbor's laundry, a stray dog, and a paint can that we honestly don't have time to get into right now, his father made a decision. Ishaan was going to boarding school. A strict one. One with rules and schedules and absolutely no nonsense.

Ishaan felt like the ground had been pulled out from under him. The day his parents dropped him off, he stood at those big iron gates and watched their car drive away, and something inside him went very, very quiet. Not a peaceful quiet. The kind of quiet that happens when something beautiful has been turned off.

For weeks, Ishaan moved through the boarding school like a little ghost. He didn't paint, didn't draw, didn't daydream in that wonderful sparkly way he used to. He sat in classes and stared at pages that still mocked him and felt the familiar shame creep up the back of his neck. His marks were terrible. His teachers were every bit as puzzled and impatient as his old ones. He ate his meals quietly. He slept. He woke up. He did it all again.

And then, on an otherwise completely ordinary Tuesday, the art teacher got sick.

Now, the replacement who walked through that classroom door was not an ordinary substitute teacher. Oh no. This was Ram Shankar Nikumbh, and he arrived like a small, cheerful, slightly chaotic weather event. He had a big laugh that took up more space than he did, a bag that seemed to contain approximately everything ever invented, and an energy that made you feel like something good was about to happen even if you couldn't quite say what.

Mr. Nikumbh didn't stand at the front and lecture. He didn't hand out worksheets. He walked around the classroom looking at the students with these bright, curious eyes, like he was seeing each of them for the very first time and finding them absolutely fascinating. He told jokes that made even the most serious students snort unexpectedly. He did impressions of grumpy teachers that were so accurate and so hilarious that the whole class dissolved into helpless laughter.

But here's the thing about Mr. Nikumbh. Underneath all that joy and silliness, he was watching. Noticing. And what he noticed most was the small, quiet boy in the third row who stared out the window with the emptiest eyes he'd ever seen on a child.

That night, after school, Mr. Nikumbh did something no teacher had ever done before. He looked at Ishaan's work. He looked at his marks, his notebooks, his drawings. He held up those notebooks and he really, truly looked at them. Not with a red pen ready to circle mistakes. With actual, genuine, trying-to-understand attention.

And slowly, a light came on in Mr. Nikumbh's eyes.

He recognized it. Because here's a secret that Mr. Nikumbh had never told most people — he had been exactly like Ishaan once. The letters had danced for him too. The numbers had played tricks on his eyes too. He knew what it felt like to sit in a classroom and feel stupid when you weren't stupid at all. He knew what it felt like to have a mind full of starlight when the world only wanted to see report cards.

What Ishaan had was called dyslexia, which is a wonderful, complicated word that basically means his brilliant brain was wired differently from most people's brains. It didn't mean anything was wrong with him. It just meant he saw the world differently, processed it differently, learned differently. And it meant he needed to be taught differently.

Mr. Nikumbh went to work. And let me tell you, this man was creative in ways that made your head spin. He made letters out of clay so Ishaan could feel their shapes with his fingers. He made words into little songs so they'd stick in a different part of Ishaan's memory. He played games and told stories and found a thousand different roads that all led to the same place. He sat with Ishaan every afternoon, just the two of them, working patiently and joyfully, treating every tiny breakthrough like it was something worth celebrating.

Which it was.

The first time Ishaan read a sentence correctly, Mr. Nikumbh did a little dance so embarrassing that Ishaan burst out laughing for the first time in months, and honestly, that laugh was worth more than a thousand gold medals.

Something began to wake up inside Ishaan. Something that had gone to sleep and pulled the covers over its head. He started to draw again, slowly at first, then with more and more confidence. His pictures were extraordinary — full of color and movement and feeling, the kind of art that made you stop and stare and feel things you couldn't quite name. Mr. Nikumbh hung them on the classroom wall, right in the center, where everyone could see them.

Other teachers were skeptical. Mr. Patel, who had transferred to the boarding school around the same time because the universe has a funny sense of timing, looked at Mr. Nikumbh's methods and twitched his caterpillar mustache disapprovingly. He gave a lot of speeches about "proper education" and "standards" that sounded very important and meant very little. But Mr. Nikumbh just smiled cheerfully and carried on, because he'd met a lot of Mr. Patels in his life and he knew that the best response to a Mr. Patel is to simply be so brilliantly effective that they eventually have nothing left to say.

And then came the art competition.

Mr. Nikumbh announced that the whole school would have an art competition, and that every student and every teacher would participate, and the paintings would be judged by the students themselves, fairly and honestly. There was a lot of grumbling from teachers who felt this was undignified, particularly Mr. Dubey, who spent three days complaining that he couldn't possibly be expected to paint while also occasionally sneaking off to practice painting in secret, which Mr. Nikumbh noticed and found absolutely delightful.

The day of the competition came, and the school hall was turned into a gallery. Students and teachers bent over their canvases, brushes flying, tongues sticking out in concentration. The room smelled like paint and possibility.

Ishaan painted.

He forgot everything else. He forgot the letters that danced and the numbers that flipped and the shame that lived in the back of his neck. He just painted, and what came out of him was breathtaking — a swirl of colors and light and feeling that seemed to contain everything he'd ever thought and felt and imagined. Fish glowing like lanterns. A boy floating in a sky full of stars. Colors that looked like they were singing.

When the votes were counted, Ishaan's painting had won. Unanimously. Even Mr. Dubey voted for it, though he coughed and looked at the ceiling when anyone glanced his way.

But the most important moment wasn't the winning. The most important moment was when Ishaan's parents came for the prize-giving ceremony, and his mother saw her son's painting hanging in the center of that hall, enormous and radiant and full of life, and she put her hand over her mouth because she couldn't quite believe it, and her eyes filled up with tears of the best kind.

And Ishaan's father, serious, important, briefcase-carrying Mr. Awasthi, stood in front of his son's painting for a very long time without saying anything. And when he finally turned to look at Ishaan, something in his face had changed. Something had softened and opened up, like a window being pushed outward for the first time in years. He saw his son. Really saw him. Not a boy who was failing, but a boy who had been misunderstood, and who was extraordinary in ways that nobody had taken the time to discover.

He knelt down and hugged Ishaan, and Ishaan, who had been waiting for exactly this without knowing he was waiting for it, hugged him back with everything he had.

Mr. Nikumbh watched from across the room and smiled a small, quiet smile that was entirely different from his big, room-filling laugh. This smile was private. It was the smile of someone who had gone fishing in very still water and found something golden.

Now here's what I want you to think about, just for a moment before you drift off. Ishaan didn't change. His brain didn't change. The letters still danced a little and probably always would. What changed was that someone took the time to understand him. Someone looked at him with patient, curious, generous eyes, and said, "I see something wonderful here. Let me help you show it to everyone else."

Every single person in this world has a thing, some particular, specific, glowing thing that they're extraordinary at, and sometimes that thing is easy to spot, and sometimes it's buried under a pile of report cards and misunderstandings and bad days. But it's always there. Always.

Maybe your thing is painting like Ishaan. Maybe it's making people laugh, or building things, or remembering facts about dinosaurs that make everyone else's heads spin, or listening so well that your friends feel better just by sitting next to you. Whatever it is, it's real, and it matters, and one day — maybe soon, maybe later — the right person will come along and see it shining there, and they'll help you show the whole world.

And if no one has seen it yet, don't worry. Don't you dare give up. Because the people who see the world differently, who see fish where other people see puddles and galaxies where other people see blank walls — those are the people who change everything.

Just like Ishaan.

Now close your eyes. Let the colors drift in, all those wonderful swirling colors. Let the letters rest tonight, they've worked hard enough. Let your magnificent, magical, one-of-a-kind brain go quiet and soft and dreamy.

You're extraordinary, you know. Just exactly as you are.

Goodnight.

dangal.6-8:
Alright, snuggle up little ones, get those blankets nice and cozy, and let me tell you one of my absolute favourite stories. It's about a papa who had the biggest dream, two daughters who were even braver than that dream, and a whole lot of mud. Yes, mud. You'll see why in a minute.

Once upon a time, in a little village in India called Balali, there lived a man named Mahavir. Now Mahavir was not just any man. He was a wrestler! A really, really good wrestler. He had arms like tree trunks and a heart full of fire, and more than anything in the whole wide world, he wanted to win a gold medal for India. Can you imagine? A shiny, glittery gold medal that says you are the best wrestler in the entire world!

But you know what happened? Life got busy, things got in the way, and Mahavir never quite got his gold medal. So he put away his wrestling dreams like an old toy in a box, moved to his little village, got a job, and started his family. And guess what? He had daughters! First came Geeta, then came Babita, and oh, how he loved them.

Now here is where our story gets really fun. One day, Mahavir heard some of the neighbours talking. Apparently, Geeta and Babita had gotten into a little bit of a squabble with some boys from the village. And do you know what those two little girls did? They outsmarted every single one of those boys! They were quick and clever and strong and absolutely nobody could catch them. Mahavir watched with his mouth hanging wide open. I mean really wide open. Like a fish. Can you believe that?

And right then and there, something in his big heart woke up. He thought, wait a moment. Maybe my daughters can win that gold medal. Maybe they can do what I never could!

So the very next morning, very early, when the sun was just peeking over the rooftops and the birds were still yawning, Mahavir woke Geeta and Babita up. The girls blinked and rubbed their eyes. What's happening, Papa, they asked. And Mahavir said, we are going to train! We are going to wrestle!

Now, Geeta and Babita were not exactly thrilled about this. Not even a tiny little bit. They had to wake up before sunrise every single day. They had to run and run and run through the fields. They had to do exercises that made their legs feel like wobbly noodles. They had to eat plain food and no sweets. Oh, the sadness of no sweets! And the worst part of all? They had to cut their long, beautiful hair short so it wouldn't get in the way during practice.

There was a very silly uncle who helped Mahavir with the training. He was a round, cheerful, bumbling sort of fellow who was always tripping over his own feet and saying the wrong thing at the wrong moment. He meant well, truly he did, but he was just wonderfully, hilariously useless most of the time. The girls secretly called him Silly Chachu behind his back, which, honestly, was a perfect name for him.

Geeta and Babita grumbled a lot at first. They really did. But then something magical started to happen. They started getting stronger. They started getting faster. They started winning. First they wrestled the boys in the village, and they won! Then they went to small local competitions, and they won those too! People would come just to watch these two amazing girls from Balali, and the whole crowd would go absolutely bananas cheering for them. Geeta and Babita started walking just a little bit taller.

But here is the really exciting part. Geeta, the older one, was so good that she got selected to go train at the National Sports Academy! A big, fancy place with a big, fancy coach. Papa was so proud he looked like he might burst like a balloon.

Now, the coach at the academy, whose name was Coach Pramod, was very full of himself. He had a big moustache that he twirled constantly and wore a shiny tracksuit and thought he knew absolutely everything about everything. He was the kind of person who talks very loudly in restaurants and tells everyone else they're doing it wrong. You know the type. He decided that everything Mahavir had taught Geeta was old-fashioned and silly and she needed to learn everything completely brand new his way.

Poor Geeta got a little bit confused. She had learned one way from her papa, and now this twirly-moustached coach was telling her a completely different way. She started to forget some of the beautiful tricks her father had taught her. And instead of getting better, she started losing. She would come home to visit and she and Papa would argue because she thought the new way was right and he thought the old way was right and both of them were so stubborn! Oh, it was quite a mess.

Babita, who was watching all of this, would just quietly shake her head and go back to her training. Babita was the sensible one, you see.

Now, Mahavir decided that if the academy wouldn't listen to him, he would simply go there himself and secretly coach Geeta on the side. Every morning before the official training started, Papa and Geeta would meet secretly and work on all the moves that had made her great in the first place. It was like a secret mission! Like spies, but with wrestling moves instead of gadgets.

Coach Pramod found out, because he was always snooping around, and he got very upset. He twirled his moustache so hard he nearly pulled it right off his face. He decided the best thing to do was to lock Mahavir in the equipment storeroom on the day of Geeta's most important match so he couldn't watch or help or cheer. Can you imagine anything more silly? Locking someone in a room full of sports equipment! Papa sat in there surrounded by cricket bats and badminton rackets and just waited patiently, because truly, what else can you do when you're locked in a room full of sports equipment?

And so Geeta had to go to the biggest match of her life, the Commonwealth Games final, completely on her own. No Papa in the stands. Just Geeta, the mat, and the memory of everything he had ever taught her.

Guess what happened next!

Geeta stood on that mat and she took a deep, slow breath. And in her head, she could hear her papa's voice. She could hear him saying, if you get a gold medal, you will be remembered forever. You will be winning not just for yourself, but for every girl who was told she couldn't do it.

And something wonderful happened inside Geeta's heart. All those early mornings, all those running through muddy fields, all those wobbly noodle legs, all those years of hard work, they all came rushing back to her at once like a big warm wave. She remembered every single trick, every single move, every clever little thing her papa had whispered in her ear during their secret morning sessions.

She wrestled like she had never wrestled before. She was quick as a sparrow and strong as a tree and clever as a fox. The crowd was going absolutely bananas again. And when the final whistle blew, Geeta had won! She had won the gold medal! The real, actual, shiny gold medal for India!

Everyone in the arena went completely wild. People were jumping and shouting and crying happy tears all at once. And somewhere in a room full of cricket bats and badminton rackets, Mahavir heard the roar of the crowd and knew, he just knew, that his daughter had done it.

When they finally let him out, and he and Geeta finally saw each other, she ran to him and hugged him so tight. And this big strong man who had wrestled all his life had to wipe his eyes because sometimes even the strongest people cry the happiest tears. He whispered to her, you have made me the proudest papa in the whole world. And Geeta whispered back, I did it for you, Papa. And for every girl like me.

And Coach Pramod? Well, he was so embarrassed about the whole storeroom situation that his moustache actually drooped. He quietly shuffled away and nobody paid him any attention at all, which was honestly the most perfectly fitting ending for him.

Babita went on to become an incredible champion too, just like her sister, because hard work and a big heart are really quite an unstoppable combination.

And the little village of Balali? Oh, they had the biggest, happiest celebration you can possibly imagine. There was music and dancing and I'm quite sure there were sweets, finally, lots and lots of sweets, for everyone.

So you see, little ones, the story of Mahavir and Geeta and Babita is really a story about believing in people even when the whole world says you're being silly. It's about waking up early and doing the hard thing even when you really, really don't feel like it. And it's about how a papa's love and a daughter's bravery together can do things that nobody ever thought possible.

Now then. Your eyes are looking quite sleepy, and that is a very good sign. Close them gently. Think about all those little birds still yawning over Balali as the sun comes up. Think about fields of soft green grass and a cool morning breeze. Think about Geeta holding up that golden medal, shining so bright it looks like a little piece of the sun.

You, my darling, can do anything you set your heart to. Absolutely anything. Now drift off to sleep, and dream the biggest, most wonderful dreams you can find. Goodnight, little ones. Goodnight.
dangal.3-5:
Okay little one, snuggle up tight. Pull that blanket all the way up to your chin. That's it. Now close your eyes and listen, because tonight I'm going to tell you a story about two very brave little girls and their very, very determined daddy.

Once upon a time, in a small and sleepy village in India, there lived a man named Mahavir. Mahavir had the biggest, bushiest mustache you have ever seen in your whole entire life. It was so big that sometimes birds would try to sit on it. He had to shoo them away every morning. Whoosh, whoosh, little birds.

Now Mahavir had a dream. A big, sparkly, beautiful dream. He wanted someone in his family to win a gold medal for India. A real gold medal. The shiniest one in the whole wide world. But Mahavir had gotten older, and his knees were a little creaky, so he couldn't do it himself anymore. His knees went creak creak creak when he walked down the stairs.

So Mahavir waited. He waited and waited for a son who could wrestle and win that medal for India.

But you know what happened? He got daughters instead. First came Geeta. Then came Babita. Two little girls with bright, bright eyes and the loudest, most wonderful laughs you ever heard.

And Mahavir thought, oh dear, oh dear. But then one day, something very funny happened. Geeta and Babita got into a little argument with two boys from their village. And those two silly boys went home with mud on their faces and hay in their hair and very confused looks on their faces. Geeta and Babita had sent them home looking like little scarecrows.

And Mahavir saw this and his eyes went very wide and his big mustache wiggled and he said, wait a moment. Wait just one moment.

He realized something wonderful. His daughters were strong. His daughters were brave. His daughters could be champions.

Now here is where the story gets really fun, little one. Mahavir decided he was going to train Geeta and Babita to be wrestlers. Real wrestlers. The kind who compete and win big shiny medals.

Every single morning, before the sun even woke up, before the rooster even thought about crowing, Mahavir would call out, Geeta! Babita! Wake up, wake up, it is time to train!

And Geeta and Babita would groan. Oh no. Not again. They would drag their sleepy little feet and yawn so big you could see all their teeth.

Daddy made them run around the fields. Round and round and round. He made them practice their moves in the mud. Splish, splash, splosh. There was mud everywhere. On their faces, in their ears, even in places mud really should not be.

And the village was watching, and some of the silly villagers scratched their heads and said, girls wrestling? That is the most ridiculous thing we have ever heard. Those silly villagers kept making very funny confused faces every single day.

But Geeta and Babita kept going. Every morning. Round and round. Splish splash splosh. Because their daddy believed in them, and slowly, slowly, they started to believe in themselves too.

Now Geeta grew older and she went away to a big training school in the city. And at the city school there was a coach who had a very important job title and a very small amount of actual good ideas. He wore a fancy tracksuit and walked around looking very pleased with himself. But most of his ideas were not very helpful at all. He was like a peacock. Very pretty feathers, not very much useful sense.

And for a little while, Geeta forgot some of the things her daddy had taught her. And she lost some of her matches and she felt very sad inside.

But then she remembered. She remembered all those early mornings. She remembered running round and round the fields before the sun woke up. She remembered her daddy with his big mustache and his creak creak creak knees, who believed she could be the very best in the whole world.

And she called her daddy. And her daddy, even though he was far away in their small sleepy village, helped her remember everything she knew. Everything that was already inside her, strong and bright like a little flame.

Now the most important day came. The big competition. The biggest one of all. The Commonwealth Games. There were wrestlers from countries everywhere. Big countries. Small countries. Countries with very long names that are hard to say before bedtime.

And that silly fancy coach put Mahavir in a room with a lock on it, because he thought he was being very clever. But Mahavir was not worried. He knew his daughter. He had taught her everything. And sometimes the best thing a daddy can do is trust that his little girl carries everything she needs, right there inside her heart.

And Geeta went out on that mat. And she was nervous. And her tummy was doing little flips. But she breathed in deep, and she was strong, and she was clever, and she was brave. And she won. She won the gold medal. The shiniest, most beautiful gold medal in the whole wide world.

And even though Mahavir could not see it happen, when they told him, that big mustache went wiggle wiggle wiggle and his eyes got very shiny. Because his little girl had done it. His brave, wonderful little girl.

And Geeta stood on that platform and she thought of her daddy, all those cold early mornings, all that mud, all those round and rounds. And she smiled the biggest smile.

Now little one, your eyes are getting heavy, aren't they. That's okay. You can close them now. Because the very best thing about this story is that Mahavir never stopped believing in his girls. Never ever ever. And his girls never stopped believing in themselves.

And that is the most wonderful thing of all.

Goodnight, my brave one. Goodnight.
dangal.9-12:
Alright, snuggle up tight, pull those blankets all the way up, and let's go on a little adventure tonight. Close your eyes if you want, or just let your mind drift along with the story, because this one is really, really good. It's about a dad, two amazing girls, and a whole lot of mud, sweat, and heart.

Once upon a time, in a small, dusty village in the state of Haryana, there lived a man named Mahavir Singh Phogat. Now, Mahavir was not just any ordinary man. He was a wrestler. And not just a so-so, kind of okay wrestler — he was a brilliant wrestler, the kind who could flip a person onto their back before they even had time to blink. He had big shoulders, a bigger heart, and the biggest dream you can possibly imagine. He wanted to win a gold medal for India. A real, shiny, heavy gold medal at the Commonwealth Games, the kind you could hang around your neck and feel like you were carrying a piece of the sun.

But life, as it sometimes does, had other plans. There were no funds, no support, no one willing to give young Mahavir a proper chance. So he had to hang up his wrestling shoes, take a regular job, and move to his little village, where he settled down with his wonderful wife, his house, his modest little income, and his enormous, unfulfilled dream. The dream didn't die though. It just sort of went to sleep inside his chest, like a little ember waiting for a breeze.

Mahavir told himself, that's alright. I may not be able to win this medal myself. But maybe, just maybe, my son will. And so he waited. And waited. And when his wife was expecting their first child, he started eating almonds and doing specific exercises that he was absolutely convinced would help bring a son into the world. He consulted a village elder. He avoided certain foods. He followed every piece of advice anyone gave him with tremendous enthusiasm.

And then the baby arrived.

A girl.

A perfectly wonderful, loud, hungry, absolutely beautiful baby girl. They named her Geeta.

Now Mahavir, being a loving father, took a deep breath, smiled, and said — well, the next one will surely be a boy. And he went back to his almonds.

Baby number two arrived.

Another girl. Equally wonderful, equally loud. They named her Babita.

Then came number three.

A girl.

And number four.

Also a girl.

The whole village found this very, very funny. They'd come to the house shaking their heads and chuckling, saying things like, "Arre Mahavir, it seems like you are running a girls' school, not a household!" And Mahavir would smile politely through slightly gritted teeth, because what could he say? He loved his daughters. He truly did. But the dream, oh, the dream of that gold medal was feeling very far away.

Now here is where our story takes the most wonderful, unexpected, gloriously muddy turn.

One afternoon, Mahavir came home to find that Geeta and Babita — who were around ten and nine years old at this point — had gotten into a rather spectacular argument with two boys from the village. Not just any argument, mind you. The kind that ended with those two boys going home completely disheveled, their hair sticking out in seventeen different directions, their clothes covered in dirt, their faces wearing expressions of absolute bewilderment. The boys had apparently said something rude to the girls, and the girls had responded in a very direct, very efficient, very physical manner.

Mahavir stared at the sheepish, muddy faces of his daughters. He looked at the two boys shuffling away in the distance. And then something inside him — that little sleeping ember — whooshed awake like a bonfire.

These girls, he thought. These girls can wrestle.

His wife, who was a sensible and long-suffering woman with the patience of an absolute saint, was not immediately convinced when Mahavir came to her with his new plan. "I want to train Geeta and Babita," he said, eyes shining. "I want to make them wrestlers. Champions. I want them to win that gold medal that I couldn't win."

His wife looked at him for a very long time. "They are girls," she said carefully.

"The greatest wrestlers," said Mahavir, completely undeterred.

She agreed, with one condition — he had to give them one year. Just one year of training. If after a year they showed no real promise, the whole thing would be dropped and life would go back to normal. Mahavir shook on it immediately, probably a little too quickly, which made his wife narrow her eyes slightly, but a deal was a deal.

And so, the training began.

Now, if you imagined training to look like a fun little class where everyone stretched gently and got juice boxes afterward, I am sorry to inform you that Mahavir's training was nothing of the sort. It began at five o'clock in the morning. FIVE. In the MORNING. When the sky was still dark and the stars were barely done twinkling and every single cell in a person's body was screaming, please, please let me keep sleeping.

Geeta and Babita did not take this well at first.

They dragged their feet. They groaned. They made faces that could have been in a dictionary next to the word "unhappy." They whispered complaints to each other at night, giggling sleepily about how their father had turned into a very enthusiastic alarm clock who unfortunately could not be smacked with a pillow.

And the food changes! Oh, the food changes were tragic. No oily snacks. No sweets. Lots of chicken and daal and things that were, as Babita declared very seriously, "deeply unfair for a Sunday."

The other big change — and this one caused quite a scene — was their hair. Long hair was not practical for wrestling. And so, one somewhat dramatic afternoon, off came the braids. The girls went to school the next day with short hair and the whole school, as schools unfortunately tend to do, made fun of them. Boys laughed. Girls whispered. It stung, the way unkind words always do, right in the soft middle part of your chest.

But here is something that the story knows, even if Geeta and Babita didn't quite see it yet — their father wasn't asking them to do any of this because he didn't love them. He was asking them because he loved them enormously, in that particular way that believes in someone even more than they believe in themselves. He saw something in them that they couldn't yet see in their own mirror.

There was a girl in the village named Omkar — a friend of Geeta and Babita's — who was getting married. She was only a little older than them, and at the wedding, she whispered something to Geeta and Babita that settled into their hearts like a warm stone.

"Your father is giving you a gift," she told them quietly, amid all the wedding noise and bangles and flower garlands. "My father never thought about my future, never thought I could be anything. At least yours thinks you can be champions. At least yours is fighting for your tomorrow."

And from that moment, something shifted. A new kind of fire, small at first and then growing steadily larger, lit up in the hearts of both sisters.

They trained harder. They got up at five without grumbling. They wrestled in the muddy pit their father dug in the backyard. They ran through the village in the early morning while the dogs watched them curiously and the roosters hadn't even properly decided whether to crow yet. They got stronger. And faster. And considerably muddier.

And then came the first real competition.

Mahavir had entered Geeta into a local wrestling tournament. The problem was, there were no other girls competing. The organizers scratched their heads. The audience looked confused. And the first opponent, a boy considerably bigger than Geeta, looked extremely confident. Perhaps a little too confident. The kind of confident that is just one good wrestler away from becoming very surprised.

Geeta won.

Not easily. Not without effort. But she won, and Mahavir stood at the side making absolutely no effort to contain his joy, while the crowd went from confused to impressed in the span of about thirty seconds.

Geeta began winning tournaments. Then Babita followed. These two girls from a tiny, dusty village in Haryana were suddenly names that people were saying at dinner tables, in sports offices, in newspaper columns. The Phogat sisters. Have you heard about the Phogat sisters?

Now, all stories need a bit of wobbling in the middle, and ours is no different. When Geeta was selected to train at the National Sports Academy — a big, fancy, prestigious institution in Delhi — she went off with stars in her eyes and her father's proud embrace around her shoulders.

At the academy, there was a coach. Oh, this coach. Let me describe him to you. His name was Coach Pramod Kadam, and he was the sort of person who believed that he knew everything there was to know about wrestling, which was, as it turned out, significantly less than he thought. He wore his authority like a slightly too-tight shirt. He puffed up his chest at every opportunity. He had a little clipboard that he clutched as though it contained the secrets of the universe, when actually it mostly just had schedules on it.

He told Geeta that her father's training was all wrong. Old-fashioned. That she should forget everything Mahavir had taught her and learn the "proper" way. And Geeta, who was seventeen and newly free and surrounded by new friends and new experiences, started to listen. She changed her technique. She grew her hair back. She started losing.

Meanwhile, back in the village, Mahavir watched the news of her losses with a worried heart. He made the trip to Delhi, this man who had never really left his village, carrying tiffin boxes of home food and a mind full of notes and observations, because he had been studying his daughter's opponents very carefully. He knew what she was doing wrong. He knew how to fix it.

But Coach Kadam saw Mahavir coming and basically treated him like an inconvenient fly at a picnic. He told Mahavir he was not allowed to coach Geeta. That he was interfering. That he should go back to his village and leave the professionals to handle things. He had Mahavir turned away at the gate on multiple occasions, which gave the security guard a great deal of confusing paperwork and gave Mahavir a great deal of determination.

What did Mahavir do? He found ways to communicate with Geeta anyway. Little notes. Observations. Cousins delivering messages. He was relentless, not because he was trying to control his daughter, but because he could see so clearly what she couldn't see — that she was wrestling someone else's way when she had a perfectly wonderful way of her own.

And Geeta, in hotel rooms and training halls and quiet moments before competitions, began to remember. She began to remember the muddy backyard. The five AM mornings. The feeling of her father's voice coaching her through something hard. She began to remember who she was.

She and Babita were always each other's greatest support. They talked late into the nights the way sisters do, in that language that is half words and half just knowing, about pressure and fear and what it means to carry a dream — yours and someone else's, all wound together.

The Commonwealth Games arrived like a big, bright, slightly terrifying destination at the end of a very long road.

Geeta was going to compete.

Now, the coach, in one final act of spectacular silliness, decided that the best thing to do before the gold medal match was to lock Mahavir in a storage room. I know. I KNOW. A storage room. With mops. And old equipment. Because he was convinced that if Mahavir coached Geeta from the sidelines, it would somehow undermine his own authority, which was already looking fairly wobbly. The coach managed to do this with the help of some extremely confused officials and a very large padlock, and then stood back looking very pleased with himself, which was honestly the most absurd part of the whole thing.

Geeta went into that final match without her father at the sideline.

And at first, things were hard. Really hard. The opponent was strong and strategic and Geeta was behind on points. In the stands, Mahavir's nephew — Geeta's cousin Omkar, who had trained alongside her — was relaying information desperately, trying to be her connection to everything her father had taught her. But it was Geeta who had to reach inside herself, into all those early mornings and muddy afternoons and hard lessons and her father's voice saying you can do this, you have always been able to do this.

She remembered a move. A particular, brilliant, audacious move that her father had drilled into her a hundred times in that backyard pit. A move that could only work if you were brave enough and fast enough and absolutely committed.

She did it.

The match flipped. Points piled up. And when the final whistle blew, Geeta Phogat was the Commonwealth Games gold medalist.

The storage room, it should be noted, was eventually opened by a very apologetic attendant who had heard all the knocking, and Mahavir walked out to the news of his daughter's victory with tears running freely down his face and absolutely zero dignity about it, and he didn't mind even slightly.

He had wanted that medal for India. And India had it. His daughter had it. His daughter who had woken up at five in the morning and run through the dark and trained in the mud and kept going when it was hard and found her own strength when she needed it most.

There, in that little village in Haryana, four girls had grown up being told, in big ways and small, that their futures had already been decided for them. And one father had said — no. Absolutely not. My daughters will decide their own futures. And they will be magnificent.

And they were.

So tonight, as your eyes get heavier, and the story settles around you like a warm blanket, think about that muddy backyard. Think about five in the morning and not wanting to get up but getting up anyway. Think about Geeta in that final match, reaching inside herself for something her father had put there with love and hard work and belief.

The best things anyone can ever give you are not things at all. They are the belief that you can, and the practice of doing it anyway.

Goodnight, champion. Sleep well. Tomorrow, whatever it brings, you are already braver than you know.
