She pressed her little nose against the train window the whole time, watching trees and fields and rivers zoom past. But here's where things got a little bit tricky. At one of the stations, the train stopped, and Munni saw a little lamb — yes, an actual fluffy baby lamb — just standing on the platform going baaaa baaaa baaaa. And Munni, being Munni, absolutely had to go say hello to it.

She hopped off the train. She petted the lamb. She giggled her silent giggle. And then... the train left. Without her. Can you believe that? Poor little Munni was all alone on a big busy platform, and her mama was on that train not even knowing her little girl had got off!

Now, Munni was lost. Really, truly lost. She wandered and wandered until she ended up in a big city called Delhi, with no idea where she was, no way to say her name or where she lived, and not a single person she knew nearby.

But THAT is when our hero shows up. Guess who?

His name was Pawan Kumar Chaturvedi, but everyone called him Bajrangi. Now, Bajrangi was a very tall, very gentle, slightly goofy man who was an absolute devotee of Lord Hanuman. He wore a little Hanuman pendant around his neck, he said his prayers every single morning, and most importantly — and this is the really important bit — he could not tell a lie. Not even a tiny one. Not even to get out of trouble. He'd tried once and his face went all red and wobbly and he just blurted out the truth anyway. That was just the kind of person he was.

Bajrangi found little Munni sitting alone and looking very confused, and his heart just melted like butter on a warm roti. He couldn't just leave her there, could he? Of course not! He took her home, and his best friend Mamu's family took Munni in like she was their own.

Bajrangi's friend Rasika thought Munni was just the most precious thing, and Munni thought so too — she followed Bajrangi around everywhere like a little duckling follows its mama duck. Bajrangi called her Munni because they didn't even know her real name. She couldn't tell them, after all.

But here's the thing. After lots of trying to figure out where Munni was from, they discovered a very important clue. Munni was actually from Pakistan! A whole other country, far away, on the other side of a big border with lots of rules and fences and very serious-looking guards.

Now, most people would have said, oh dear, that's very complicated, let me find another way. But Bajrangi said, right, I am going to take this little girl home to her mama. Full stop. No arguments.

His friends said, Bajrangi, you don't even have the right papers to go to Pakistan! You can't just walk in!

And Bajrangi said, I'll figure it out.

Did he have a plan? Not exactly. Did he have a visa? Absolutely not. Did he have the courage of someone who truly, madly, deeply wanted to do the right thing? Oh yes. One hundred percent yes.

So off they went, Bajrangi and little Munni, on the most wonderfully ridiculous journey you can imagine. They crossed the border in a very creative way that involved a lot of tiptoeing and one extremely confused goat who kept following them. Munni found the whole thing hilarious, by the way. She kept clapping her hands and bouncing up and down while Bajrangi shushed her and tried to look invisible, which, for a very tall man, is quite difficult.

Once they were in Pakistan, Bajrangi realised he had a bit of a problem. He didn't speak the local language very well, he had no idea where Munni's village was, and he had accidentally introduced himself to several people in completely the wrong way because he was so nervous. He told one shopkeeper he was a dancing potato. Not on purpose. It just came out that way.

But people were kind. Wonderfully, surprisingly kind. A family invited them in for food. A little boy showed them which road to take. A funny old man with a very large moustache that wobbled when he laughed gave Bajrangi directions while his moustache went wobble wobble wobble. Munni was absolutely delighted by that moustache. She kept pointing at it and doing her silent laugh and the old man laughed too and everyone was just so jolly.

Now, there was a bit of a funny problem. A policeman named Inspector Nawab had heard about this mysterious man wandering around Pakistan without papers, and he was DETERMINED to catch him. Inspector Nawab thought he was very very clever and very very sneaky. He had a big official hat that was slightly too large and kept falling over his eyes at important moments. He'd jump out from behind things going AHA and then his hat would fall down and he'd have to push it back up and by then Bajrangi and Munni had already toddled off somewhere else.

There was also a journalist named Chand Nawab — yes, also Nawab, confusing I know, try to keep up — who had a little camera and was always looking for a big exciting story. He started following Bajrangi around too, and at first he was a bit of a nosy nuisance, but then something happened. He actually watched Bajrangi. He watched this silly, gentle, completely honest man carrying a little girl all over the country just to bring her home safely with no reward, no payment, nothing in it for himself at all. And Chand Nawab's heart got very full and a little bit crinkly the way hearts do when they see something really truly good.

Chand Nawab started helping them. He used his camera. He told Munni's story to people. And slowly, wonderfully, the story of the little lost girl and her big silly guardian spread from person to person to person like a lovely warm wave.

Meanwhile, Munni's mama had never stopped looking for her little girl. Never ever ever. She had been searching and searching, her heart aching every single day. And when she saw the video of her daughter on a little phone screen, being carried along on the shoulders of a big goofy man in a Hanuman pendant, she burst into the most beautiful happy tears.

Inspector Nawab with his wobbly hat tried one more time to be very official and important and stop everything. He puffed out his chest and said there were rules and regulations and proper procedures. But then he looked at Munni. Just looked at her. And her big bright eyes looked right back at him. And his very serious official face did something it hadn't done in a long time. It smiled. And then it did something even more surprising. Inspector Nawab stepped aside.

And then the most magical thing happened. People gathered. On both sides of the border, people came together, all different, all from different places, speaking different languages, wearing different clothes, but all of them there for the same reason — to see a little girl go home to her mama.

Munni ran. Her little legs went as fast as they possibly could, pigtails flying, and she ran and ran and ran, and her mama opened her arms so wide and caught her and held her so tight and Munni — our little Munni who had never spoken a single word — looked up at her mama's face and said her very first word.

She said mama.

The whole crowd went absolutely silent for one beautiful second. And then everyone erupted. Cheering, laughing, crying the happy kind of tears. Even the Inspector's hat fell off and this time he didn't pick it up, he was too busy clapping.

And Bajrangi? Big, gentle, goofy Bajrangi with his Hanuman pendant and his inability to tell even the tiniest lie? He stood there and watched, and his whole face was so full of joy it practically glowed. Munni turned around and looked at him one last time with those big bright eyes, and she gave him a smile so enormous it could have powered the sun.

He walked back home with a light step and a full heart, and I think Hanuman himself must have been very pleased that day.

So my darlings, that's the story of Bajrangi and Munni. A story about being kind even when it's hard, being honest even when it's tricky, and the very wonderful truth that love doesn't need a passport or a permission slip or even words. It just needs a brave and gentle heart.

Now close your eyes, my loves. Let your breathing go slow and soft. Think about all the people who love you, right here, right now, close by. And know that you are as safe and as held as Munni the moment her mama caught her.

Goodnight, little ones. Sleep tight. Sweet, sweet dreams.
bajrangi.3-5:
Okay little one, snuggle up tight, pull that blanket all the way up to your chin, yes just like that, and let me tell you about the most wonderful, most surprising, most heart-melting adventure of a very big, very kind man named Pawan.

Now Pawan, everybody called him Bajrangi. Do you know why? Because he loved Bajrang Bali, Lord Hanuman, more than almost anything in the whole wide world. He had little statues of Hanuman. He had pictures of Hanuman. He even talked to Hanuman when he needed help. And Hanuman, well, Hanuman always listened.

Bajrangi was a big, strong man with the biggest, softest heart you ever saw. He could not tell a lie. Not even a tiny one. Not even to get out of trouble. If you asked him something, out came the truth, every single time. His friends would shake their heads and laugh. But that was just Bajrangi. Honest as the morning sun.

Now one day, something extraordinary happened.

Bajrangi was sitting at a train station, all the hustle and bustle around him, chai wallahs calling out, pigeons flapping about, when he noticed something. A tiny little girl, all by herself, sitting very still, looking around with the biggest, most curious eyes in the world.

She was maybe as old as you, little one. Maybe just a little older.

Bajrangi looked left. He looked right. He scratched his head. Where was this little girl's mama? Where was her papa? Nobody was coming. Nobody was looking for her. She was all alone.

Now most people might have just walked away. But Bajrangi? No no no. That big heart of his would not let him do that. He sat down right next to her. He made a silly face. And the little girl, instead of crying, looked at him very seriously and then burst into the most wonderful giggle you ever heard.

Bajrangi named her Munni. Sweet little Munni.

But here was the tricky part, the mysterious part, the part that made everything into a great big adventure. Munni could not speak. Not one single word. She talked with her eyes, with her hands, with her expressions, and somehow, somehow, Bajrangi understood everything she was trying to say.

And slowly, with a lot of pointing and nodding and funny hand signals, Bajrangi figured out that Munni was not from his country at all. She was from Pakistan. A whole other country, far far away, on the other side of a big border with tall gates and very serious looking guards who wore very big hats.

Oh my goodness, thought Bajrangi. How do we get this little one home?

Now India and Pakistan, you see, they were neighbours, but getting across the border was not simple like hopping over a fence. There were rules and papers and stamps and more rules. Bajrangi tried to do everything the proper way. He went to offices. He waited in very long lines. He talked to men sitting behind very tall stacks of paper.

And every single person he talked to said no.

There was one particular officer, oh he was something else. He had a very grand moustache that he was extremely proud of. He twirled it constantly. He puffed out his chest. He stamped papers very importantly. But really? He was absolutely, completely, totally confused about everything. He once stamped his own hand by mistake. He once got his moustache stuck in a drawer. He was, in short, wonderfully, hilariously useless.

Bajrangi would just sigh and take Munni's hand and they would walk back out into the sunshine.

But Bajrangi did not give up. No no no. Giving up was not something Bajrangi knew how to do.

He made a friend along the way, a funny, chatty journalist named Chand Nawab who talked so fast and got so excited about everything that he once tried to film a story and forgot to press the record button three whole times. He became Bajrangi's helper and his very good friend, and together the three of them, Bajrangi, Munni, and Chand Nawab, set off on the most amazing journey.

They walked through fields of golden grass. They crossed little bridges over gurgling streams. They met farmers who shared their food. They slept under skies so full of stars it looked like someone had spilled a whole jar of glitter up there.

And everywhere they went, when people saw this big gentle man carrying this tiny girl with the curious eyes, something wonderful happened. Hearts opened. Doors opened. People helped. Because kindness, you see little one, kindness speaks every language there is. It does not need papers or stamps or big moustached officers.

And then one day, Munni looked up and she knew. She knew these roads. She knew these smells. She knew this place.

Home.

And when her mama came running, oh, when her mama came running with tears streaming down her face and her arms wide open, and Munni ran as fast as her little legs could carry her and jumped right into those arms, well. Even the big strong Bajrangi cried. He cried big happy tears. And Chand Nawab cried. And probably the goats standing nearby cried a little bit too.

And just before Bajrangi had to turn around and go back home, Munni looked at him. She took a deep breath. And for the very first time, with her small, sweet voice, she said one word.

Bajrangi.

He turned around with the biggest smile the world has ever seen.

And that is the story of a big kind man, a tiny brave girl, and how love and honesty can get you all the way across the whole wide world.

Now close your eyes, little one. Close them very slowly. You are safe. You are loved. And somewhere tonight, Bajrangi is probably talking to Hanuman, smiling his big smile, fast asleep.

Just like you are going to be. Right now. Sweet dreams.
bajrangi.9-12:
Alright, alright, shuffle those pillows around and get yourself all cozy, because tonight I have an absolutely wonderful story for you. Pull that blanket up to your chin, take a nice deep breath, and let me tell you about the most big-hearted, adventure-filled journey you've ever heard. It's the story of a gentle giant named Pawan, a tiny girl who couldn't speak, and a friendship so powerful it crossed mountains, borders, and even the grumpiest of grumpy border guards. Ready? Good. Here we go.

Now, our story begins in a little village nestled in the hills of India, where there lived a young man named Pawan Kumar Chaturvedi. But nobody called him that, because that's a mouthful. Everyone called him Bajrangi. And why did they call him Bajrangi, you ask? Because he was the world's most devoted fan of Lord Bajrang Bali — that's Hanuman, the mighty, loyal, and wonderfully brave monkey god. Pawan had a little temple in his heart for Hanuman, and he visited an actual temple every single morning without fail. He was the kind of person who couldn't tell a lie even if you paid him a mountain of gold and threw in a free pizza. Couldn't do it. His nose didn't grow like Pinocchio's, but his face went completely red and his voice got all wobbly. Lying just wasn't in him.

Pawan was big and strong and a little bit, shall we say, slow with the books. He hadn't exactly been the shining star of his school exams. But what he lacked in academic sparkle, he made up for in the most enormous, warm, overflowing heart you could ever imagine. Think of your favourite stuffed animal — the one that's been with you forever — and imagine if that stuffed animal came to life as a person. That would be Pawan.

So there he is, living in Delhi, trying to sort out his life, when one ordinary, unremarkable Tuesday — which was about to become a very remarkable Tuesday — everything changed.

At a railway station, in the middle of all the noise and the rushing crowds and the chai sellers calling out and pigeons doing what pigeons do absolutely everywhere, Pawan noticed a little girl. She was maybe six years old, tiny as a sparrow, with the biggest, most curious eyes you've ever seen. She had gotten completely, utterly, totally separated from her mother in the chaos of the station. The train had pulled away, and there she was — alone on the platform, clutching nothing but the little dupatta around her shoulders, looking around with those wide eyes.

Now, most people rushed past. Busy, busy, busy. But not Pawan. Pawan stopped like someone had pressed his pause button. He crouched down to her level and tried to talk to her, and here's the thing — the little girl couldn't speak. Not a single word. She was mute. But she could understand everything, and her face said plenty. Right now, her face said, "I am lost and a little scared but I am also watching you very carefully to decide if you are trustworthy."

Pawan, being Pawan, immediately bought her a samosa, because food is always a good first step.

The little girl's name, he would eventually figure out, was Shahida. And very slowly, through pointing and nodding and the kind of sign language that people invent on the spot when they really need to understand each other, Pawan pieced together her story. She was from Pakistan. She had come to India with her mother to visit a famous shrine, and somewhere in the enormous, magnificent madness of a crowded Indian railway station, they had been separated, and the train had left without little Shahida.

Now here's the thing. In those days — and still today — India and Pakistan are like two cousins who had a very big argument a long time ago and haven't quite sorted it out since. The border between them is serious business. You can't just stroll across. You need papers, permissions, passports, and about forty-seven different official stamps. Pawan had none of these things. Shahida had none of these things either.

But Pawan had made a promise. Not out loud — just in his heart, in the way that really counts — that he would get this little girl home.

And so began the most wonderfully chaotic, heartwarming, slightly ridiculous adventure.

First, they tried the official way. The police. Pawan marched up to a police station, Shahida trotting beside him, and explained the situation. The officer on duty was a round, mustachioed fellow named Inspector Dandapat who had the most magnificent mustache you've ever seen — it curled at the ends like a pair of sleeping caterpillars — and who was deeply, passionately committed to his afternoon nap schedule. He looked at Pawan. He looked at the little girl. He looked at his watch. He told them it was "very complicated" and "come back next Tuesday" and "have you tried filling out Form 27-B?" and then he went back to his office and his biscuits.

No help there.

Pawan tried the Pakistani embassy next. Now, the embassy had a different kind of problem. The person at the front desk was a nervous, bespectacled young man named Ranjeet, who was terrified of doing anything that wasn't written in a manual. Ranjeet's manual did not have a chapter called "What To Do With Lost Small Children Who Cannot Speak." He flipped through it three times, sweating gently, and then told them they needed documents that Shahida simply didn't have.

So. No official way.

There was only one thing left to do. Pawan would take Shahida to Pakistan himself. Unofficially. Which is an extremely polite way of saying — secretly, quietly, holding their breath, hoping nobody looked too closely.

Now, getting across the border without papers sounds like the kind of thing only a very clever spy could do. But Pawan wasn't a spy. He was just a big, honest, determined man who could not lie and who loved Hanuman and who had decided that this small girl was getting home if it was the last thing he did. And somehow, that combination turned out to be more powerful than any spy training.

They found a way through. A forgotten, mostly dried-up river path that a very old and wonderfully eccentric goat farmer showed them — in exchange for help carrying his goats, which took forty-five minutes because one particular goat named Birbal absolutely refused to cooperate and kept sitting down in protest. Shahida found this hysterical and did that silent laugh that is somehow the best kind of laugh — shoulders shaking, eyes squeezed shut, the whole production.

And then they were in Pakistan.

Now, here's where the story gets even more wonderful, because Pakistan turned out to be full of kind, funny, generous, complicated people — which, of course, it always was, just as India is. Pawan had grown up hearing that the two countries were so different. But he kept finding, every single day, that people on both sides just wanted their chai in the morning and their families safe and their cricket team to do well.

In Pakistan, they met Chand Nawab. Oh, Chand Nawab — you would love him. He was a local journalist with a big video camera, an even bigger opinion of himself, and absolutely no professional success whatsoever. He'd been trying to make it big in news for years and had somehow managed to accidentally film the back of his own head more times than anything newsworthy. He was bumbling, he was loud, he wore a waistcoat he was extremely proud of, and he had a laugh like a donkey discovering it had won a prize.

When Chand Nawab stumbled across Pawan and little Shahida — an Indian man, walking around Pakistan with a lost Pakistani child, not bothering anyone, just genuinely trying to do the right thing — he thought he had found the story of his career. And he was absolutely right, though not in the way he expected.

He started filming. He started following them. He got in the way tremendously. But also — and this is the thing about people like Chand Nawab — he was, under all the bumbling, a good person. And slowly, without meaning to, he became their friend. And then their helper. And then their champion.

Meanwhile, there were obstacles. Oh, there were obstacles.

There was a border security official named Major Chaudhry who had decided, with great personal conviction, that Pawan was some kind of spy or troublemaker. Major Chaudhry was the kind of person who wore his uniform even at breakfast, who had a filing cabinet for his filing cabinet, and who absolutely believed that rules existed to be followed no matter what, even if those rules were making a small child cry. He was not evil, exactly. He was just very, very stiff. Like a cardboard box that had decided to become a person.

Every time Pawan and Shahida got close to finding her village, Major Chaudhry would appear, walkie-talkie crackling, mustache bristling, ready to make things very difficult. But Pawan — honest, big-hearted, completely unstrategic Pawan — kept slipping away from him, not because he was crafty, but because he was simply too sincere for Major Chaudhry to process. You can't really catch someone who isn't running away, just walking toward something good.

They visited mosques. They visited shrines. Pawan, the devoted Hindu, quietly sat outside and waited while people prayed inside, because he respected what he didn't fully understand, which is one of the most important things a person can do. Shahida reached up and held his hand every time. That's how you know two people have become family. Not because they look alike or believe exactly the same things, but because one hand reaches for the other without even thinking about it.

And then, finally — oh, my loves, finally — they found her village. A tiny, green, beautiful place tucked in the hills. And her mother. Her mother, who had been searching and crying and praying for weeks and weeks and had never stopped looking.

The moment when Shahida saw her mother and ran — that run, those arms opening, that collision of mother and child — well. Let's just say that even Major Chaudhry, standing stiffly nearby, had to very suddenly pretend to be very interested in something on the horizon while his eyes did something that official border security officials' eyes are absolutely not supposed to do.

But the story wasn't quite over, because Pawan had been noticed. He was an Indian man, without papers, on Pakistani soil. This was serious. There was a lot of official frowning. There were forms, and officials, and the kind of bureaucratic confusion that makes everything take three times longer than it should. Pawan, because he genuinely could not lie, kept telling the absolute truth to everyone, which confused the officials enormously because nobody ever does that.

And here is where Chand Nawab — lovely, ridiculous, waistcoat-wearing Chand Nawab — did the best thing of his life. He took that footage he'd been collecting. All of it. Every moment of this big, honest man carrying a tiny girl across a country just to take her home. And he put it online. He broadcast it. He sent it everywhere.

And the people — the people of Pakistan, the people of India, watching on their phones and their televisions — they saw it. And they felt it. Because kindness, when you actually see it, is impossible to ignore. It's like a light in a dark room. You can't look away from it.

Suddenly, everyone knew about Pawan and Shahida. And suddenly, Major Chaudhry found himself in the very interesting position of being the cardboard-box official standing between the world's most beloved lost-child reunion and its happy ending. His phone was ringing. His superior's phone was ringing. His superior's superior's phone was ringing. People lined the roads.

And so they made a space. A corridor. And Pawan walked, and on both sides of him were crowds of people — Pakistani people who had fallen in love with this strange, sincere, enormous-hearted Indian man — and they were clapping, and cheering, and some were crying, and some were doing all three at once.

And little Shahida, who had not spoken a single word in her entire life, who had been silent and quiet through all of it — the train stations and the border crossings and the goats and the hiding and the finding — Shahida ran to him.

And she said his name.

"Bajrangi."

Just that. Just one word. But oh, what a word. A whole story in one word. A whole friendship. A whole journey.

And Pawan — big, strong, never-crying Pawan — cried. Enormously. With absolutely no shame at all. Because some things are too full to hold.

And then he walked back across the border, and she stayed with her family, and the two countries went back to being complicated neighbors who hadn't sorted out their argument. But for one day, in one small place, because of one honest man and one brave little girl and one very persistent journalist in a waistcoat, something real and true and good had happened.

And that is enough. That is more than enough. Sometimes that's everything.

So here's what I want you to think about as you drift off tonight. Pawan wasn't special because he was the strongest, or the smartest, or the most important person. He was special because he couldn't look away from someone who needed help. Because he kept one promise he'd only made to himself. Because he was honest, even when it would have been so much easier not to be.

You've got that in you too, you know. Every single one of you.

The world is full of borders, some on maps and some in hearts. And every now and then, someone walks right across them with nothing but kindness, and changes everything.

Alright now. Close those eyes. Feel how warm and safe and cozy you are right here, right now. Take a slow breath in... and let it go. Let Bajrangi and Shahida walk off into the quiet hills of that story, together for one last moment before she goes home and he goes home, both of them carrying something precious — a friendship that crossed every border there is.

Sleep well, my love. Dream big, gentle dreams.

pathaan.6-8:
Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets nice and tight, and let me tell you about one of the most amazing adventure stories you've ever heard. This is the story of a hero named Pathaan, and trust me, by the end you're going to want to be just as brave and clever as he is. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, there was a special hero named Pathaan. Now Pathaan wasn't just any ordinary person. He was a secret agent for India, which means his job was to travel the whole wide world and make sure everyone stayed safe and happy. He had twinkling eyes, a great big smile, and the most magnificent hair you've ever seen on anyone ever. And he was SO good at his job that even the birds and the butterflies probably knew his name. Well, maybe not the butterflies. But still.

Now Pathaan had been away from home for a very, very long time. So long that he had almost forgotten what it felt like to sit in his own cozy room. But that's the thing about heroes, you see. Sometimes being a hero means making big sacrifices, which is a fancy grown-up word for giving something up because you love people so much. Pathaan loved India so much that he gave up his comfortable home and his quiet life to keep everyone safe. Isn't that something?

But here's where the story gets really exciting. Are you still awake? Good, good, keep those eyes open just a little longer.

There was a very silly villain named Jim. Now Jim thought he was incredibly scary and terribly clever, but honestly? He was kind of like that one kid in class who always tries too hard to be the toughest one and ends up tripping over his own shoelaces. Jim had decided, for reasons that made absolutely no sense whatsoever, that he wanted to cause trouble for India. Big trouble. The kind of trouble that would make everyone very sad and scared.

Jim had a whole group of helpers who were just as bumbling as he was. They wore matching outfits and always seemed to be bumping into each other and knocking things over. One of them once tripped over a bucket during a very important meeting, and Jim had to pretend he wasn't absolutely furious about it. Can you imagine? A big important villain meeting, and someone just kicks a bucket right across the floor? Clang, clang, clang! Oh dear.

Jim's big plan involved something called a very dangerous thing, which he kept in a very fancy box with about seventeen different locks on it. He was SO proud of those locks. He talked about them constantly. "Seventeen locks!" he would say, puffing out his chest. "Nobody can open seventeen locks!" His helpers would all nod very seriously and then immediately forget how many locks there were and have to ask again.

Now, someone had to stop Jim and his silly gang. And that someone was going to be Pathaan.

But wait! Pathaan couldn't do it alone. Because the best adventures always have the best teams.

Pathaan was going to get some help from a brilliant, wonderful friend named Rubai. Now Rubai was incredibly smart, possibly the smartest person in any room she ever walked into, and she knew it, and she was right. She was quick and funny and knew about seventeen different languages and could solve puzzles faster than you could say "what's for breakfast." She and Pathaan had to learn to trust each other, which, as you probably know, is one of the most important things in the whole world.

At first, they weren't sure about each other. Pathaan thought he could do everything by himself, because sometimes heroes make that mistake. And Rubai thought Pathaan was a little too show-offy. Which, honestly, fair enough. But as they worked together and went on adventure after adventure, they discovered something really lovely. They were much, much better as a team. Together they were unstoppable. Like peanut butter and jelly. Like moonlight and stars. Like you and your favourite stuffed animal.

And then! Oh, guess what happened next! There was ANOTHER helper who joined them. An old friend of Pathaan's named Tiger. Now Tiger was also a secret agent, equally brave and wonderful, and when Pathaan needed help the most, Tiger came zooming in like the most magnificent surprise you've ever seen. Because that's what real friends do. They show up when things get hard. Even if they have to travel very far to do it.

So now you had Pathaan, Rubai, and Tiger, all working together, and honestly Jim and his gang simply did not stand a chance.

The adventures they went on together were absolutely spectacular. They went to snowy mountains where everything sparkled like someone had spilled a million diamonds across the ground. They went to busy, colourful cities where the streets smelled like spices and flowers. They went to places so beautiful that even the clouds seemed to stop and look around for a moment just to appreciate it all.

And every single time Jim's gang tried to do something troublesome, Pathaan and his friends found the most wonderfully clever ways to stop them. No crashing or bashing, just pure cleverness and teamwork and a healthy amount of running, which Pathaan was extremely good at, by the way. The man could RUN. His hair flowing in the wind, his feet barely touching the ground. It was something to see, truly.

One time, Jim's helpers tried to sneak past Pathaan disguised as delivery people carrying an enormous stack of boxes. Pathaan simply waited until they walked by and then quietly switched the address on the package, and they ended up delivering themselves to the local police station entirely by accident. They stood there so confused, still holding the boxes, blinking at the officer behind the desk. Can you believe that? Pathaan didn't even have to do very much at all. Sometimes being clever is better than anything else.

Another time, Rubai discovered that Jim's whole plan depended on a special password, and she figured out what it was in about forty-five seconds while eating a snack. Just sitting there, munching away, and suddenly she put down her food and said "got it." Just like that. Pathaan stared at her for a long moment and then just slowly nodded like, yes, okay, this person is extraordinary, I accept this completely.

But the most important moment in the whole story came when things looked really difficult. Jim had managed to put his plan into motion and it seemed, just for a moment, like maybe he might actually get away with it. His seventeen locks were doing their job. His helpers were being slightly less bumbling than usual. And Pathaan, Rubai, and Tiger were very far away.

But here is what Jim never understood, because villains so rarely do. He thought that doing bad things made him powerful. But Pathaan knew that love makes you powerful. Love for your home, love for the people you protect, love for your friends standing right beside you. And when you have that kind of love in your heart, you can do things that seem absolutely impossible.

Pathaan looked at Rubai. Rubai looked at Tiger. Tiger cracked his knuckles, which he always did when things were about to get very interesting. And then the three of them came up with the most brilliant, most creative, most wonderfully unexpected plan you could ever imagine.

I won't tell you every single detail because some things are best left to the imagination, but I will tell you this. Jim's fancy seventeen-lock box? Unlocked. Jim's big plan? Completely, totally, wonderfully stopped. And Jim himself? He sat down very heavily on the ground, crossed his arms, and said "oh, COME ON" in the most defeated, pouty voice you've ever heard. His helpers all looked at each other and started slowly backing away as if they had never met Jim and had simply wandered in from somewhere else entirely.

India was safe. Everyone was happy. The sun came out from behind the clouds, and somewhere, probably, birds were singing a very cheerful song about the whole thing.

Pathaan got to come home. And when he did, he walked through the streets and felt something warm in his chest that had been missing for a very long time. He was home. He was really, truly home. And all the people he had kept safe, even though they didn't always know his name or his face, were going about their lovely ordinary days, laughing and eating and playing and dreaming, and that was enough. That was everything.

Rubai and Tiger came with him, because good friends don't just say goodbye after adventures. They stay. They share a meal. They sit together quietly and feel grateful for each other.

And somewhere, in a very small, very cold room, Jim was trying to explain to someone why his seventeen locks hadn't worked, and absolutely nobody was listening to him at all.

So what did we learn from Pathaan today, my loves? We learned that home is worth protecting. We learned that friendship is the most powerful thing in the world. We learned that clever is better than loud, and that love is better than meanness, and that the best adventures are always shared with people who believe in you.

And most importantly, we learned that no matter how far away you go, and no matter how many silly villains with too many locks on their boxes try to cause trouble, the good people always find their way back to each other.

Now then. The story is done, the heroes are resting, and you know what? I think it's time for you to rest too. Close your eyes, feel how warm and safe and cosy you are right here. No villains here, only soft pillows and sweet dreams and people who love you very much.

Goodnight, little ones. Sleep tight. Dream of adventures and good friends and coming home.
pathaan.3-5:
Okay little one, snuggle up tight. Pull that blanket all the way up to your chin. That's it. Perfect. Now close your eyes and listen, because I'm going to tell you a very special story tonight. It's about a hero named Pathaan.

Now Pathaan was not just any hero. He was the bravest, kindest, most wonderful spy in the whole wide world. And do you know what a spy is? A spy is someone who goes on secret adventures to keep everyone safe. Just like how I keep you safe. But Pathaan did it for the whole country. For everyone. For all the mommies and daddies and little ones like you who were snuggled up safe in their beds.

Pathaan loved his country so so much. It was like his heart was made of the colours of the flag. That's how much he loved it.

Now Pathaan had been away for a very long time. He had been on so many adventures in so many faraway places. And even though he was very brave, sometimes he felt a little lonely. Because being far from home for a long time can make anyone feel a tiny bit sad. Even the bravest people in the world.

But then something happened. He got a message. A very important message. His country needed him. And just like that, all the tiredness went away. Because when someone you love needs you, you just go. Don't you? Of course you do.

So Pathaan jumped right up and said, I'm coming. I'm on my way.

Now on this adventure, Pathaan met a very good friend. Her name was Rubai. And Rubai was also a spy. She was clever and funny and incredibly brave, just like Pathaan. At first they weren't sure about each other. You know how sometimes you meet someone new and you're a little bit shy? It was like that. But very quickly they figured out that they were the best of friends. The kind of friends who look out for each other. The kind of friends who say, don't worry, I've got you.

And that is a very very good kind of friend to have.

Now. Every good story has a silly villain. And this one had a very silly villain indeed. His name was Jim. Now Jim thought he was very very scary. He wore a big dramatic coat and he practiced his mean face in the mirror every single morning. He'd go, grrrr. Like that. And then he'd look at himself and say, yes, very scary, very good, well done Jim.

But actually Jim kept making mistakes. He'd come up with a big plan and then trip over his own shoelaces. He'd try to be sneaky but then sneeze at exactly the wrong moment. Achoo! And everyone would turn around and see him. He was really just a very confused man who needed someone to give him a nice cup of warm milk and tell him to calm down.

Jim had a plan though. A very silly plan. He wanted to cause trouble for lots and lots of people. He had collected something he was not supposed to have, and he was keeping it hidden, and he thought nobody would ever find out.

But he did not count on Pathaan.

Pathaan was very very clever. He figured out all of Jim's silly plans. Every single one. And each time Jim thought he had outsmarted everyone, Pathaan would be one step ahead going, nope, not today, thank you very much.

There was one moment where it looked like things might not work out. Jim had done something really not nice and Pathaan's heart felt heavy. Have you ever felt that? When something feels really hard and you wonder how it will ever be okay again? Pathaan felt that.

But do you know what he did? He thought about all the people he loved. All the families sitting at home. All the little ones sleeping in their cozy beds. And he thought, I cannot give up. Not now. Not ever.

And so he didn't.

With the help of Rubai and some other very good friends, Pathaan came up with the most brilliant, most wonderful, most clever plan you can imagine. And it worked. It worked so beautifully. Jim looked around and realized that all his silly scheming had come to absolutely nothing. He stood there with his big dramatic coat and his carefully practiced mean face and all he could do was sputter and say, but but but how, and Pathaan just smiled that warm smile of his.

Because kindness and cleverness and loving your people will always, always beat silliness and grumpiness and being mean.

Jim was sent to a very long timeout. A very very long one. And everyone else was safe.

And Pathaan? Pathaan finally got to come home. And when he did, the whole country felt warm. Like when you come inside from the cold and you smell something yummy cooking and someone wraps a blanket around you.

That's how it felt.

And Pathaan looked up at the stars that night, the same stars you can see right now if you peek out your window, and he whispered thank you. Thank you for letting me take care of you.

And the stars twinkled back. Like they were saying, thank you too, Pathaan. Thank you too.

Now you my little one, you are also very brave and very loved. Just like Pathaan. And just like him, wherever you go, whoever you become, there will always be people cheering for you. Always.

So now it's time to close those sleepy eyes. Let your arms go all soft and heavy. Let your thoughts go quiet like a still, still lake.

You are safe. You are loved. And everything is just exactly right.

Goodnight, little one. Goodnight.
pathaan.9-12:
Alright, alright, scoot over and make some room, tuck those feet under the blanket, yes both feet, I can see that one sticking out. There we go. Comfy? Good. Because tonight I have a really, really good one for you. It's got a hero who travels the whole wide world, a best friend who is absolutely brilliant, a villain who is, well, let me just say he makes some very questionable decisions, and a mystery that takes us all the way from frozen snowy mountains to sunny beaches to the bustling, beautiful streets of our very own India. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, there was a man named Pathaan.

Now Pathaan wasn't just any ordinary fellow. He wasn't the kind of person you'd see at the grocery store debating which brand of biscuits to buy. No no no. Pathaan was a spy. A secret agent. The kind of person who could walk into a room full of problems and walk out with all of them solved before anyone even finished their cup of chai. He worked for a very important and very secret organization that protected India, and his whole entire life, every single day, every single breath, was devoted to keeping his country and its people safe.

But here's the thing about Pathaan that made him different from other heroes in stories. He wasn't loud about it. He didn't go around saying, look at me, I'm so brave, please clap. He was quiet about his love for India. It lived deep inside him, like a warm little flame right in the center of his chest, and it never, ever went out, even on his hardest days.

And Pathaan had some very hard days.

You see, a little while before our story begins, something terrible had happened. Pathaan had been on a mission, a very important one, and things had gone wrong in a way that wasn't his fault at all, but he still felt responsible. He felt like he had let people down. And so his bosses, in a decision that was honestly a little bit unfair if you ask me, decided he could no longer be an active spy. They said, Pathaan, you're done. Hand in your badge. Go live your life somewhere.

And so Pathaan disappeared. Not in a dramatic poof-of-smoke way, but in a quiet, sad, drifting kind of way. He wandered. He went here and there and everywhere. Moscow, where it snowed so much you couldn't see your hand in front of your face. Dubai, where the buildings were so tall they tickled the clouds. Afghanistan, Spain, Morocco. He was like a boat that had come untied from its dock and was just floating wherever the current took it.

But even untied boats don't float forever. Something was coming that would pull Pathaan right back into the adventure he was made for.

That something had a name. And the name was Jim.

Now, Jim. Oh, where do I begin with Jim. Jim was the villain of our story, but I want you to picture him very carefully, because he is not the terrifying, shadowy kind of villain. Jim was more like, you know that kid in class who was really smart and really talented and should have used all that talent for good things but instead decided to be unnecessarily dramatic about absolutely everything? That was Jim. He wore very intense outfits. He gave very long speeches. He believed, with his whole dramatic heart, that India had wronged him, and he had decided he was going to get his revenge.

His plan, and I am not making this up, was to release something called a biological weapon. Now in simple terms, that means a kind of invisible, sneaky illness that could make lots of people very sick. Jim had gotten his hands on this terrible thing and was planning to use it to cause chaos and hurt people all across India.

Very bad plan, Jim. Very bad indeed.

His helpers were a group called the Outfit, and they were, to put it kindly, not the sharpest pencils in the box. They wore matching outfits which I think was meant to be intimidating but mostly just made them look like they'd gotten lost on their way to a very intense summer camp. Their leader on the ground was a fellow who was constantly making plans that sounded very impressive when he said them out loud and then fell apart completely the moment Pathaan showed up.

Which brings us to how Pathaan got pulled back in.

India's intelligence agency, RAW, that's the organization that handles all the super secret spy stuff, realized something enormous and scary was happening. They needed their best people on it. And their director, a sharp, no-nonsense woman named Nandini who had the kind of focused energy that made you want to sit up straight and pay attention, knew exactly who she needed.

She needed Pathaan.

There was just one tiny problem. Pathaan had, technically, been let go. He wasn't officially a spy anymore. He was just a wandering fellow in various international locations feeling a bit sorry for himself.

But Nandini didn't become the head of India's intelligence agency by letting technicalities stop her. She made some calls. She pulled some strings. And she found Pathaan.

When they reached him, Pathaan was sitting somewhere cold and grey and a little bit lonely. And when they told him India needed him, something happened to that little flame inside his chest. It flickered. And then it blazed.

He was back.

Now, Pathaan couldn't do this alone. The mission was too big, too complicated, stretched across too many countries. He needed backup. And backup came in the most wonderful form, a woman named Rubina.

Rubina was extraordinary. She was one of the smartest people Pathaan had ever met in his entire life of meeting extremely smart people. She knew languages he'd never even heard of. She could solve a puzzle in the time it took most people to find the puzzle pieces. She had this brilliant, quick mind that worked like a supercomputer, except warmer and with better fashion sense. She also had courage that was, frankly, a little bit ridiculous. The kind of courage where she would look at a genuinely impossible situation and just go, yes alright, let's do this, as if she were deciding to try a new flavor of ice cream.

Rubina had her own complicated past. She had once been on the other side, working with people who weren't the good guys, but not because she was bad. She had her reasons, her grief, her story. And somewhere along the way, she had found her way to the right side. People can do that, you know. Change. Choose better. It's actually one of my favorite things about people.

At first, Pathaan and Rubina weren't sure what to think of each other. There was a lot of are you trustworthy and I'm watching you and hmm you seem capable but I'm going to pretend I'm not impressed. But when you go on adventures together, when you solve impossible problems side by side, when one person saves the other from a truly ridiculous situation involving an extremely confused group of Outfit members in what I can only describe as a chaotic snowball fight of a confrontation, well, you become friends. Real friends. The kind who would do anything for each other.

And they did do anything for each other. Over and over again.

The two of them traveled to find the pieces of Jim's terrible plan. They went to cold places and hot places and places where they really had no business being if you thought about it logically, but logic was taking a back seat on this trip. They discovered that the biological weapon had been split into separate components, hidden in different parts of the world, because Jim had seen enough movies to know you don't keep all your terrible plans in one basket.

At every stop, they ran into the Outfit's enthusiastic but deeply incompetent agents. There was one memorable moment, and I really wish you could have seen it, where a whole squad of Outfit members had set up what they thought was a very clever trap, complete with a countdown and everything, very theatrical, very Jim, and Pathaan and Rubina just sort of walked around it while the Outfit members stared at their own gadgets in confusion going wait this isn't how it was supposed to go. Then Rubina did something very clever with a door, Pathaan said something very witty about their trap, and they were gone before the Outfit could figure out what had happened.

It happened like that a lot.

But Jim, for all his drama and flair, wasn't a complete fool. He was dangerous in the way that very passionate, very hurt, very wrong people can be dangerous. He believed in what he was doing. He thought he had been abandoned, thrown away by the very country he had once served, and that pain had curdled inside him into something dark and bitter. He wanted India to feel what he felt. Lost. Afraid.

This is where the story gets a little sad, just for a moment, and I want you to know it's okay to feel a little sad right here because it means you're paying attention.

Pathaan understood Jim's pain. He didn't agree with what Jim was doing, not even a little, not one single bit, but he understood the feeling of being cast aside. Of giving everything and feeling like it wasn't enough. Of drifting, untethered, with that flame inside getting smaller and smaller. Pathaan had felt all of that. The difference was that Pathaan's love for India, for the people in it, for the millions of ordinary wonderful sleeping dreaming laughing crying living people who had nothing to do with whoever had wronged Jim, was bigger than his hurt. Pathaan couldn't look at those people and say, well I'm sad so none of this matters.

Jim could. And that was the difference between them.

The final showdown, and oh it was quite something, happened when Jim finally had all the pieces of his weapon and was ready to launch his plan. He was in a very remote location, very dramatic, very him, with all his Outfit followers around him looking both menacing and slightly confused as usual.

And Pathaan came.

He came because India needed him. He came because Rubina was already there, having figured out Jim's location first with her extraordinary brain and having gotten herself into a spot of trouble as a result. He came because that flame in his chest was roaring now, warm and bright and absolutely refusing to go out.

The confrontation was not a quiet one. There was a lot of running and extremely creative use of various objects that were definitely not meant to be used the way Pathaan used them. There was a go-kart involved at one point, I will say that much. The Outfit members kept getting in each other's way in a sort of magnificent domino effect of incompetence. One of them tripped over another one's very dramatic cape, and they both went sliding into a third one, and honestly it was almost impressive how thoroughly they managed to undo their own plans without any help at all.

Jim and Pathaan faced each other at last.

And Pathaan said something very simple. He said, the people of India never hurt you. They don't even know your name. They're just people. They're just living their lives, going to school, making dinner, tucking their children in at night. You don't get to hurt them for something that has nothing to do with them.

Jim, in his heart, in the very deep part of him that his anger hadn't quite managed to reach, heard that. He heard it in a way that moved something in him. He had been so focused on the people who had wronged him that he had stopped seeing everyone else. Stopped seeing that the world was full of people who were just trying to get by.

He didn't give a big speech about it. Jim was not capable of doing anything without a big speech, so actually he did give a speech, but it was a slightly different kind of speech, a smaller one, a tired one. And in the end, the weapon was destroyed. Safely. Cleverly. With help from Rubina who had, of course, already figured out the technical aspects of dismantling it while everyone else was busy with the confrontation.

The Outfit scattered like startled pigeons, bumping into each other on the way out, several of them running in completely the wrong direction, at least two of them ending up accidentally locked in a supply closet for reasons that remain unclear.

And it was over.

India was safe.

Pathaan stood in the quiet aftermath and breathed. Just breathed. The flame in his chest was warm and steady and full.

Nandini called him. Are you alright, she asked. He said yes. She said, good, because we have another mission. He laughed. An actual real laugh, the kind that comes from deep down where the real feelings live.

Rubina was there beside him, and she rolled her eyes at the phone call but she was smiling too. Two friends at the end of a very long, very ridiculous, very important adventure, standing together in the quiet.

Pathaan was home. Not in a place, not at an address, but in himself. In his purpose. In that warm certain knowledge that he was exactly where he was supposed to be, doing exactly what he was made for.

And India slept safely that night. All those millions of people, going about their ordinary wonderful lives. Tucking their children in. Telling them stories. Pulling blankets up over cold feet, yes both feet, don't leave that one out.

Safe and warm and never knowing how close things had come, or who had stood between them and danger without asking for a single thank you.

That, my loves, is what a real hero looks like. Not loud. Not looking for applause. Just steady. Just full of love. Just keeping that little flame burning no matter how windy it gets.

Alright now. Story's done. Eyes are getting heavy, I can tell. Let your thoughts go all soft and slow. Imagine you're somewhere warm and safe, because you are. You absolutely are. Let your breathing get quiet and easy. The world is good tonight. The heroes are out there doing what they do.

And you, my darlings, can rest.

Goodnight.

jawan.6-8:
Alright, snuggle up little ones, pull those blankets up nice and cozy, and let me tell you a really really good story tonight. This one has a hero who is SO clever, a team of the most amazing friends you've ever heard of, and a super silly bad guy who just cannot seem to get anything right. Ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, there was a man named Vikram. Now Vikram was not just any ordinary man. He was tall, he was brave, and he had the most magnificent hair you have ever seen in your whole entire life. Can you imagine? Just absolutely wonderful hair. But more importantly, Vikram had the biggest heart of anyone in the whole kingdom, and he truly truly cared about people who needed help.

Vikram worked at a very special place called a jail. But this was not a sad jail, oh no no no. Vikram made sure it was actually quite a nice place, because he believed that people deserved kindness and second chances. He had all sorts of people there, and he treated everyone with respect and warmth. He was basically the coolest person in the whole building, and everyone knew it.

Now here is where the story gets really interesting, so listen close!

Vikram had a plan. A big, clever, sneaky, absolutely brilliant plan. You see, there was a very bad man in the story named Kalee. Now Kalee was one of those villains who thought he was SO smart and SO powerful, but honestly? He was mostly just very full of himself and a little bit ridiculous. He wore very fancy suits and he walked around like a peacock who just discovered a mirror. He would snap his fingers and expect everyone to jump, and when things went wrong, which they very often did, he would stamp his foot and make the most hilarious pouty face. His helpers were not much better either. They bumped into each other, they tripped over their own feet, and one time one of them accidentally sat on an important pile of papers and couldn't find them for a whole week. It was quite something.

Kalee had been doing something very unfair for a long time. He was taking money that was supposed to help farmers and doctors and regular people, and he was stuffing it all into his own pockets. Terrible, right? The farmers could not grow enough food. The doctors did not have enough medicine. And Kalee just kept buying more and more fancy suits. Can you believe that?

Well Vikram had had ENOUGH of all that nonsense.

So here is what he did. Vikram came up with the most wonderfully clever disguise plan. He dressed up in different costumes and went out into the world to fix things and help people. One day he might look like a train conductor, the next day a delivery man, and one time he even dressed up as someone selling balloons at a fair, which honestly sounds like a lot of fun. Nobody knew it was the same person doing all these good things. He was like a superhero with a disguise kit instead of a cape!

And Vikram did not do any of this alone. Oh no no no. He had the most amazing team of friends helping him. These friends were all people who had been through hard times but were incredibly brave and incredibly smart. There was a woman who was so clever she could figure out any puzzle you put in front of her. There was another friend who could run faster than almost anyone. There was someone who was brilliant with computers and could type so fast that their fingers were practically a blur. And they all worked together like the best team you could ever imagine, like puzzle pieces that fit together perfectly.

Now Vikram also found out something very important during all of this. Something about his own family, something that had been a mystery for a long long time. It turned out that someone he loved very much had been a hero too, long before Vikram was doing any of this. This made Vikram feel so many feelings all at once, like when you are happy and a little sad and very proud all mixed together into one big feeling soup. Have you ever felt feeling soup? It is quite intense.

There was also a very dedicated police officer named Narmada who was trying to figure out who this mysterious disguised helper was. She was sharp as a tack, this Narmada. She kept finding little clues and following them and getting closer and closer to the truth. She was not a bad person at all, she just wanted to understand what was happening. And guess what? Eventually she and Vikram became the most wonderful allies, because they realized they both wanted exactly the same thing. They both wanted fairness. They both wanted the people with no voice to finally be heard. When you meet someone who wants the same good things as you, that is a very special kind of friendship indeed.

Now, the big moment. The part of the story where everything comes together.

Vikram and his brilliant team decided it was finally time to make sure Kalee could not keep doing his unfair things anymore. But how do you stop a silly pouty villain in a fancy suit? You do not chase him around or get into any trouble. You use your brain! Vikram and his friends gathered up all the proof of everything Kalee had been doing wrong. All the secret papers, all the hidden information, all the things Kalee had hoped nobody would ever find. They put it all together like the world's most important school project.

And then, in the cleverest move of all, they made sure everyone found out the truth. The whole country heard what Kalee had really been up to. Farmers heard it. Doctors heard it. Teachers and shopkeepers and grandmas and grandpas and everyone heard it. And you know what happened to Kalee when the truth came out? He started sweating through his fancy suit. His hair went all floppy. He kept trying to explain himself but every single excuse that came out of his mouth was more silly than the last one. His helpers bumped into each other trying to run away and ended up in a big confused pile, which was honestly a little bit funny even if they had been behaving badly.

Kalee tried one last time to act very big and very important, he puffed out his chest and tried to look frightening, but with everyone watching and everyone knowing the truth, he just looked like what he really was. A very small person in a very expensive suit who had forgotten that real power does not come from money or fancy things. Real power comes from having people who trust you and believe in you. And nobody trusted Kalee anymore. Not one single person.

He was led away, still muttering about his suits and how unfair everything was, and honestly it was a bit hard not to giggle just a little.

And with Kalee out of the way, something wonderful began to happen. The money that was supposed to help farmers? It actually went to farmers. The medicine that was supposed to reach hospitals? It actually got there. Little by little, things started to get better for all the people who had been struggling for so long. And that, my little sleepyheads, is what Vikram had been working toward the whole entire time. Not for glory, not for people to cheer his name, but just for things to be a little bit fairer and a little bit kinder for everyone.

Vikram and his team sat together after it was all done, tired and happy, like how you feel after a really really good day at the park. The kind of tired where your whole body is relaxed and warm and you just want to close your eyes and smile. His friends laughed and talked and reminded each other of all the funny things that had happened along the way, like that one time someone's disguise hat blew off at exactly the wrong moment, or the time Kalee's helper accidentally delivered the wrong box to the wrong place and looked completely baffled about it for twenty whole minutes.

And Vikram, brave wonderful Vikram with his magnificent hair and his enormous heart, felt something settle quietly inside him. He thought about the person in his family who had been a hero before him. He thought about how love can travel through time, how the bravery of someone who came before you can light a little lantern in your own heart. He felt connected to something bigger than himself, and it made him feel peaceful and full of warmth.

The moon was out now, big and round and silvery, peeking through the windows of all the homes where good people were sleeping soundly, finally a little safer than they had been before.

And far away, in the cozy places where children were tucked into their beds with their blankets pulled up to their chins, the night was quiet and soft and perfect.

Just like right now.

Just like where you are, all snuggly and warm.

You know, the best heroes are always the ones who help people just because it is right. Not for trophies or applause, but just because someone needed help and they could give it. Maybe you can be a little hero like that too, in your own small wonderful ways, every single day.

But that is a thought for tomorrow.

For right now, let your eyes get heavy. Let your breathing get slow. Let all the little thoughts floating around in your head drift away like bubbles.

Goodnight, little ones. Sleep tight. Dream of clever plans and wonderful friends and moonlight and kindness.

Everything is okay. Everything is warm. 

Off to sleep now.
jawan.3-5:

He walked and talked and moved in a completely different way. It was like the best game of pretend you have ever seen. He was playing a character. A new person. Now here is where the story gets really exciting, little one. Stay with me. Don't fall asleep just yet.

A world that was kinder. A world that was fairer. A world where nobody was left behind.

And then came the big day. The day everything came together.

Vikram and his six wonderful friends and his new friend Narmada all worked together. They told everyone the truth about Kalee. They showed people his naughty, greedy ways. And you know what happened to Kalee? He started sweating through his very shiny suit. He started fumbling and bumbling and tripping over his own feet. All his fancy plans fell apart like a tower of blocks when the cat walks through it. Crash! Clatter! Boom! Down it all came.

And the people, all the ordinary wonderful people, they stood up. Farmers and teachers and doctors and bus drivers and shopkeepers. They all raised their voices together. And when everyone raises their voice together for something good and true, even the silliest, greediest person in the shiniest suit cannot ignore it. Kalee had nowhere to hide. And that was that.

But here is my favourite part of the story. The part I really want you to remember as you drift off to sleep tonight.

Vikram, you see, was not just a clever hero. He was a person who had been hurt before. A long time ago. He carried sadness in his heart the way you sometimes carry a heavy backpack. But through all of this adventure, through all this helping and planning and pretending, he found something. He found that love is very, very strong. The love of his friends. The love of doing the right thing. The love of his family, which kept him going even on the hardest days.

And at the very end, Vikram stood in the sunshine. Not hiding anymore. Not pretending. Just himself. Vikram. With his big heart and his good people all around him. And he smiled the most tired, happy, wonderful smile.

The farmers could breathe again. The sick people got their medicine. Kalee sat in a corner looking very sorry and very much like someone who had learned a very important lesson about being kind.

And everyone, all of them, sat down together for a big, warm meal.

See little one, the world has its silly Kalees sometimes. People who forget to share. People who forget to care. But the world also has its Vikrams. And its Narmadas. And its six wonderful brave friends. And someday, when you are big and tall, you will be one of those good people too. I just know it.

Now the stars are out. The moon is watching over you. Your blanket is warm. Your pillow is soft. And you are safe, and you are loved, so so loved.

Close your eyes now.

Sleep tight, my little one.
