Alright, alright, scootch over and make some room, pull that blanket up to your chin, and let me tell you about one of the most remarkable, most daring, most absolutely bonkers adventures I have ever had the pleasure of telling you about. This one has disguises, secret identities, a hero with a heart so big it barely fits in his chest, and a villain so silly you'll want to laugh out loud — but you can't, because it's bedtime, so you'll have to save that for morning, okay? Okay. Good.

Now, are you ready? Here we go.

Once upon a time, not in some faraway kingdom with dragons and castles, but right here in our beautiful, noisy, colourful India, there lived a man named Azad.

Azad was not your ordinary fellow. He had the kind of face that could look like absolutely anyone — cheerful, serious, old, young, a street vendor, a professor, a grandpa selling chai. He was a master of disguise, you see. And he used this spectacular talent not to play pranks at school, though honestly that would have been tempting, but to do something far more important. He used it to help people who had nobody else to help them.

But here's the really interesting bit — Azad didn't work alone.

He worked with a team. And not just any team. His team was made up of the most unexpected group of heroes you could ever imagine. Six women who had all, at some point in their lives, been treated unfairly by the world. Six women who had been told they were too small, too quiet, too powerless to make a difference. And together, with Azad, they had decided to prove every single one of those wrong people absolutely, completely, spectacularly wrong.

They called themselves a special squad, and they operated in secret, like the most exciting underground club you've never heard of — because if you had heard of it, it wouldn't be much of a secret, now would it?

Now, Azad — our wonderful, clever, disguise-wearing hero — had a story. And like all the best stories, it began a long time ago, with his mother.

Her name was Narmada, and she was the kind of woman who made everyone around her feel like the sun had come out on a cloudy day. She was a doctor. A real, dedicated, brilliant doctor who worked in the places where nobody else wanted to work — dusty villages, forgotten corners of the country where people were sick and had no money and no help. She fixed people up not because she was getting rich doing it, because she absolutely was not, but because she believed with every single cell in her body that every person deserved to be taken care of.

Azad had grown up watching his mother do this, and it had carved itself into his heart like writing in stone. He had decided that he too would spend his life fighting for people who couldn't fight for themselves.

But here's where things get complicated, as they always do in the best stories.

There was a man. A very, very rich man. His name was Kalee — and honestly, you could not have picked a more perfectly suited name for someone so spectacularly unpleasant. Kalee had so much money that he had genuinely lost count of it, which sounds like a nice problem to have until you realise that having too much money and too little conscience is actually a terrible, terrible combination.

Kalee had gotten his enormous fortune by selling medicines. Now, medicines sound very helpful, don't they? And they can be! But Kalee was not selling good medicines. He was selling medicines that didn't work properly to hospitals and the government — charging mountains of gold coins for them while the medicines themselves were as useful as a chocolate teapot. And when people in hospitals didn't get better because the medicines were bad, Kalee just shrugged his very expensive shoulders and counted his money and ordered another fancy dinner.

He was, in short, a complete and utter rascal.

And he had friends — or rather, he had people he paid to be his friends, which is a very different and much sadder thing. These friends were politicians and businessmen who helped keep his sneaky little operation running. They wore very nice suits and had very important titles and were, to put it politely, absolutely useless at being decent human beings.

Chief among Kalee's bumbling band of overpaid helpers was his assistant, a man called Dhruv, who had the personality of a soggy biscuit and the self-awareness of a houseplant. Dhruv carried a very important-looking folder everywhere he went. Nobody, including Dhruv, was entirely sure what was in it. But it made him feel significant, so there it was.

Now, Azad had known about Kalee for a long time. And he was determined — absolutely, unshakeably determined — to stop him.

But Azad also had a secret.

A very big one.

You see, Azad's mother, the wonderful doctor Narmada, had once tried to stop Kalee herself, years ago. She had gathered all the evidence, all the proof of his rotten medicine scheme, and she had tried to make sure the right people found out about it. But Kalee, being a man with entirely too much money and entirely too little shame, had used that money to make her voice go very, very quiet.

And Azad, who had been only a boy when this happened, had never, ever forgotten.

So he grew up. And he trained. And he became this extraordinary, shape-shifting, never-give-up sort of person who dedicated his entire life to making things right — not just for his mother, but for every family that had suffered because of people like Kalee.

Now, here's where the story really gets going, because one day, Azad and his squad decided it was time for their biggest plan yet.

It was so ambitious, so elaborate, so wonderfully complicated that even explaining it takes a bit of doing, so pay attention, because this is the good part.

Azad disguised himself — and I mean fully, impressively, even-his-own-grandmother-wouldn't-recognise-him disguised himself — as the chief of a very important prison. Yes, a prison! He walked in there with his fake moustache and his very official-looking uniform and his extremely convincing serious face, and absolutely everyone believed he was exactly who he said he was.

From inside this prison, he and his team began their operation. They started quietly, carefully, like people pulling a very long thread that was attached to a very big sweater, knowing that eventually the whole thing would unravel.

They found prisoners who had been locked up unfairly — people who had gotten in trouble not because they were bad, but because powerful people like Kalee had pointed fingers at them when things went wrong, because powerful people never, ever want to take the blame themselves. And Azad helped them. He listened to their stories and made sure those stories got out into the world where people could hear them.

He also did something rather genius: he started collecting evidence. Real, solid, can't-argue-with-this evidence about all of Kalee's dodgy dealings. Every fake medicine, every bribed official, every rotten decision that had hurt ordinary people — Azad and his team collected proof of all of it, piece by piece, like the world's most important jigsaw puzzle.

Meanwhile, Kalee was having a perfectly dreadful time, and it was entirely his own fault, which made it considerably less sympathetic.

He started noticing that things were going wrong for him. Shipments of his terrible medicines were being mysteriously redirected. His very important friends in very important places were suddenly getting nervous phone calls from investigators. His assistant Dhruv kept running in and out of rooms looking flustered, his ever-present folder now bulging with panicked notes and incomprehensible scribbles.

"What do you MEAN someone is asking questions?" Kalee would bark, and Dhruv would blink at him over the folder and say something deeply unhelpful like, "Yes sir, that is precisely the situation, sir," before shuffling out again.

Kalee began to suspect someone was behind all this chaos. He hired detectives. He hired detectives to watch the detectives. He became so suspicious of everyone around him that he started wearing his very expensive hat pulled down low over his face everywhere he went, which made him look less like a powerful villain and more like a mushroom in a good suit.

But he couldn't figure out who Azad was, because Azad kept changing. One day he was a delivery person. The next day he was an elderly school teacher. The day after that he was somehow a famous classical musician, and nobody could explain how. He was extraordinarily good at this.

And all the while, the wonderful squad of six women was working tirelessly. One was gathering documents. One was getting information out to journalists. One was making sure that the families of people who had been hurt by Kalee's bad medicines knew that someone was finally, finally fighting for them. They were brilliant and brave and they looked out for each other always, teasing one another in the way that only people who deeply love each other can, and celebrating even the small victories with enormous enthusiasm and sometimes cake.

Now, the moment that everything came to a head was extraordinary.

Kalee, having completely lost his cool in the most dramatic fashion possible, decided to confront whoever was behind it all publicly. He made a big, blustery speech in front of a room full of cameras and reporters, wagging his finger and puffing up his chest, insisting that everything he had ever done was perfectly legal and above board and anyone who said otherwise was a liar.

And that, dear listener, was exactly the moment Azad had been waiting for.

Because Azad stood up. Right there, in that very room, in front of all those cameras and all those reporters. And he wasn't in disguise this time. He was just himself — steady and calm and looking directly at Kalee with the kind of expression that says, very quietly, that this is over.

And then the evidence came out. All of it. Every single piece, presented clearly and carefully, in a way that even Dhruv with his extremely full folder could not have wriggled out of explaining. The fake medicines. The bribes. The families who had suffered. The years and years of ordinary people being let down by someone who was supposed to be providing something as important as medicine.

The room went very, very quiet.

And then it went very, very loud.

Kalee looked around desperately for help, but his very important friends in their very nice suits were all suddenly extremely busy studying their shoes. Dhruv quietly put down his folder for perhaps the first time in years and just sort of stood there, looking like a man who had finally understood that he had been on entirely the wrong team.

The authorities, who had been handed everything they needed to act, finally did their jobs. Kalee was taken away, spluttering and complaining about his hat getting squashed, which really did seem to be his primary concern given the circumstances.

The squad erupted.

You know that feeling when something you've worked incredibly hard for finally, finally works? When all the late nights and the scary moments and the times when you weren't sure if it was going to be okay turn out to have been worth it? That feeling bubbled up and overflowed in that room, and there was hugging, and cheering, and someone definitely cried a little, and someone else pretended they weren't crying while absolutely crying, and it was wonderful and messy and completely perfect.

Azad stood quietly in the middle of all of it, and he thought about his mother.

He thought about her voice, the one that had been silenced for so long. And he felt, for the first time in a very long time, that it had been heard. That all the people like her — the doctors and the teachers and the ordinary families who had just wanted someone to help them — they had been heard too.

Later, when things had calmed down and the cameras had gone home and the dust had settled, Azad went to see his mother.

And Narmada, who had never stopped believing in doing what was right even when it was hard, looked at her son and said nothing for a moment. She just held his face in her hands the way parents do when words aren't quite enough.

"I told you," she said finally. "I told you one person can make things right."

"You told me a lot of things," Azad said.

"And were any of them wrong?"

He thought about it seriously. He really did.

"No," he admitted. "Not a single one."

And she laughed, and he laughed, and the squad was there too, all crowded into that small room that suddenly felt enormous because it was so full of warmth.

They shared a meal together that evening, all of them. It was noisy and chaotic and somebody knocked over a glass of water and blamed it on somebody else and there was a good-natured argument about who made the better chai that went on for quite some time without any resolution, and it was, in every possible way, exactly how the best evenings end.

Now then.

That's the story of Azad and his wonderful, courageous, slightly ridiculous, deeply loving team who took on a very silly, very greedy villain and beat him — not with anything frightening, but with truth and cleverness and the unshakeable belief that ordinary people deserve to be protected.

And the lesson, if you want one — and I think tonight you do — is this. You don't have to be big or loud or powerful to do what's right. You just have to care enough to keep going. You have to find your people, the ones who'll work alongside you and eat dinner with you and knock over glasses of water with you. And you have to remember that the truth, told clearly and bravely, is more powerful than all the fancy suits and full folders in the world.

Now.

It is very late.

Your eyes are heavy, aren't they. Yes they are. I can tell.

Pull that blanket a little higher. There you go. Just like that.

Dream about something good tonight — maybe about the moment when everything you worked hard for finally works out. That feeling is out there waiting for you, real as anything.

Goodnight, my love.

Sleep tight.
